20812-history-of-the-english-people-volu:
Richard the Second gave up his crown in September 1399, and Parliament took that act as law. John Richard Green opens volume three of his History of the English People at that fall. A solemn act of deposition sealed the change of kings.

Green wrote English history as the story of the people, not just of courts. Trade, towns, faith, and law share space with kings and wars. Volume three runs from Parliament's rise through years of deep change. His fresh approach shaped how schools taught the past, and this volume shows his sweep at its most confident.
22808-the-gray-madam-1899:
The Gray Madam is a mystery story dated 1899, named for a gray-clad woman whose appearance at a door leaves nothing behind it. The catalog record names no author. Ghost or spy, the gray madam of the title belongs to the 1890s taste for uncanny visitors in respectable houses.

Shaken by the contact, the narrator tore the front door open and looked out. She expected to find the woman waiting on the steps, or standing on the sidewalk out front. But no one matching her was anywhere visible. I came back inside wondering if I was a hallucination's victim, or just an everyday fool. That doubt, hallucination or folly, powers the tale. The story keeps one foot in the ghost story and one in the detective's notebook.
allen-keynotes-leading-remedies-1899:
Henry C. Allen taught prescribers to seize the one strange, clear sign in a case, and Key-Notes and Characteristics of 1899 is his handbook. The second edition gathers leading remedies of the materia medica, each summed up by its keynote symptoms. Allen compares rivals side by side throughout.

A keynote might be a craving, a fear, or the odd hour when pain strikes. Match that sign, Allen held, and the remedy often follows at once. Few homeopathic books were reprinted so often in the next century, which shows how well his sharp, short method suited daily practice.
arrhenius-dissociation-modern-theory-sol:
Harry C. Jones translated and edited The Modern Theory of Solution for Harper's Scientific Memoirs in 1899. The volume gathers the founding papers of the new physical chemistry in English. Wilhelm Pfeffer's work on osmotic pressure opens the set. Jacobus van't Hoff follows with his own study of osmotic pressure in solutions.

Svante Arrhenius contributes his paper on the dissociation of substances dissolved in water. In it, salts in water split into charged ions, a bold claim for its day. Francois Raoult's laws on solutions close the group. Together the memoirs launch the ionic theory. English readers gained the sources in one volume.
arxiv-2512-00799:
Taha Anwar wrote a 2025 teaching review on the roots of the Standard Model of particle physics. That model rests on local gauge symmetry, the idea that physics stays the same when certain internal labels are twisted from place to place. It is one of the great achievements of modern science.

Yet its main equation, the Lagrangian, is usually taught to students who already have deep training. Anwar builds a gentler bridge aimed at advanced undergraduates. The path runs through quantum electrodynamics, the theory of light and electrons, as the worked example. A clearer on-ramp could bring more students into modern particle theory.
arxiv-2512-00899:
Raka Dabhade, Jebraan Mudholkar, Siddhesh Durgude, and Arpit Kottur propose a first filter for promising planets in a 2025 paper. The hunt for habitable exoplanets, worlds around other stars, is a central goal of modern astrophysics. Missions like Kepler and TESS have found vast numbers of candidates.

No team can study every candidate in depth. Follow-up time on big telescopes is scarce, so targets must be ranked. The authors offer a first-order filter, a quick screen that flags the most promising candidates for detailed characterization. A good early screen keeps rare, Earth-like worlds from being lost in the pile.
arxiv-2512-01099:
Daria Smirnova, Hamid Nasiri, Marta Adamska, Zhengxin Yu, and Peter Garraghan study the energy cost of choosing models in a 2025 paper. Modern AI systems can call many tools and models to do complex tasks. Large language models often orchestrate those choices, deciding which model handles each step, based on written descriptions of what each model does.

That qualitative approach ignores energy use, which varies widely between models. The authors propose energy-aware, data-driven model selection inside LLM-orchestrated systems. Picking models by measured performance and energy, not just description, could cut the power bill of compound AI systems substantially.
arxiv-2512-01399:
Martin Thummler and co-authors model bright light made by quantum dots under strong fields. When a strong laser hits a dot, it can emit light at many times the laser tone. That effect is called high-order harmonic generation. Tests show it fades for small dots at long laser tones.

No model could yet match that fade for tiny dots. The team built one based on a real-space tight-binding view. Their model tracks electrons on a grid of sites in the dot. It aims to match the size trend seen in tests. A sound model guides new light sources based on dots.
arxiv-2512-01499:
Over a decade past its discovery, the Higgs boson still anchors particle physics. Its links to heavy particles and gauge bosons are now well gauged. Much else is not. The shape of its self-interaction is still weakly known. Its links to light fermions are also loose.

An overview lays out Higgs theory in the Standard Model and in its effective extension. That extension adds new terms that new physics could fill. The review maps what is known and what is open. It gives scope teams a shared base for the next round of Higgs tests at colliders.
arxiv-2512-01699:
Fadhila Chehami and co-authors report self-organized freeform waveguiding inspired by nature. Butterfly wings gain iridescent hues from complex photonic forms. Those forms grow from local rules, with no central plan. They still yield advanced optical traits like band gaps.

The team shows waveguides that form by like self-organization. No in-situ tuning or top-down design is used. Local rules alone set the final path for light. Self-formed guides could cut fabrication cost for photonic chips and sensors. Freeform guides bend in curves set by growth rules, which suits implants and wearable optics where straight channels waste precious space.
arxiv-2512-02299:
Asked a health question, a language model may get several documents that disagree, and which one it trusts decides whether its answer helps or harms. Boya Zhang and four co-authors build HealthContradict in 2025, an expert-verified dataset for testing how models reason over long, conflicting biomedical material.

Each of its nine hundred twenty cases pairs a health question with a factual answer backed by scientific evidence, plus documents in conflict. The study asks how models use context and how contradictions bend their responses. As medical chatbots spread, measuring their behavior under conflicting evidence is a basic safety exercise.
arxiv-2512-02999:
Dhimiter Canko and Mattia Pozzoli compute a full set of three loop Feynman integrals for collider physics. Producing two vector bosons at hadron colliders is a key process at the Large Hadron Collider. Precision predictions for it need next to next to next to leading order corrections in quantum chromodynamics.

The authors compute all planar three loop master integrals for the leading color part of those corrections. The integrals fall into nine four point families with massless internal lines and two massive external legs. Such integrals are reusable bricks for many precision predictions at current and future colliders. Bricks of this sort get used for years. Each new rate that needs them can stack on the set in place and skip months of fresh work.
arxiv-2512-03099:
Graph neural networks can sort and predict, but they rarely explain why. Haribandhu Jena, Jyotirmaya Shivottam, and Subhankar Mishra tackle that gap in this 2025 work. These networks are now used in drug research, social network study, and recommendation tools.

One fair way to explain a result is the Shapley value, which scores each part's share. But exact scores need a huge number of checks, far too many for real graphs. The authors use quantum methods to speed that task, in a tool called QGShap. Fast, faithful reasons could help experts trust network outputs. For practitioners, faster Shapley scores could bring explanations to graphs with millions of links.
arxiv-2512-03199:
Face recognition works worse on tilted or blocked faces. Justin Norman and Hany Farid test a fix in this 2025 work. Real-world photos often have poor quality, non-frontal poses, and objects hiding part of the face.

The authors ask whether AI-driven pose correction and image restoration lift accuracy. Their study checks if straightening a head pose helps the model name the person. The answer matters for security and photo tools that rely on faces. It also warns where such fixes might fail or mislead. The study also shows the risk that restored faces might fool systems in harmful ways.
arxiv-2512-03299:
Some curves hide groups that are hard to compute. Justin Chen, Heidi Goodson, Rezwan Hoque, and Sabeeha Malikah study one family in this 2025 work. They look at hyperelliptic curves given by a simple prime-power equation.

A variety is called degenerate when its Hodge ring is not built from divisor classes. Degeneracy makes Sato-Tate groups, which describe statistical patterns of the curve, hard to find. Few examples and techniques exist in the literature. The authors add both, aiding number theory and cryptography research. New examples of degenerate curves help map where Sato-Tate computations break down.
arxiv-2512-03399:
Aligning one AI system is not enough for good outcomes. Joe Edelman and a large team argue for full-stack alignment in this 2025 work. Even a system perfectly aligned to its operator can cause harm if the operator's goals clash with others.

Institutions, not just models, need alignment with shared values. The authors use thick models of value, rich accounts of what people hold dear. Co-aligning AI and institutions could prevent perverse outcomes at scale. The work speaks to policy makers as much as to model builders. Thick value models resist thin metrics that miss what communities actually care about.
arxiv-2601-07299:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by Zhengdao Li and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers Cauchy-Gaussian overbound for heavy-tailed GNSS measurement errors. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. Overbounds of heavy-tailed measurement errors are essential to meet stringent navigation requirements in integrity monitoring applications. The work proposes to leverage the bounding sharpness of the Cauchy distribution in.

The core and the Gaussian distribution in the tails to tightly bound heavy-tailed GNSS measurement errors. The authors develop a procedure to determine the overbounding parameters for both symmetric unimodal (s.u. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07599:
Lior Dvir, Nadav Torem, and Yoav Y. Schechner work out the statistics of a sensor that counts single photons. A SPAD, or single photon avalanche diode, records the timing of detection events. Given a fixed photon flux, those timings follow a pattern the authors derive. The raw signal relates to the flux in a nonlinear way, and it is naturally random.

From the likelihood of the raw signal, the team derives a score function for it. Likelihood and score functions are basic tools for estimating light levels from noisy data. SPADs power depth cameras, lidar, and low-light imaging. Exact statistics help engineers squeeze better estimates from each photon. The paper gives imaging scientists a firmer base for working with these sensors.
arxiv-2601-07899:
Valery Asiryan and Randall L. Rathbun compute evidence against a hoped-for factorization in the cuboid problem. The perfect cuboid is a famous unsolved geometry puzzle about boxes with integer edges and diagonals. Sharipov's second cuboid polynomial is a degree ten polynomial in two coprime integer parameters. Written as a quintic in the squared variable, it gives an associated monic quintic polynomial. Their 2026 preprint reports computational evidence on that quintic.

A quadratic-cubic factorization would split the quintic into simpler pieces and open an attack route. Evidence against it closes that route for the cases computed. Negative results matter in long-unsolved problems because they redirect effort. Computer searches now play a real role in such eliminations. The paper serves number theorists and cuboid problem specialists. It narrows where a solution can hide.
arxiv-2601-07999:
Tiantian Feng and coauthors sort cases of cognitive impairment from speech, with care for dialect. VoxCog joins speech foundation models that make a point of knowing speech dialects. People with Alzheimer's disease or mild cognitive impairment often speak in ways that tests can pick up. Changes include slower speech and sounds drawn out for longer. Those changes look much like dialect based shifts in sound, the authors note. Their 2026 preprint gives an end to end approach for more than one language.

Care for dialect guards against a real flaw: to take dialect for disease. A sorter blind to dialect can flag sound speakers in an unfair way. Multilingual coverage widens the test beyond English speakers. Speech is cheap to collect, so a fair speech test could screen widely. The paper serves speech technology and dementia research communities. It treats dialect knowledge as a feature for fairness, not noise.
arxiv-2601-08199: R. Hu, J. Li, S. Fan, and F. Xu wrote a 2026 arXiv paper, printed in Physics Letters B, on three-nucleon forces for a new local two-nucleon potential set in position space. Three-nucleon forces shape the form of small cores and how dense core matter can get. The chiral form comes from chiral effective field theory and has served first-principles studies well. Hard tasks remain in how to set low-energy constants and how to apply cut-off rules called regulators.
arxiv-2601-08299: Mingzhe Li, Yang Kuang, and Zhicheng Hu solve the Gross-Pitaevskii equation with a multi-mesh adaptive method. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that wave functions in this equation vary sharply by region. Some components swing fast while others stay smooth. A single mesh, even adaptive, can cost too much because it must suit the roughest component. The authors give different components their own meshes instead. The equation models Bose-Einstein condensates, so cheaper solves help physicists scan wider parameter ranges.
arxiv-2601-08899:
Yunhua Ding checks how a break in key space rules would show up in tests that hunt for a faint spin shift in neutrons. Such tests look for an electric dipole moment, a tiny split in how a neutron acts in fields. A split could hint at new laws past the known set. Ding works in a frame that lets space rules bend in set ways.

He works out the first order shift in spin spin rate from such a bend. He does the same for tests that hold charged bits in a ring. The sums tell test teams which bend terms their gear can see, and how strong a bound a null result sets. A reader in core physics gets a map from odd lab shifts to deep rule breaks.
arxiv-2601-09399:
Thomas Abbott and a large CHIME team present the second catalog of fast radio bursts from the CHIME telescope. Their 2026 arXiv paper covers bursts caught between July 2018 and September 2023. Fast radio bursts are millisecond flashes of radio energy from far beyond our galaxy.

The catalog lists 4,539 bursts from 3,641 distinct sources. Among them are 981 bursts from 83 sources known to repeat. A sample this large lets astronomers study burst rates, energies, and environments with real statistics. It also sharpens the hunt for what makes some sources fire again and again while most stay silent after one flash.
arxiv-2601-09599:
Luigi Bellafronte, Sally Dawson, Clara Del Pio, Matthew Forslund, and Pier Paolo Giardino compute Higgs boson decays with high precision. Their 2026 arXiv paper works at next-to-leading order in the Standard Model Effective Field Theory. Precise decay rates are needed to pin down Higgs properties at the LHC and future colliders.

The authors compute all two- and three-body Higgs decays. Corrections are included from both QCD and electroweak effects, within the dimension-six effective theory. Deviations from the Standard Model would show up as small shifts in these rates. A complete set of predictions lets experiments read those shifts as constraints on new physics.
arxiv-2601-09899:
Richard Kerner surveys the astronomy of the Islamic golden age through European eyes. His 2026 arXiv paper began as an invited talk at the ICRANET-Isfahan astronomical meeting in November 2021. It draws on a chapter of his book Our Celestial Clockwork, published the same year.

The paper briefly sets out the mathematical and astronomical achievements of the Islamic world in its golden era. Those scholars preserved, criticized, and extended Greek astronomy for centuries. Their work later fed the European revival of the science. A European perspective on that debt is the paper's stated angle.
arxiv-2601-09999:
Chu-An Liu fixes a flaw in how forecasts are joined. A joined forecast blends many single views into one. Past work found big gains from such blends. But the errors of a blend can link from one time step to the next.

Liu shows that this link can be strong. He then gives a plain fix. Add a share of the last error to the next blend. That step can lift gains a lot. At times it beats the gain from the blend itself. The fix is cheap and needs no new data. It fits any blend that shows linked errors.
arxiv-2601-10099:
Priyanka Cingirikonda, Marina Kounkel, and Joseph Mullen use fast spin stars to find close pairs. A star that spins fast is most oft in a pair. The mate sits close, at a few AU or less. That range is hard to probe by most pair hunts.

So fast spinners flag pairs that would else be missed. The team uses them as tags of pair rates. They ask how pair rates shift with how dense the star field is. Dense fields may break or make pairs at a new rate. The work turns a spin trait into a census tool.
arxiv-2601-10599:
F. Pierucci and co-authors argue that AI safety must be framed at the level of institutions, not single models. Large language model systems now act as agents inside human social and technical systems. So alignment, the match between a system and human aims, cannot be a trait of one model alone. It depends on the settings where the agents act.

The team sets out a governance framework aimed at safety across whole distributions of agents and outcomes. It treats rules, oversight, and shared norms as part of the safety problem. The frame shifts debate from model traits to the systems that deploy them. Policy readers get a structured way to think about guarding advanced AI at scale.
arxiv-2601-10699:
Luciano Navarro-Coydán, J. Alberto Vázquez, Israel Quiros, and Ricardo García-Salcedo seek cosmic acceleration without a vacuum energy term. In f(R, L_m) gravity, the action mixes curvature with the matter Lagrangian in a nonlinear way. They study a class where matter terms carry powers that could drive late-time expansion on their own.

The authors follow scaling solutions that settle into a de Sitter phase, the steady exponential expansion our universe now shows. They also set bounds on the model's parameters. If matter-driven terms can do the job, the cosmological constant may not be needed. The paper tests that hope against the structure such a theory must have.
arxiv-2601-10799:
P. Datta and a large collaboration report the BigBite Calorimeter, an instrument built for Jefferson Lab. The calorimeter is made of lead glass and measures electron energies. It forms the electron arm of the BigBite Spectrometer. That spectrometer served the Super Bigbite program in Hall A, which measured neutron electromagnetic form factors with high precision.

The paper covers the design, construction, installation, and performance of the device. Form factors describe how charge and magnetism spread inside the neutron. Precise values test our picture of quarks inside matter. Instrument papers like this one are the record that lets later teams trust, reuse, and improve the hardware behind the physics.
arxiv-2601-11199:
Aiman Al Masoud, Marco Arazzi, and Antonino Nocera tackle a safety flaw in search-based AI. Their 2026 preprint builds a shield for retrieval-augmented generation. Such systems pair a language model with search over big text stores. The pair can write with facts pulled fresh from the store.

The risk sits in what the search hands to the model. Most designs send all found text straight into the prompt. That can leak private or locked facts to the model and then to users. It also opens a path for prompt injection attacks. The team's frame shares facts on a need-to-know basis. It aims to block leaks while the model still writes good text.
arxiv-2601-11399:
S. Ortiz-Gomez and six coauthors trace young compact groups of galaxies. Their 2026 preprint studies star-forming compact groups in detail. Compact groups pack a few galaxies into a tight space. They are a stage before galaxies fall into big clusters.

Pre-processing is the frame for the study. It says galaxies can quench star birth in small groups first. Only later do they fall into a cluster's hot core. The team checks physical and morphological traits in the groups. Morphology is the shape and structure of each galaxy. A star-forming sample shows groups before quenching bites. That snapshot can show how the group setting starts the change.
arxiv-2601-11499:
Dimitar Nedanovski, Svetoslav Nenov, and Dimitar Pilev time the first success in evolution. Their 2026 preprint studies Differential Evolution, a search heuristic. First-hitting times mark when a search first finds its target. The team frames them through conditional hazards.

Past analysis used Markov-chain kernels or drift arguments. The hazard frame skips both of those classic routes. Survival odds of a target set split into a product. Each factor is a conditional first-hit chance at one step. Hazard identities then give tail bounds for the wait. Those bounds tell how long success may take to arrive. Such results help set budgets for stochastic search runs.
arxiv-2601-11999:
A. Lefebvre-Lepot, M. A. Mehmood, C. Perrin, and E. Zatorska derive a one-dimensional flow model for grains with a rough coat. The grains are hard spheres that act through thin film forces when close. Each grain also has a thin rough layer that cuts how fluid can pass.

From that micro picture, they derive a macro model with roughness built in. Such models help predict how dense grain flows move in pipes and mixers. A derived model rests on firmer ground than a guessed one. It ties coat traits to bulk flow in a clear way.
arxiv-2601-12099:
Leonardo S. Goodall, Dor Shilton, Daniel Austin Mullins, and their co-authors test if large models can label ethnographic texts well. Such labels could speed cross-cultural work by pulling structured data from field texts. They tested seven top models on one shared task.

The task was to label 121 ritual traits in 567 text excerpts. Skill was limited in their tests. It fell well below the level needed for trusted auto labels. The result is a caution for teams that hope to swap human coders for models in this field.  The low scores held across all models in the test.
arxiv-2601-12199:
Muhammad Umar Farooq and Oscar Saz identify Arabic dialects in streaming speech with a method drawn from speech recognition. Their tool, CTC-DID, treats dialect tags as a label sequence for each utterance. That is the same trick CTC loss uses for words in ASR.

Dialect calls in a stream must be fast and firm as speech runs. A limited label set keeps the task lean. Good dialect tags help route speech to the right ASR and language tools. The work tests this CTC frame for that job.  A stream tool must keep pace with live speech input.
arxiv-2601-12499:
Meiru Zhang, Zaiqiao Meng, and Nigel Collier study why language models fail multi hop questions. Multi hop questions need facts from several spots, joined in a chain. Even with huge context windows, models still miss such questions a lot. A known cause is position bias: models overlook facts at certain spots in the text.

The key unknown is where the chain breaks. A model might fail to locate the needed evidence at all. Or it might find the evidence but fail to join it up. The team name these the recognition bottleneck and the synthesis side of failure. Their title states a weakest link law for these failures. Pinpointing the break tells builders what to fix first.
arxiv-2601-12599:
Michael Kinyon and Desmond MacHale give elementary proofs of two classic theorems about rings. A ring is commutative when the order of multiplication never matters. Jacobson theorem says a ring must be commutative if each element raised to some power returns itself. Herstein generalized that result with a weaker demand on the power gap.

In both theorems, the power may depend on the element in question. The original proofs of such results can be deep and hard. Elementary proofs matter because they open the results to more readers and courses. They can also reveal which steps truly carry the weight. Short, clean proofs of famous theorems are prized in algebra. This work adds two to that shelf.
arxiv-2601-12999:
Jia-Shu Niu, Ying Zhang, and Hui-Fang Xue report on BE Lyncis, a pair of objects in orbit around each other. They describe it as a highly stretched binary system. It hosts what they call the nearest known black hole to Earth.

The team used light data from the TESS space telescope. They also used a long set of peak light times that spans 39 years. From this they find that one member is a high swing Delta Scuti star. It pulses as it orbits. The orbit takes about 15.9 years and has a very high stretch. That mix makes the system a rare test case for star and black hole work.
arxiv-2601-13099:
Abdellah El Mekki and a large team built a data set for Arabic machine translation. Arabic splits hard by place. Most day to day talk uses local dialects, not the standard form taught in school and used in news. Yet most translation tools train on the standard form and cope poorly with dialect input.

Their set is called Alexandria. It is large, built by the speech groups, and turned by human hands. It spans many domains and many dialects. The goal is tools that serve the tens of millions who speak dialect first. For builders of language models, the set gives a fair test and train base that past sets lacked.
arxiv-2601-13299:
Ethan Seefried and co-authors built the first open large set of hard engineering diagrams with full marks. Such diagrams show parts, links, and sense marks in dense webs. A machine that can parse them could aid design, checks, and repair in many fields.

Their set is called Enginuity. It spans many domains of engineering, not one trade. Marks state part ranks, how parts join, and what marks mean. That depth is what past sets lacked. For vision and language teams, the set gives a train and test base for diagram sense. It may help turn static plans into data a tool can use.
arxiv-2601-13499:
Yang Liu, Zhejunyu Jin, Jie Liu, and Peng Yan drive skyrmions with current in frustrated altermagnets and find a twist on old lore. A skyrmion is a tiny swirl of magnetism that can move as one bit. It has two acts, its place and its helicity, the twist of its swirl.

Old lore held the twist locked to the Hall angle of the path. The team finds the twist is free of that lock. It turns one way at a rate set by the square of the current push. A free twist is a new knob for skyrmion tools. For magnet teams, a knob that turns with push squared is both a test mark and a design path.
arxiv-2601-13599:
Linrui Ma, Yufei Cui, Kai Han, and Yunhe Wang study how diffusion language models build text in 2026. In these models, text takes shape from noise, with each part able to see all the rest. That two-way view helps the whole piece hang together. Many fast designs split text into blocks and build block by block. That choice adds a left-to-right bias.

The team argues that the block style can break the broad sense of the whole. Their work, called Diffusion In Diffusion, tries to win that broad fit back. It keeps the speed gains of block-wise work where it can. The goal is text that stays true to its full theme from start to end.
arxiv-2601-13699:
S. O. Kara sets out a way to encode a class of particle theories for quantum simulation in 2026. The theories are leptophilic, meaning they act mainly on leptons like electrons. They extend the Standard Model with a new U(1) gauge force. The work targets near-term and future quantum devices.

Kara shows the lepton charge pattern maps well onto qubit registers. Gauge symmetries and anomaly cancellation rules are built into the quantum states themselves. A scalable code like this lets small quantum machines test new physics. It also shows how theory rules can guide quantum program design.
arxiv-2601-13799:
Luigi Romano, Ole Morten Aamo, Jan Åslund, and Erik Frisk extend a new kind of friction model in 2026. The frame is Friction with Bristle Dynamics, or FrBD. It blends analytic formulas for the friction coefficient with equations for bristle-like elements. Friction here can depend on rate and state, not just speed.

Their focus is linear viscoelastic rheology, how materials flow and spring back. Such models suit control tasks, where a firm grip model guides motion. Tire and road work needs friction laws that react in time. FrBD aims to give that with a clear structure.
arxiv-2601-14299:
Ambarish Gurjar and L Jean Camp study network defense data in this 2026 paper. Defenders face a steady stream of attacks, logged as raw alerts from intrusion detection systems. The sheer volume of alerts forces hard choices about what to handle first. Triage today rests mostly on high-level risk classes.

The authors widen how risk is measured. They look at alerts through their technical traits, as usual. They also sort alerts by their temporal patterns, how they unfold in time. Their title names the goal: predicting when tail risk, the rare worst cases, will escalate. The work aims to help defenders spot a bad surge before it peaks.
arxiv-2601-14399:
Lukas Heinrich and Tom Magorsch build a faster inference tool in this 2026 paper. Their target is the quark-gluon plasma, the hot matter made in heavy-ion collisions. Its transport coefficients describe how that matter flows and drags. The team estimates those values by simulating quarkonium suppression, the loss of bound quark pairs in the plasma.

The simulator solves a Lindblad equation for an open quantum system in a large Hilbert space. That makes each run costly, so parameter estimation is expensive. The authors make the Monte Carlo simulation differentiable, so gradients can guide the search. Gradient-based optimization then finds good parameter values with far fewer runs.
arxiv-2601-14799:
Qihua Liang and five co-authors build a multi-modal tracking system in this 2026 paper. Multi-modal object tracking integrates multiple complementary inputs, such as thermal, depth, and event data. It has attracted considerable attention for its strong performance. Current general-purpose multi-modal trackers mainly unify various modal tracking tasks through prompt learning. Those tasks include RGB-thermal, RGB-depth, and RGB-event tracking.

Such trackers still overlook the effective capture of spatio-temporal cues, how targets move through space and time. Their model, UBATrack, is a spatio-temporal state space model for general multi-modal tracking. Readers get a tracker designed to follow motion itself, across whichever sensors are available.
arxiv-2601-15099:
Ángel Vaca and Joan Gutiérrez-Florensa build a better gauge of frequency in power grids. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with instantaneous frequency, the local rate of the grid's wave at each moment. Grid operators watch it to keep the system stable.

The authors use the complex Teager-Kaiser energy operator, paired with a dynamic-signal identity. They derive a new formula for the local frequency. The formula spells out the envelope-curvature terms that older gauges hide. Making those terms explicit corrects a bias that affects the standard estimators long used in power systems.
arxiv-2601-15199:
Andrés Guzmán, Federico Malizia, and István Z. Kiss study how contagion spreads when contacts come in groups. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with hypergraphs, networks where one link can join many people at once. Group contacts can change spread dynamics a lot.

Standard analysis treats pairwise and group links as if they were independent. The authors drop that assumption. They study cross-order hyperdegree correlations, links between a node's pairwise degree and its group degree. The work shows how those ties reshape the way a contagion moves through a whole human population.
arxiv-2601-15799:
Sanghoon Lee, Tilen Čadež, and Kyoung-Min Kim study mobility edges in disordered systems in a 2026 arXiv paper. A mobility edge separates states that spread from states that stay localized. Such edges are common in one-dimensional quasiperiodic systems once exact self-duality breaks. Their origin is usually read one Hamiltonian at a time. Each system seems to set its own edge positions. The authors show that view is wrong.

Edge positions are structurally constrained across related Hamiltonians. The link comes from an isospectral duality between the systems. Isospectral means the systems share the same spectrum. A shared spectrum ties their edges together. The result turns isolated facts into a pattern. For theorists of localization, patterns across models are far more useful than case-by-case numbers.
arxiv-2601-15999:
Yongsheng Han, Raj Thilak Rajan, and Geert Leus recover hidden network structure from data in a 2026 arXiv paper. Graph topology identification is central in networked systems. Often the wiring is hidden while node data are available. The task is to infer the graph from the signals on it. Conventional solutions use probabilistic models or complex optimization. They often suffer from non-convexity, which traps solvers. Others need strong assumptions, like acyclicity or positivity.

The authors propose covariance matching, per the title. Matching the data's covariance to a graph model offers a different route. Covariance is estimable from observations alone. A cleaner formulation could avoid the traps of older methods. Many fields need hidden wiring: brain networks, power grids, and social systems among them.
arxiv-2601-17299:
Shyam S. Sharma and five co-authors study single radio pulses from the pulsar PSR B0329+54. Each pulse links straight to the process that made it. Pulses also trace the shape of the magnetic field near the star. By matching pulses across radio bands, the team reads where in the magnetosphere each band comes from.

Such maps test how pulsar radio beams form and spread. They show if high and low bands share one zone or split apart. Pulsars are precise cosmic clocks, but their radio engine is still not fully known. Single-pulse work gives some of the sharpest clues. It turns brief flashes into a map of a star's hidden zones.
arxiv-2601-17499:
Recent JWST views of the supernova remnant Cassiopeia A open this study of star death. Cassiopeia A is the wreck of a core-collapse supernova. Its ejecta form a fine network of filaments. One odd feature stands out, nicknamed the Green Monster. It looks pockmarked, with near-round holes and rings. The authors use such detail to rebuild the star that died.

From wreck shape, they infer progenitor traits and blast mechanics. That reverse work tests how massive stars end their lives. It links what telescopes see now to physics from centuries past. Cassiopeia A is near and bright, so it serves as a key case. Its lessons guide reads of far remnants too.
arxiv-2601-17599:
Saarthak Johri, Neil Ash, and Monica Valluri ask what warps galactic disks. Dark matter halos in the ΛCDM model are triaxial, or stretched in three axes. Most also tumble, in a motion called figure rotation. The team studies 40 isolated halos with stellar disks from the TNG50 simulation. They track about four billion years of change.

They test if halo tumbling and tilt drive disk warps. Warps are bends seen at disk edges in many galaxies. A clear cause would link dark halo shape to bright disk form. TNG50 gives a rich, controlled test set. The work helps observers read warp photos. It ties a visible trait to dark structure.
arxiv-2601-18099:
Akbar Saadat builds a frame for comparing how blurred two photos of the same scene are. His 2026 preprint deals with defocus, the blur that comes from being out of focus. For three decades, defocus has given strong depth cues in images. Yet reading depth from flat images stays a hard, basic problem in 3D recovery. Heuristic methods wrestle with the ill-posed task of guessing a blur that changes across the scene.

The frame estimates the relative Gaussian blur between an image pair. A relative measure can be steadier than an absolute one. It can feed depth maps for cameras, robots, and photo tools. The work attacks a small piece of the depth problem with a focused tool.
arxiv-2601-18399:
Mehmet Velioglu works on a plant task that is hard to watch: how tall the thick layer grows where two liquids part. Plants that split oil from water, or one drug base from the next, rely on tanks where the mix sits and sorts by weight. The height of that thick zone tells staff if the tank is safe and if it works well.

To read that height by eye is costly, and the view is often blocked by foam or glass. Velioglu trains a smart model that learns from physics as well as from data. The model needs just cheap flow counts at the tank mouth, not a clear view inside. A firm count could warn staff early when a tank starts to drift out of its safe range.
arxiv-2601-18499:
Kratveer Singh and seven colleagues ask if quantum links can show up when key facts about the link are not known. Links of that kind rest on the phase of each wave, a kind of clock set by lasers or wave gear. In most labs the phase must be set with great care, or the link washes out. Here the phase stays firm but hid, and no one sets it by hand.

The team show a kind of pair link that can still be read in that hid case. The read looks at the joint trait of two quantum bits, not at each bit on its own. That joint read can stay sharp while the hid phase roams. The trick could ease the load on labs that build links with many bits. It may also open new tests of basic quantum rules.
arxiv-2601-18599:
Shannon Starr studies a set of counts that grow out of a classic chain in the maths of wholes. The counts sit in a grid, row by row, set by a rule that sums their past kin. Such grids show up when staff count how a whole can be split into parts in set ways. The name of the grid comes from a past scholar who charted its first rows.

Starr looks at the edge of the grid where the row is long but the column count stays small. In that edge zone the counts take a clean form as the rows grow. A clean form lets staff guess far rows with no long sums. It also shows how the grid's shape is set by a few deep rules. Work of this kind feeds the maths of counts and splits, a base for codes and for chance.
arxiv-2601-18999:
Fangzhou Wu, Sandeep Silwal, and Qiuyi Zhang rethink how language model servers reuse past work. A key-value cache stores past steps so new text builds fast, but memory is small and old items must be dropped. The default rule drops the least recently used items, which copes poorly as queries stream in.

The clash grows when many models share workers: load balance and cache hits pull in opposed ways. The team shows random rules can boost cache gains, while learned rules balance load. Their joint view helps serve many models on shared hardware with less waste.
arxiv-2601-19099:
Yosub Shin, Michael Buriek, and Igor Molybog test whether visual models can match a map to a street photo. Vision language models ace many picture tests, yet they stay shaky on spatial tasks that link a top down map to a ground level view. Their bench, m2sv, poses exactly that match as a task.

Each item pairs a north up overhead map with a street view shot taken at the same real place. The model must infer which way the camera faced. Skill at this match matters for robots and aids that must tie what they see to where they are on a map.
arxiv-2601-19199:
Libo Sun and four co-authors give phone agents a memory that grows so they survive app updates. Mobile agents powered by big models can run tasks on a phone by tapping through screens. But apps update often: looks change, flows move, and agents trained on old screens fail.

Beneath the new paint, what each screen does and what the user wants stay much the same. Their agent, MAGNET, keeps a memory that evolves with the apps, storing the stable meaning. Agents that track meaning over surface change could stay useful across the churn of consumer software.
arxiv-2601-19399:
Samir Sadok, Stéphane Lathuilière, and Xavier Alameda-Pineda let a speech model keep what labels leave out. Speech models often lean on named attributes like pitch, content, and speaker identity. Those named parts cannot capture the full richness of a natural voice.

Their framework, RT-MAE, adds trainable residual tokens that soak up whatever the named attributes miss. A masked autoencoder design forces the model to rebuild hidden parts of speech from the rest. Models that admit what their labels miss should sound more like real speech. They should also score more like it, when they rebuild a voice or judge a clip.
arxiv-2601-19499:
Mehdi Heydari Shahna, Seyed Adel Alizadeh Kolagar, and Jouni Mattila work on control systems for mobile robots. They use reinforcement learning, where a robot learns a task by trial and error. Learned policies can perform very well, yet they rarely come with a formal promise that the robot will reach its goal. Safety rules in industry are strict, and unproven behavior is hard to certify.

The authors add a stabilizer with a Lyapunov-like guarantee to the learned controller. In plain terms, the added part keeps the robot's motion pointed toward the goal in a provable way. Trial-and-error learning still shapes the fine details of the motion. The mix aims to keep the skill of learning while adding the proof that factories and standards demand. It is a step toward robots that learn and can still be trusted.
arxiv-2601-19999:
Will Brian and Alan Dow introduce a new guessing principle in set theory. Diamond principles predict sequences with great accuracy and are tools for building mathematical counterexamples. Parametrized diamonds tie each principle to a cardinal invariant, a measure of the size of the continuum's combinatorics. Each known example gives a diamond-like principle forcing its invariant to be the smallest uncountable size.

Their principle is tied to the Laver property, a notion from forcing theory. It also connects to nontrivial automorphisms of a classic quotient algebra. The construction shows the pattern of parametrized diamonds extends further than known. Such principles calibrate the strength of set-theoretic assumptions. The work adds a new instrument to that calibration.
arxiv-2601-20399:
Gaku Omiya, Pierre-Louis Poirion, and Akiko Takeda analyze a randomized subspace method for stochastic optimization under heavy-tailed noise. Subspace methods cut the cost of each step by working in a lower-dimensional slice of the problem. Most theory for the nonconvex case gives bounds in expectation, and high-probability bounds are scarce even under mild noise.

The authors first prove a high-probability convergence bound under sub-Gaussian noise, matching the known order of cost. They then extend the study toward heavy tails. Guarantees that hold with high probability, not just on average, matter when one bad run is costly.
arxiv-2601-20599:
Hyunjun Na and Donghwan Lee study regularized gradient temporal-difference learning, a family of methods for evaluating a policy from off-policy data with function approximation. These methods are widely used, but their convergence theory rests on a restrictive assumption: that the feature interaction matrix is nonsingular. In practice that matrix can become singular.

Singularity leads to instability or degraded performance in the learning updates. The authors add regularization to tame the problem. Sturdier evaluation methods matter because off-policy learning reuses logged data, from games to clinical records, where collecting fresh data under the target policy is impossible.
arxiv-2601-20799:
Adérito Araújo and two co-authors build step-by-step solvers that respect the shape of a wider class of systems. Their 2026 paper gives a frame for Jacobi Hamiltonian integrators. Such systems conserve key quantities over time. Jacobi manifolds widen the stage on which they live. A good solver keeps that structure at each step. Naive methods leak the very things that define the motion.

The build rests on two lifts. One turns Jacobi structures into Poisson ones. The other raises the dynamics to a cleaner space. There, known structure-keeping methods apply. The team also shows uses for the scheme. The work serves long simulations where slow drift ruins the result.
arxiv-2601-20899:
Kenil Solanki, Gaurav Bhandari, S. D. Pathak, and Vikash Kumar Ojha study the spin of light where quantum gravity may leave fingerprints. Their 2026 paper examines photon angular momentum near the Planck scale. The framework is a relativistic generalized uncertainty principle. It builds in a minimal length at the Planck scale. That tiny floor changes the rules for the gauge field. The authors work with a Lorentz covariant version of the theory.

Using Noether's theorem, they derive the energy-momentum tensors of the modified field. Both canonical and symmetric Belinfante forms are computed. From them come the gauge spin and orbital angular momentum currents. Splitting a photon's spin from its orbital part is a subtle art. Planck-scale corrections could shift that split. The paper maps the shift within a consistent formalism.
arxiv-2601-21099:
M. Berton and ten co-authors open a survey of radio emission from a puzzling class of galaxies. Their 2026 paper is the first in the NOCTURNE series. It studies the radio spectrum of narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies. The origin of radio emission in active galactic nuclei is still debated. Several mechanisms can contribute at these frequencies. They include relativistic jets and the jet base. Outflows, star formation, and the hot corona also play roles.

Disentangling those parts takes broad, careful spectra. Narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies are a sharp test case. Their black holes are light and feed fast, which may favor some mechanisms. The series aims to characterize their radio output in full. This first paper sets out the spectrum. It gives the community a base for judging which engine dominates.
arxiv-2601-21299:
Tingyu Zhao and István A. Kovács work on cleaning noise out of network data. Networks are a standard way to picture complex systems, from cells to societies. Real network data, though, often carry noise, bias, and missing links, and the weights on links can be wrong.

Bad weights can spoil every later study built on the network. The authors present a way to filter noise out of the whole network at once. Cleaning the data first makes later claims about groups, hubs, and spread more reliable. The approach is meant for the messy data that real projects actually collect.
arxiv-2601-21699:
Hojae Han, Heeyun Jung, Jongyoon Kim, and Seung-won Hwang ask whether small language model agents can handle multi-step reasoning on tight budgets. Reinforcement learning has empowered agents that search and use tools over many turns. The wins so far rest on heavy training with large models.

Under real resource limits, small agents fall into a weak regime. Few rollouts mean sparse exploration, sparse credit, and unstable learning. The authors study how such agents can still reason across hops. Their question is practical: most deployments cannot afford the high-cost regime, so reasoning must be made to work in the cheap one.
arxiv-2601-21799:
Daniel Kressner and Peter Oehme present a new numerical method for a recurring task in scientific computing. Many applications need the Fréchet derivative of a matrix function. A measure of how the function's output changes when the input matrix is nudged in a chosen direction. For large-scale matrices, computing it directly is far too costly.

The authors build their method on Krylov subspaces, small spaces that capture the action of a large matrix on the vectors that matter. Their 2026 preprint approximates the needed derivative action on a vector within that reduced space. Faster derivative estimates feed sensitivity analysis, uncertainty studies, and the training of models that treat matrices as learnable objects.
arxiv-2601-21899:
Forecasting air quality for the whole planet is hard for two reasons. Pollution patterns differ sharply from place to place, and models trained in one region often fail in places they have never seen. The 2026 preprint behind this entry proposes a framework called OmniAir to meet both problems.

OmniAir is built for station-level prediction worldwide. Instead of letting a station's identity be only its location, it encodes stable physical features of the environment into identities that can generalize. It also learns the topology, the pattern of links between stations, in a dynamic way. Reliable forecasts for unmonitored regions would help health agencies warn people who currently get no local air quality information at all.
arxiv-2601-22199:
Syed Tanzim Mubarrat and co-authors weigh two ways to teach bots with games. Class work on bots builds clear thought, fresh ideas, and skill at hard tasks. But the field is steep, and many who start it drop out. Games can lift drive and keep class fun. So can game traits, like points and badges, laid on plain class work.

Which of the two helps more was not clear. The team gives the first full check of both, done to a strict gold rule for such checks. From the check they draw design tips for class staff. The split counts, since schools must choose where scarce funds go: full games, or game traits on top of class work as it stands.
arxiv-2601-22499:
Elhadj Moustapha Diallo and a team design secure links in a stacked smart-radio setup, under strict odds of breach. Their 2026 preprint joins three kinds of reflecting surfaces: one on a drone, one that sends and reflects at once, and one for indoors. Users move, paths get blocked, and foes may team up or jam.

The team seek settings that keep the breach chance below a set cap. They serve both indoor and outdoor users from the one stack. Such work fits dense, mixed next-wave networks. It treats safety as a design rule, not an afterthought.
arxiv-2601-22699:

Sentence completion suits likelihood scoring; symbol picks suit direct comparison. Matching the form to the task gives a truer grade. The lesson is simple and wide: test design bends results. Evaluation teams can use it at once. The work cleans up a common source of noise.
arxiv-2601-22899:

bernstein-evolutionary-socialism-1899:
Eduard Bernstein's Evolutionary Socialism appeared in German in 1899, and Edith C Harvey's English translation followed in 1909. Bernstein, a German socialist in London exile, had worked closely with Engels. His book questioned core claims of Marxism from inside the movement itself.

Bernstein argued that capitalism was not collapsing, that the middle class was not vanishing, and that trade unions and votes could win real gains step by step. Revolution, he said, should give way to steady reform through democracy. The case for evolutionary over revolutionary socialism made the book the founding document of social democracy, and it split socialist parties for a generation.
bosanquet-philosophical-theory-state-189:
Bernard Bosanquet published The Philosophical Theory of the State in 1899, and the text here follows the second edition of 1910. Bosanquet, a leading British idealist, set out to state what the state truly is when seen by philosophy. His answer draws on Rousseau and Hegel: the state embodies the general will of its citizens.

The general will, on his account, is not the sum of selfish wants but the shared mind that makes social life possible. Laws and institutions express that common self, and the citizen finds freedom in obeying them. The book became British idealism's definitive work of political philosophy. Its claims about state and person still start arguments.
brown-arthur-mervyn-1799:
Arthur Mervyn bears the subtitle Memoirs of the Year 1793, and Brown set it in plague-struck Philadelphia. The narrator recalls meeting a sick man slumped by a wall late one evening. He takes the stranger to be ill with the pestilence, yet stops to help him anyway.

That stranger is young Arthur, whose path runs through theft, fraud, false charges, and love. Yellow fever had emptied the streets of the young nation's chief city that year. Hawthorne later praised the book in strong terms, quoted on its title page. Of all Brown's novels, this one reaches widest in scope and drive.
brown-edgar-huntly-1799:
Brown offered Edgar Huntly to the public in 1799 and said its aim was new from the start. In his preface he rejects Gothic castles and worn-out horrors as tools for moving readers. In their place he puts frontier danger and the perils of the western wilds.

Young Edgar follows a sleepwalker into rough country and lands among caves, wild beasts, and frontier war. A murder puzzle drives the plot while the hero's own mind grows less steady. The dark and winding caverns became famous in their own right. Many readers now treat them as an early American picture of the hidden mind.
brown-ormond-1799:
Ormond, or The Secret Witness came out in three volumes in 1799, signed only B. C. Brown. A Latin motto from Phaedrus warns that those who plot harm for others often fall as victims themselves. The tale is set in Philadelphia during the yellow fever years.

Constantia Dudley, a brave and clear-headed young woman, holds the center of the story. Against her stands Ormond, a smooth schemer with a hidden past who trusts that good ends excuse any means. Brown pits her virtue and reason against his charm and force. The result is among his darkest tests of how much freedom a person can bear.
budge-egyptian-magic-1899:
E. A. Wallis Budge, Keeper of Egyptian Antiquities at the British Museum, published Egyptian Magic in 1899. He wrote this classic survey for general readers rather than specialists. Amulets, secret names, and words of power organize his chapters.

Budge explains the spells Egyptians used for protection and the afterlife. Ceremonies, magical figures, and written charms receive vivid examples from museum objects. He treats Egyptian magic as a system with its own logic. The book's conclusions have dated in places since 1899. Its storytelling still brings ancient Egypt's enchanted world close. Many readers began their interest in Egyptology with Budge's tour.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jerusalem-a-d: A 1913 entry on Jerusalem — the holy city, 71 to 1099. Adrian Fortescue unfolds its fateful ages. Titus razed the ancient walls. The caliphs ruled the sacred stones. The crusaders freed the sepulchre. Its 1099 capture is famed. Its 70 fall is famed. Its 614 Persian sack is famed.
chesnutt-conjure-woman-1899:
Charles W. Chesnutt published The Conjure Woman in 1899, his sly, foundational set of conjure tales in dialect. The tales tell of slavery-era North Carolina through Uncle Julius, a former slave with a storyteller's cunning in frame. Chesnutt, a Black writer from Cleveland, smuggled sharp truths about slavery inside charming folk frames for white readers.

John, a northern grape grower, narrates while Julius, his coachman, answers each plan with a conjure tale. Goophered grapevines, a man turned to a tree, and a conjured mule carry memories of cruelty and wit. Each tale quietly serves Julius's present ends, a job, a church, a schoolhouse saved from the buyer's axe. Chesnutt lets the reader see what John cannot, the history inside the humor of the old man's tales. The book founded a tradition of Black frame tales that later writers took up.
chopin-awakening-1899:
Kate Chopin published The Awakening in 1899, and the reviews nearly ended her career. Critics called the novel morbid and unwholesome, and Chopin was frozen out of literary society. She had written, instead, the book that would invent modern feminist fiction for later generations of readers.

Edna Pontellier, a Kentucky-born wife and mother summering in Creole Louisiana, begins to wake to her own desires. She learns to swim, takes up painting, moves out of her husband's house, and loves where she should not. Grand Isle and New Orleans frame her search for a self beyond wifehood and motherhood. The sea that taught her freedom receives her at the end. The novel's rediscovery in the 1960s made Chopin a central American writer.
cia-0000009699:
The general situation of the Viet Cong, the North Vietnamese Army, and the Khmer Communists is treated together in a July 1971 item. The heading shortens all three forces to initials: VC, NVA, and KC. By 1971 the three movements fought connected wars across Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia.

A combined survey let analysts judge the whole Indochina battlefield rather than its pieces. Strength, supply, and morale in one country affected the others directly. The file's wide frame reflects how the war itself had widened. Readers get the regional picture as Washington's analysts assembled it in the middle of 1971.
cia-0000009899:
Viet Cong policy toward prisoners of war is studied in a September 1967 CIA paper. Policy papers step back from incidents to find rules: how captives should be taken, held, fed, and used. The southern enemy's practice varied by unit, so any stated policy met messy reality.

Knowing the stated rules still helped judge individual reports. A camp that broke its own side's policy was a different problem from one that followed it. The paper also served legal and negotiation thinking about the war's conduct. It preserves the enemy's captivity doctrine as Washington understood it in 1967.
cia-0000011499:
Burma won freedom from Britain in 1948 and at once faced revolts that nearly tore it apart. In July 1951 the CIA judged the survival chances of its non-communist government. Communist rebels were among several armed movements fighting the young state, and China's new communist regime loomed across its border.

The paper weighs the strength of the government in Rangoon against the rebels pressing it. It also asks how much outside help the regime could count on. The estimate captures the early Cold War fear that mainland Southeast Asia might fall, piece by piece, to communist forces.
cia-0000012299:
The theory behind Soviet war-making is the thread in a Helms memo of November 1961. It went to the DIA director, its quoted title beginning 'The Theo...' and cut short. The subject is again the journal Military Thought, where Soviet officers argued doctrine in print. Washington's analysts read those arguments the way coaches study an opposing team's playbook.

The memo passes one such piece along the channel built that autumn. The Pentagon's hunger for the colonel's military detail shows in the steady requests. For readers, the page marks the demand signal from the customers who turned raw secrets into plans.
cia-0000012399:
May 1, 1961, London: meeting number eleven falls on a date with its own weight in the file. One year earlier, to the day, Francis Gary Powers had fallen from the sky over the Soviet Union. Now a Soviet colonel sat in London giving the West what the U-2 could no longer photograph, in sessions his handlers numbered like chapters.

The eleventh session's record continues the intensive spring run. The date's irony hangs over the page without needing comment. For readers, it shows the spy business keeping history's calendar: anniversaries marked by work, not ceremony.
cia-0000013299:
American prisoners held in Viet Cong Inter-Region 5 are counted in a CIA report from October 1971. The inter-regions were the middle layer of the southern enemy's command structure. They stood between the central office above and the provinces below. The report covers where the captives sat inside that chain of command. It shows which headquarters held them, moved them, and answered for them to the levels above in the system.

The head-count by region is the report's core contribution. It files the jailed under the commands that held them in 1971. For readers, the page shows the captivity system organized like the war itself, in layers.
cia-0000013599:
Security conditions in Mexico City get a CIA survey in September 1968, weeks before the Olympic Games opened there. The capital was seething that year. Students filled the streets in protest, and the government answered with troops. The paper surveys the metropolis's undercurrents as the world's athletes and cameras prepared to arrive in the middle of a political crisis.

The survey weighs the protest movement, the police, and the risk of violence. Within weeks, troops fired on students at Tlatelolco square. For readers, the paper is the city's portrait on the eve of the Games, drawn before its darkest night.

Inside, the possible peace feeler is recorded as it was heard. Feelers of this kind tested whether talks could begin at all. Most such feelers failed quietly at the time. Yet each one mapped a little of the ground on which later, serious talks could stand. The paper weighs where each might move and what that meant for American interests. It captures the Arab world at the start of a revolutionary decade. The postwar order there was cracking, and no one in Washington could be sure what would replace it.
cia-0000132099: A 1996 CIA document presents the agency's internal probe of the Bay of Pigs affair. The failed 1961 invasion of Cuba had set off a painful reckoning inside the agency at the time.
