conrad-heart-of-darkness-1899:
Joseph Conrad published Heart of Darkness in 1899, a short novel told by a sailor named Marlow. Marlow takes a job piloting a steamboat up the Congo River. His task is to find Kurtz, an ivory trader deep in the interior. The trip moves through stations marked by greed, waste, and cruelty.

As Marlow gets closer, he hears more about Kurtz and his power over local people. The meeting at the end is bleak and hard to forget. Conrad drew on his own time in the Congo under Belgian rule. The book remains a sharp and debated study of empire and moral collapse.
cumont-textes-monuments-mithra-tome1-189:
Franz Cumont published the first tome of his Textes et monuments figurés relatifs aux mystères de Mithra at Brussels in 1899. The text is in French. Tome one holds his critical introduction and the collected literary and inscriptional texts for the Mithraic mysteries, the Roman cult of the god Mithras.

Cumont, a Belgian scholar, gathered every known scrap of evidence for a religion that left no scripture of its own. His introduction argued that Mithraism came from Persia through Asia Minor into the Roman army and ports. The thesis ruled the field for most of a century. The library also holds his shorter English summary of 1903. This tome is the full scholarly corpus behind that summary, and it founded Mithraic studies.
dannunzio-virgins-of-rocks-1899:
Agatha Hughes translated The Virgins of the Rocks into English in 1899. Claudio Cantelmo, last heir of a noble line, retreats to a ruined estate. He has fixed on one grand aim for his fading house.

Cantelmo means to father a son fit to be a king. On the estate he finds three sisters, the virgins of the rocks. Each sister embodies a different ideal of womanhood and fate. He must choose among them as a breeder chooses, coldly and with care. Symbol crowds every page of this strange tale. Many judges call it D'Annunzio's most symbolic work, a dream of blood and destiny.
dante-vita-nuova-rossetti-1899:
Dante set his young love for Beatrice in verse and prose in La Vita Nuova, The New Life, written about 1294. Dante Gabriel Rossetti translated it with a poet's sympathy, in the version printed in 1899. Poems written across years are framed by Dante's own story of when and why each was made.

Beatrice passes from living lady to heavenly guide within these pages, and Italian gains a literary language in the process. The book stands as the gateway to the Comedy, where Beatrice leads the poet through Paradise. Rossetti, who loved Dante above all poets, made this translation a work of devotion.
dekker-shoemakers-holiday-1599:
Dekker's Shoemaker's Holiday, first played in 1599, is the merriest of Elizabethan citizen comedies. The text here follows the Mermaid edition edited by Rhys. Dekker based it on a prose tale of Simon Eyre, the shoemaker who rose to be Lord Mayor of London.

Eyre's shop hums with apprentices, jokes, and songs while love plots cross the lines of rank. A young gentleman works disguised at the bench to win his bride. The Lord Mayor's feast ends the play in pure good cheer. Generations have loved its picture of working London, proud, kind, and ready to laugh at lords and itself alike.
della-tramutatione-metallica-sogni-tre-1: Della tramutatione metallica sogni tre, 1599. The three metallic dreams. This book preserves that work. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
descriptive-mentality-from-the-head-face: Descriptive Mentality from the Head, Face and Hand, 1899. The head reading. This book preserves that manual. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
dewey-school-society-1899:
John Dewey published The School and Society in 1899, a short book from his lectures in Chicago. Dewey argues that schools should mirror the life of a real community. Children learn best by doing: cooking, weaving, building, and solving shared problems. The old school of sitting still and reciting lessons fails the child, he says.

He links school reform to democracy itself. A school that trains obedience cannot serve a free society. Dewey's laboratory school at Chicago tested these ideas in practice. The book founded progressive education as a movement. Its core claims still shape debates about classrooms today.
die-geheimsymbole-der-chemie-und-medicin: Die Geheimsymbole der Chemie und Medicin des Mittelalters, 1899. The medieval symbols. This book preserves that study. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
digha-nikaya-rhys-davids-1899: Volume one of the Dialogues of the Buddha, the Digha Nikaya translated by Rhys Davids. These long discourses record the Buddha's teachings on doctrine and practice. This edition preserves those foundational Buddhist texts. The archive guards it with care.
dubois-philadelphia-negro-1899:
W E B Du Bois published The Philadelphia Negro: A Social Study in 1899. Du Bois, then a young scholar at the University of Pennsylvania, spent over a year in the city's Seventh Ward. He interviewed thousands of Black residents door to door, a scale of fieldwork new in American social study.

Du Bois mapped jobs, wages, families, churches, and crime in the ward, and traced the history of Black Philadelphia. He showed that poverty and crime followed barred doors and low pay, not racial character. The study founded urban sociology in the United States and set a standard for later field research. Its care and fairness still impress readers today.
encyclopaedia-biblica-vol1-1899:
Thomas Cheyne and John Sutherland Black edited the Encyclopaedia Biblica, whose first volume appeared in 1899, covering A to D. It was the critical answer to Hastings: a dictionary of the Bible built on the higher criticism. Scholars from many countries contributed.

Articles treat the literary, political, and religious history of the Bible, plus its archaeology, geography, and natural history. The writers question old dates and authorships with cool, learned rigor. Church readers found some of it shocking; scholars found it thrilling. The work became a landmark of critical Bible study, and its boldness still startles today.
europmc-pmc10155999:
Roux and colleagues present iPHoP, a machine learning framework that predicts the hosts of viruses found in metagenomes, in a 2023 paper. Most viruses of bacteria and archaea are now known only from DNA fished out of environmental samples. Without a known host, it is hard to say what a virus does or where it fits in nature.

The framework blends several prediction methods to raise accuracy and coverage. It aims to name a host for far more viral sequences than earlier tools could. Better host calls help scientists map how viruses shape microbial communities.
europmc-pmc10178199:
Masenga and co-authors review how oxidative stress works in metabolic syndrome in a 2023 paper. Metabolic syndrome is a cluster of problems, including belly fat, high blood sugar, and high blood pressure, that raise the risk of diabetes and heart disease. Extra body fat fuels both inflammation and oxidative stress, which then damage tissue over time.

The review traces the chemical steps by which that stress builds and spreads harm. It links the process to each part of the syndrome. It also surveys treatments that target the stress itself. Those include drugs and lifestyle change.
europmc-pmc10320099:
Kolberg and co-authors described the 2023 update of g:Profiler, a free web tool for gene list studies. A gene list study asks what shared jobs a set of genes does. The tool links gene lists to large data banks on gene roles, cell paths, and gene control.

The tool now works for 849 species, from humans to plants, fungi, and pests. Users can also upload data for any other species. Kolberg added a new filter that picks out the gene terms that drive a result. New graphs show how those terms connect to each other. Old data banks stay saved back to 2015, so past work can be checked again.
europmc-pmc10391899:
Marassi and Fadini reviewed in 2023 how three chronic diseases drive each other. The three are type 2 diabetes, heart and vessel disease, and chronic kidney disease. Each is common, and they often strike the same person. Doctors have coined one shared name for the linked trio: cardio-renal-metabolic disease.

High blood sugar can damage the heart and kidneys in well-known ways. Marassi notes that the heart and kidneys also harm each other directly. Less clear is how heart or kidney disease then worsens blood sugar control. The review gathers proof for each link in the chain. It builds the case for care plans that treat the trio as one illness, not three.
europmc-pmc10457199:
Zhao led a gene study of blood proteins tied to inflammation in 2023, with the Estonian Biobank Research Team among the partners. The team measured 91 such proteins in 14,824 people. It then searched each genome for spots that raise or lower a protein level. Such spots are called protein quantitative trait loci.

The search found 180 spots, 59 near the protein's own gene and 121 far away. Zhao merged these with disease gene data to test which proteins cause illness. One protein, lymphotoxin-alpha, stood out in multiple sclerosis. A second, CD40, raised risk for one joint disease yet lowered it for two others. One more, CXCL5, was tied to ulcerative colitis and ran high in patient guts.
europmc-pmc10499599:
Takeuchi and a large team linked gut microbe sugar use to insulin resistance in 2023. Insulin resistance is the core fault behind metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes. In it, body cells respond weakly to insulin, the hormone that lowers blood sugar. Gut microbes help digest food, and their sugar use may feed the fault.

The team joined stool chemistry, microbe gene reads, and blood data in humans. Stools of resistant people held more simple sugars that the body can absorb. Takeuchi tied that surplus to microbe sugar paths and to swelling signals. Some gut bacteria tracked with resistance, others with healthy response. The healthy-response set eased the fault when fed to mice.
europmc-pmc10667099:
Wadden led the SURMOUNT-3 trial in 2023 on a weight drug given after a lifestyle program. Adults with obesity first spent 12 weeks on strict diet and activity coaching. Those who lost at least 5% of body weight moved to the drug phase. In all, 579 people got tirzepatide or a dummy shot once a week for 72 weeks.

The drug arm lost far more weight, Wadden reports. Mean extra change was a loss of 18.4% on the drug, versus a gain of 2.5% on the dummy. A further loss of 5% or more hit 87.5% on the drug and 16.5% on the dummy. Gut side effects were the most common harm, mostly mild or moderate.
europmc-pmc10767899:
Zdrazil and co-authors described the ChEMBL database in 2023, a free store of drug-like compounds and their test results. Staff curate each entry by hand for quality. The bank has grown in size and in data types since its 2009 launch. Past reports ran in 2012, 2014, 2017, and 2019.

Deposited data now slightly outweigh data mined from papers, Zdrazil reports. Chemical probe data flow in on a set schedule through a European consortium. Screens for anti-Covid compounds were added in release 27, with patent data close behind. New flags mark natural products and chemical probes. About 270,000 test records now carry a note on how the compound acts.
europmc-pmc11031399:
Barthélemy and a large team test a precise blood measure for Alzheimer disease against spinal fluid tests in this 2024 study. New Alzheimer treatments that slow the disease make it vital to spot who can benefit. Spinal fluid tests are approved but need a spinal tap. The team measured a blood ratio of a tau protein form, called plasma percent p-tau217, in two patient groups.

The groups held 1,422 people in Sweden and 337 in the US, the authors report. Brain scans served as the truth standard for amyloid plaques and tau tangles. The blood test matched approved spinal fluid tests at sorting plaque status, with accuracy scores from 0.95 up to 0.97 for plaques. For tangles it scored from 0.95 up to 0.98 and generally beat the fluid tests. The main checks focused on people with mild memory impairment.
europmc-pmc11093599:
Ju and a large team show that a protein-building enzyme doubles as a lactate tagger in stomach cancer in this 2024 study. Lactylation is a chemical tag that lactate, a sugar breakdown product, adds to proteins. The known tagger was doubted, since its fuel is about a thousand times scarcer than a rival fuel. The team tested an enzyme called AARS1, which normally helps build proteins.

AARS1 used lactate and ATP, the cell's energy currency, to attach the tag directly, they found. It sensed lactate levels, moved into the nucleus, and tagged a growth complex called YAP-TEAD, switching it on. That complex in turn raises AARS1 levels, forming a positive feedback loop. AARS1 was higher in stomach tumours, and high levels tracked with poor patient outlook. Blocking the loop slowed cancer cell growth in their tests.
europmc-pmc1621099:
Social forces decide who gets sick and who gets care. Farmer and co-authors developed that claim in 2006 under the name structural violence: the harm done by social structures themselves. They drew on work with HIV patients in the US and Rwanda.

Racism, poverty, gender inequality, and war shape illness far upstream of the clinic. Yet medical training seldom links that analysis to daily practice, since the field prizes molecular answers. Farmer calls such inquiry desocialized. He urges biosocial thinking: treating disease as a joint product of bodies and society, built into clinical frameworks, not left as bedside intuition.
europmc-pmc1665399:
Nanoparticles slip into fish eggs, organs, and even brains. Kashiwada tracked them in 2006 using see-through medaka, a small fish whose body is transparent. Fluorescent latex particles of many sizes floated in the water.

Particles stuck to the egg shell and pooled in oil droplets. Mid-sized particles, 474 nanometers, entered eggs best. The smallest, about 39 nanometers, reached the yolk and gallbladder as embryos grew. In adults they lodged mainly in gills and gut, but also brain, liver, testis, and blood. Kashiwada concludes particles can cross the blood-brain barrier, and toxicity rose with water salinity.
europmc-pmc1779499:
Sheridan and co-authors examined in 2006 a small group of breast cancer cells marked CD44 positive and CD24 negative. Such cells had been reported to act like stem cells, which can grow and renew themselves. The team asked whether these cells can invade tissue and travel to new sites.

The researchers checked 13 breast cancer cell lines and found five where over 30 percent of cells carried the mark. Those lines made more of several invasion-linked genes, such as interleukin-6, interleukin-8, and urokinase plasminogen activator. In lab invasion tests the marked lines invaded more strongly than other lines. Yet only some of them could settle and grow in mouse lungs. The mark alone did not predict spread to the lungs.
europmc-pmc1936999:
McCarney and colleagues ran in 2007 what they describe as the first randomized trial of the Hawthorne Effect itself. The effect is the claim that people in studies change or improve simply because they are being watched closely. It threatens how well trial results transfer to routine care, yet it had never been quantified.

Inside a trial of Ginkgo biloba against placebo for mild to moderate dementia, 176 participants were randomized again. One arm got intensive follow-up with full assessments at baseline and at two, four, and six months. The other got a short baseline check and one full assessment at six months. At six months, the intensive group scored better on the cognitive test used, by about two points, and on participant-rated quality of life. The effect was significant for cognition in the main model.
europmc-pmc2125099: A medical paper on the spleen's relation to blood destruction and regeneration. The spleen again. This article preserves that hematology. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2125499: A medical paper reporting the serum treatment of twenty-six polio cases. The serum cure, tried. This article preserves that therapeutics. Its place in history is secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
europmc-pmc2128199: Calves with lung infections carried a suspect germ, and this paper tied Bacillus actinoides to their bronchopneumonia. The bovine pneumonia's cause, investigated. The young cattle's disease, traced. The article preserves that veterinary bacteriology. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2128399: A medical paper on the action of drugs on respiration, the morphine series. The opiate breath. This article preserves that pharmacology. Tomorrow's readers will find it. The historical record keeps it. Time has kept the file intact.
europmc-pmc2131299: A medical paper on microbic virulence and host susceptibility in paratyphoid infection. The germ's strength. This article preserves that bacteriology. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2131499: Family bloodlines carry their clumping factors from parent to child, and this investigation proved it using immune agglutination. The scientists traced agglutinogens across generations of donors. The inherited blood markers, established. The article preserves that genetics research for future readers.
europmc-pmc2131599: A medical paper on relation of varicella to herpes zoster, statistical observations. The link's numbers. This article preserves that epidemiology. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Tomorrow's readers will find it.
europmc-pmc2140499: A biology paper on the physiology of the respiration of fishes in relation to hydrogen ion concentration. The fishes' breath. This article preserves that physiology. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
europmc-pmc2270899:
Outeiro and co-workers visualised toxic alpha-synuclein oligomers in living cells in 2008. In Parkinson's disease, this protein misfolds and clumps; its fibrils fill Lewy bodies, the disease's hallmark inclusions. Growing evidence instead blames small prefibrillar clusters, called oligomers, as the toxic species. They had never been identified in living cells. The team used bimolecular fluorescence complementation, a method where two protein halves glow only when they meet, to watch oligomers form.

Stabilising the oligomers through the assay increased cell toxicity. Adding the protective chaperone Hsp70 rescued the cells and reduced oligomer formation. Parkinson's-linked mutations did not change how many oligomers formed. Their biochemical properties, however, differed from normal alpha-synuclein oligomers. The assay gives researchers a direct tool to test candidate therapeutics for these synuclein disorders.
europmc-pmc2516199:
Homer and colleagues showed in 2008 that a person's DNA can be picked out of a mixed sample using dense gene-chip data. Their tool was a microarray that reads hundreds of thousands of SNPs, the single-letter DNA differences that vary between people. The question was whether someone contributing only a trace to a mixture could still be identified.

The team built the statistical theory, tested its limits in simulations, and then ran real mixtures in the laboratory. They correctly detected specific people even when a person supplied less than 0.1 percent of the total DNA in the mix. The result matters for forensics, where samples are often contaminated. It also means summary statistics from large genetic studies do not fully hide who took part.
europmc-pmc2556099:
Dowd and colleagues catalogued the bacteria living in chronic diabetic foot ulcers in this 2008 study. Such ulcers often end in amputation, and the microbe communities inside them, growing as biofilms, were poorly understood. Culture methods grow only easy species, so the team used a DNA sequencing method called bTEFAP to census 40 ulcers from different patients.

The commonest genus was Corynebacterium, ahead of the usual suspects like Staphylococcus and Streptococcus. Oxygen-hating bacteria such as Bacteroides, Peptoniphilus, and Anaerococcus appeared in nearly every ulcer and made up much of each community. The authors propose that distinct bacteria form groups they call functional equivalent pathogroups. Alone, each member is harmless. Together they act like one consortium, as damaging as a classic pathogen. That would explain why these infections persist.
europmc-pmc2570799:
Knopp and colleagues tested in 2008 how well standard stool examinations find intestinal worms in Zanzibar schoolchildren. These soil-transmitted helminths infect the poorest communities, and control programmes giving deworming drugs need accurate counts. But repeated mass treatment had lowered worm burdens, making infections easy to miss. The team collected three stool samples from each of 342 children on Unguja Island and applied three laboratory techniques.

A single sample missed much. Sensitivity ranged from 20.7 percent for one method detecting Strongyloides to 84.2 percent for another detecting Ascaris. Examining three samples raised the observed hookworm prevalence by 161 percent under one technique. Combining different techniques on multiple samples came closest to the true prevalence predicted by a mathematical model. After three samples, whipworm prevalence stood at 47.9 percent.
europmc-pmc261899:
Stein and a large consortium sequenced in 2003 the genome of the soil worm Caenorhabditis briggsae and compared it with its famous relative C. elegans. The two species split about 100 million years ago yet look nearly identical and share chromosome number, genome size, and habitat. The comparison aimed to expose which features evolution has conserved.

The draft genome holds roughly 19,500 protein-coding genes, about the same as C. elegans. Clear counterparts exist for 12,200 of them, and about 800 genes have no detectable match. Gene order is extensively shared, and operons, the worm's clustered gene units, kept their arrangement in 96 percent of cases. Genome size differences came almost entirely from repetitive DNA, which makes up 22.4 percent of the C. briggsae genome. The comparison also revealed 1,300 new C. elegans genes.
europmc-pmc2627899:
Ramagopalan and colleagues showed in 2009 that vitamin D directly switches on the main gene behind multiple sclerosis risk. Multiple sclerosis clusters in sunny-poor regions, and the strongest genetic factor is a variant of the immune gene HLA-DRB1, the *1501 type. The team searched that gene's control region for a vitamin D response element, a DNA switch the vitamin's receptor can grip.

Sequencing over 1,000 chromosomes showed the switch perfectly conserved on the risk-carrying *15 haplotypes but variable on others. Binding tests confirmed the vitamin D receptor docks there. In cell experiments, adding active vitamin D raised expression from the *15 promoter, an effect lost when the switch was deleted or swapped for a non-risk version. Cell-surface protein rose only in *15-bearing cells. The authors frame this as a direct gene-environment interaction.
europmc-pmc2631699:
Maki and Tambyah reviewed in 2001 how to engineer away urinary catheter infections, the most common hospital-acquired infection. More than a million patients in American hospitals and care facilities catch one each year. Risk runs at 5 percent per day of catheter use. These infections are also the second most common cause of hospital bloodstream infection and are tied to higher death rates.

The review examines catheters redesigned to fight infection at the surface. Catheters impregnated with the antibiotics nitrofurazone or minocycline plus rifampin show anti-infective activity. So do catheters carrying a silver alloy hydrogel coating. Both significantly cut infection risk for short-term use up to two or three weeks. Silent infections trigger needless antibiotic treatment. They also breed resistant organisms. So the authors argue prevention by design beats treatment after the fact.
europmc-pmc2700099:
Le Guilloux, Schmidtke, and Tuffery released in 2009 Fpocket, a free program that finds the pockets on a protein's surface where drug molecules might sit. Structure-based drug hunting starts by docking thousands of candidate compounds into such a pocket, so spotting the right pocket comes first. Many proteins' pockets were still found by eye or by luck.

Fpocket builds a geometric mesh of the protein and marks hollow spheres that nestle against its surface, clustering them into pockets. On proteins with known bound drugs, the true pocket sat in its top three guesses 94 percent of the time. For empty proteins the figure was 92 percent. It beat the field's standard tools while running faster. The package includes benchmarking and descriptor tools, and its open code invites others to build better scoring on top.
europmc-pmc2707599:
Moher, Liberati, Tetzlaff, Altman, and the PRISMA Group issued the PRISMA statement in 2009, a guide for reporting systematic reviews and pooled analyses in health care. Clinicians and guideline writers rely on such reviews to stay current. Yet early checks showed review reports often missed basic facts about methods and quality checks.

PRISMA replaces the older QUOROM guide and reflects new ideas in how reviews should be done and described. It sets out what authors should state about their search, study choice, bias checks, and combined results. Clearer reports, the authors argue, let readers judge for themselves whether a review can be trusted and used in care.
europmc-pmc2719799:
Sequeira and co-authors scanned gene activity across many brain regions in 2009 for changes tied to suicide and major depression. Most prior work focused on serotonin, one brain messenger, yet other messenger systems likely play a part too. They sampled seventeen cortical and deeper regions from suicide cases, with and without depression, and from controls.

Suicide-linked changes clustered most in prefrontal cortex, the front planning area, and in the hippocampus, a memory area. Two messenger systems stood out as broadly altered: glutamate, the main excitatory signal, and GABA, the main calming signal. Follow-up tests on receptor subunit genes, the parts that receive those signals, matched the scan results in independent samples.
europmc-pmc2791199:
Gao and colleagues hunted for the exact protein changes that let H5N1 bird flu pass between mammals, using guinea pigs as hosts in 2009. Since 2003 the virus had caused over four hundred known human cases, most after close contact with poultry, and over sixty percent of those patients died.

Of six virus strains tested, only two spread from infected animals to healthy cage mates. Changing single building blocks in two proteins showed what made the difference. One change in the PB2 protein, at position seven hundred one, was required for spread. A second change in the HA protein removed a sugar attachment and let the virus grip cell surfaces found in mammal airways.
europmc-pmc2851599:
Parchman, Geist, Grahnen, Benkman, and Buerkle sequenced the working genes of lodgepole pine in 2010, building a genomic toolkit for a tree whose huge genome blocks whole-genome sequencing. Lodgepole pine anchors mountain forests across western North America and varies strikingly across its range. Using a high-throughput sequencer on copied gene messages, the team gathered nearly six hundred thousand reads.

Assembly produced over sixty thousand gene clusters representing roughly seventeen thousand distinct genes, plus a surprising haul of active retrotransposons, jumping genes that copy themselves around the genome. The collection yielded thousands of simple repeat and single-letter variants as ready markers, with working lab primers for many. The authors present the set as a foundation for population and adaptation studies in pines.
europmc-pmc2873499:
Harte and colleagues found in 2010 that a bacterial toxin leaking from the gut runs high in people with fatty liver disease not caused by alcohol. The toxin, endotoxin, comes from gut germ walls and can stir body-wide inflammation tied to insulin resistance. They measured it in one hundred fifty-five patients with biopsy-confirmed fatty liver and in healthy controls.

Toxin levels in patients ran nearly three times the control levels on average. Having diabetes on top of fatty liver did not push levels higher, and the toxin level tracked how insulin-resistant a patient was. Companion markers of toxin response also rose. A small follow-up group treated with diet or diet plus a fat-blocking drug let the team probe whether levels fall as the liver improves.
europmc-pmc2887799:
Harteveld and Higgs reviewed in 2010 alpha-thalassaemia, likely the most common single-gene disorder in the world. The condition cuts production of alpha-globin, one chain of the hemoglobin that carries oxygen in red cells. It clusters around the Mediterranean, Southeast Asia, Africa, the Middle East, and South Asia, and migration has raised its frequency in northern Europe and North America.

Healthy people carry four working alpha-globin genes, and losing one, two, three, or all four explains the range of severity. Losing three causes HbH disease, a moderate to severe anemia, while losing all four is lethal before birth. Most cases come from deleted genes rather than spelling errors. Because blood tests alone can mislead, DNA analysis usually confirms the exact form, which matters for family counseling.
europmc-pmc2954799:
Williams and co-authors isolated a progenitor cell group living inside normal adult human joint cartilage in a 2010 study. Cartilage repairs itself poorly, and lab-grown cartilage cells lose their character, yielding patch tissue weaker than the original.

Using a sticking test on the protein fibronectin, they pulled out clones that multiplied through many doublings while keeping normal chromosome counts. The cells showed strong activity of telomerase, an enzyme that guards chromosome ends, and in three-dimensional pellets they formed cartilage-like tissue with limited range. Such resident progenitors could give repair therapies a better starting cell than borrowed marrow cells.
europmc-pmc3038199:
Amano, Nakayama, and Kaibuchi reviewed in 2010 a protein switch that helps cells keep their shape, grip, and direction. The switch, called ROCK in short, is turned on by a small partner protein and belongs to a wider family of such control proteins. Once active, it tunes the cell's inner scaffolding, the network of fibers that lets cells contract, crawl, and divide.

Drug studies link this switch to blood vessel spasm, lung blood pressure problems, nerve injury, and glaucoma. That spread makes it an attractive drug target across several fields. The review covers the switch's structure, how it is switched on, and what it acts on inside cells. It gathers the case for blocking or tuning it in treatment. Readers get a compact map of a pathway found in nearly every tissue.
europmc-pmc3040199:
Nacke and colleagues surveyed in 2011 how land use shapes the bacteria living in German soils. They sampled nine forest and nine grassland sites covering six management styles in one region, and read a marker gene from nearly six hundred thousand bacterial sequences. Soil bacteria drive nutrient cycles and soil quality, yet how farming and forestry steer them was poorly known.

Grassland soils held a richer spread of bacterial groups than forest soils, and several major groups differed clearly between the two land uses. Beech and spruce forest soils also hosted distinct communities. Soil acidity tracked many of the shifts, while management style itself showed weak links once acidity was considered. The authors conclude that land use matters mainly through the soil conditions and trees it creates. Their dataset sets a scale few earlier soil surveys could reach.
europmc-pmc3091299:
Bell and coauthors asked in 2011 how much of the variation in DNA methylation between people is written in their DNA sequence itself. Methylation, a chemical tag on DNA, helps regulate genes and differs from person to person for unclear reasons. The team measured tags at more than twenty thousand sites in cell lines from seventy seven donors of African ancestry, alongside full genotypes and gene activity data.

Nearly two hundred tag sites tracked with nearby DNA variants, showing local genetic control is common. One variant inside a gene previously suspected of shaping methylation tracked with the genome wide pattern as a whole, though such long range effects were rare overall. Tags near gene starts generally went with lower gene activity, as expected. Many variants affected both tagging and activity of the same gene. The work shows methylation is partly inherited through the sequence, not purely environmental.
europmc-pmc3108599:
David Johnston-Monje and Manish Raizada published a 2011 study in PLoS ONE on microbes that live inside maize seeds without causing disease. They compared seed bacteria across wild relatives of maize and farmed varieties, from Mexico to Canada, to see which microbes survived domestication. Samples were grown in the lab and also read by DNA fingerprint methods.

Most seed microbes found in the wild ancestor still occur in modern maize, and a small shared core appeared in every plant type tested. Cultured microbes came from many groups, and several could help plants by freeing phosphate or making growth signals. One strain strongly boosted potato shoot growth in tests. The work suggests seeds carry a lasting microbial inheritance worth protecting in breeding.
europmc-pmc3141799:
Sarah Crowe and colleagues made the case for case study research in health services in a 2011 paper in BMC Medical Research Methodology. The approach, standard in business, law, and policy, lets researchers study a complex issue closely in its real setting. Health research has used it less, despite its fit for tangled service questions.

Drawing on their own health case studies, the authors sort the main designs, the questions each suits, and the records, interviews, and observations typically used. Strengths include depth and context; risks include weak theory and cherry-picked cases. The paper closes with design pointers and a checklist for judging case study reports, aiming to raise both use and quality of the method in health research.
europmc-pmc3170599:
Nadine Genet and colleagues reviewed the scientific literature on home care across Europe in a 2011 paper in BMC Health Services Research. Care delivered at home is growing as populations age and family carers become scarcer, yet cross-country knowledge was patchy. The team screened thousands of papers from a decade, keeping seventy-four that described whole home care systems.

The surviving studies covered eighteen countries and dwelt mostly on who receives care and how services are organised. Unequal regional access, market pressures, quality, and joining health with social care recurred as themes. Systems differed sharply between and even within countries, comparative studies were rare, and financing and Eastern Europe were barely covered. The authors call for uniform frameworks so countries can finally be compared like with like.
europmc-pmc3219299:
Cornelis de Jager and colleagues tested whether simple blood-count ratios predict bloodstream infection in emergency patients, in this 2010 paper in Critical Care. Doctors usually rely on markers such as C-reactive protein and white cell counts, which perform imperfectly. The team compared these with the lymphocyte count and the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio in patients suspected of community-acquired bacteremia.

They matched ninety-two patients with positive blood cultures against ninety-two with negative cultures. The groups differed clearly in C-reactive protein, lymphocyte count, and the ratio, but not in total white cell or neutrophil counts. The ratio gave the best overall test performance, closely followed by the lymphocyte count, and both beat the conventional markers. Because the values come free with a routine blood count, the authors suggest using them in daily practice.
europmc-pmc3224599:
Ryan Dowling, Pamela Goodwin, and Vuk Stambolic reviewed the case for the diabetes drug metformin as a cancer treatment in this 2011 article in BMC Medicine. Metformin is the most widely prescribed drug of its class for type 2 diabetes. Population, laboratory, and early clinical evidence had begun to suggest it might also fight cancer.

The authors set out two routes by which the drug could help. By lowering circulating insulin, it may starve cancers that thrive on high insulin, such as breast and colon tumors. It may also act directly on cancer cells by blocking the mTOR signaling pathway, which controls protein production and growth. The review weighs the supporting evidence and the molecular mechanisms, framing metformin as a promising repurposed therapy.
europmc-pmc3257299:
Angela Bruex and colleagues built a gene regulatory network for root skin cell development in the model plant Arabidopsis, in this 2012 paper in PLoS Genetics. The root epidermis makes just two cell types, hair cells and non-hair cells, making it a clean system for studying how fate is decided. The team wanted a systems-level view of the whole differentiation program.

The team used mutants that produce only one cell type, plus cell sorting to isolate the epidermis. They found over fifteen hundred genes differing between the two fates. About two hundred formed a core set. They then perturbed the system with seventeen mutants and two hormone treatments. Watching each core gene respond let them arrange the genes into a network. Timing data and statistical modeling helped place the genes. A family of regulatory proteins called bHLH emerged as stage-specific organizers.
europmc-pmc3285199:
Kresten Lindorff-Larsen and colleagues put eight protein force fields through a systematic trial in this 2012 paper in PLoS ONE. Molecular dynamics simulations animate proteins atom by atom, but their accuracy rests entirely on the force field, the equations approximating atomic forces. With simulations now reaching previously inaccessible timescales, the team compared the fields against hard experimental data.

They checked how well each field reproduced the structures and wobbles of folded proteins measured by NMR. They tested whether simulations of small peptides were biased toward helices or sheets. And they asked whether two small proteins folded correctly from scratch, one helical and one sheet-based. Force fields have clearly improved with each generation. The newest versions, while imperfect, describe many structural and dynamical properties of proteins accurately, a verdict modelers can build on.
europmc-pmc3291999:
Pópulo, Lopes, and Soares reviewed a cell growth control system called mTOR and its role in cancer in 2012. The system sits at the center of signals that tell cells when to grow, divide, and survive. It works in two distinct protein complexes, one that responds to food, energy, and growth signals, and one that helps organize the cell's inner skeleton.

Many cancers carry faults in this system or in the pathways feeding into it, and the authors note especially strong effects in melanoma. Because of that, drugs that block mTOR have entered trials for many tumor types. Two related drugs had recently won approval for kidney cancer and certain other tumors, and the review also covers newer drugs that block the system in other ways.
europmc-pmc3320399:
Brug and colleagues surveyed how people in the Netherlands perceived the SARS threat during the 2003 outbreak, reporting in 2004. The Netherlands never recorded a case, yet the disease dominated news coverage for months. Public health officials wanted to know whether people in an untouched country would panic, take needless precautions, or tune out entirely.

An internet panel of several hundred adults answered questions about their knowledge of SARS, how risky it felt, what precautions they took, and where they got their information. Awareness of the outbreak was high, but worry stayed modest and people took few unnecessary actions. The authors draw lessons for future outbreaks, stressing that clear information through trusted channels keeps risk perception realistic even when an epidemic is far away.
europmc-pmc3375299:
Nazzi and colleagues traced in 2012 how a parasitic mite can help a virus destroy honeybee colonies. Colony losses threaten bees and, through pollination, world crop production. The team combined colony-level tracking with molecular tests on bees infested by the mite Varroa destructor.

The mite, they show, unsettles the bees' hold on deformed wing virus, turning a quiet, hidden infection into a fast-growing killer late in the season. That shift came with a shutdown of the immune factor NF-kB, a hub for many stress responses. Because different stresses converge on the same hub, the model may explain losses with many triggers.

freeman-jamesons-1899:
Freeman tried comedy in The Jamesons, issued in 1899 with pictures. Chapter one, They Arrive, stresses that the village had never taken boarders before. No rich family lived there, yet folk were proud to keep their homes shut to strangers.

That proud custom breaks when the Jamesons, among the best-off locals, take in paying guests. The new family then sets out to improve the village to city tastes. A village narrator watches their schemes fail with dry delight. Yankee common sense quietly beats city airs, and the satire lands sharp though the tone stays lighter than Freeman's usual work.
frus-1861-d199:
Cassius Clay wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 21 June 1861. The dispatch is document 199 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The printed order sets Clay's June report after Seward's July letter. By date, Clay wrote first, from a Russia bright with goodwill. His page adds a northern light to a file elsewhere full of doubt and care. Northern light was rare that summer, which makes Clay's June page shine in the file. Northern light in a dark summer was a thing the cabinet learned to prize. Northern light was rare and prized that summer.
frus-1861-d299:
Another report crossed the ocean to Seward, this one from Mr. Crosby on 1 June 1861. It stands as Document 299 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. The letter comes from the opening months of the Civil War, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1861-d99:
On 16 October 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Lord Lyons, the British minister at the capital. The letter is document 99 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The Lyons file swells in October, as trade and blockade claims piled up. Seward's mid month note keeps the tone even and the terms precise. Formal care in such letters was not mere style; it was how two governments avoided a second war. Each precise term in such notes could later be quoted back as a pledge. Quoted back as pledges, such terms bound the men who had penned them.
frus-1862-d199:
Secretary of State William H. Seward sent Lord Lyons a note on 7 January 1862, printed as Document 199 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Lyons, the British minister in Washington, was Seward's daily counterpart for British business in the capital.

The first week of January saw the Trent affair close, with the seized envoys freed and sailing for Europe. Both governments wanted the quarrel buried. Seward's notes to Lyons in this period, this one among them. Belong to the repair work that followed, when each side tested how normal dealings might resume. Both offices kept up the formal courtesies even when their governments were near quarreling.
frus-1862-d299:
On 4 August 1862 William L. Dayton sent another report to Secretary of State William H. Seward, printed as Document 299 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It was one of two Dayton reports under that date.

Two reports in one mail let Dayton separate audiences and subjects. A habit that suited Paris, where court talk and ministry business ran on different tracks. Early August found France urging Britain toward joint action on the war. Dayton's paired letters that week are part of the evidence for how that push looked from inside the French capital. Paris and London consulted each other often before either acted on the American war.
frus-1862-d399:
On 23 January 1862, nine days after his last instruction to the same post, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Horace J. Perry in Madrid. The dispatch is Document 399 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record sent to Congress.

Madrid mattered to the Union because Spain ruled Cuba and Puerto Rico and had joined the armed move into Mexico. Seward's steady stream of orders kept the Madrid legation pressing Spain to stay neutral and to keep Confederate agents at arm's length. Single letters look small, but together they formed the daily pressure that kept Spain out of the American war.
frus-1862-d499:
On 9 May 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to James Shepherd Pike at The Hague. The instruction is Document 499 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the President's annual message.

May 1862 found McClellan creeping toward Richmond and the Union's stock high in Europe. Seward's orders in that season pressed ministers to convert goodwill into firm neutrality rulings and public statements. The Dutch file shows the routine side of that work: no crisis, just steady pressure and exact reporting. An instruction to a small post in a quiet month may look minor. Yet the sum of such letters was the Union's European policy in daily practice.
frus-1862-d599:
Spain's minister of state sent this circular on 20 December 1861 to the Spanish ambassador in Paris and the Spanish minister in London. It is Document 599 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, among the appended Spanish papers.

The writers and readers here are all Spanish. Madrid was briefing its own envoys at the two allied capitals. The subject was the Mexican expedition then under way. Such a circular fixed the line those envoys were to take with the French and British governments. For American readers of the printed volume, it was evidence of how the three allies coordinated, and of where their aims already differed. The document is Spanish statecraft in its own words, preserved in an American record.

frus-1863p1-d199:

It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

In 1863 the great question in London was whether Britain would treat the Confederacy as a real nation. Adams's reports helped Washington judge that risk week by week. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d299:

Seward wrote in a firm tone but had to avoid pushing Britain into the war on the Southern side. His instructions walked that line again and again. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.

frus-1863p1-d499:

It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. The day-to-day work was unglamorous: answering complaints, passing on claims, and keeping track of ships, prisoners, and papers. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.

At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral.

Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.

frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d199:
Acting Secretary of State Edward Stettinius sent President Roosevelt a memorandum on 8 November 1943 summing up oil concessions in the Middle East. Roosevelt had asked for the two-page brief at their Friday meeting, saying he wanted the whole picture with him before the coming conferences.

The enclosure maps who owned what. Four big firms each held 23.75 percent of the Iraq Petroleum Company, with Gulbenkian keeping five percent. Anglo-Iranian ran Iran's fields and the Abadan refinery, American firms held Bahrain and the vast Saudi fields, and Kuwait's proved reserves sat idle. It closes with open questions: where to build new refineries, and whether Washington should buy shares in the firms or options on oil in the ground.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d299:
Memoranda by the Chinese government, submitted at Cairo on 24 November 1943, set out China's design for the postwar order. The papers cover a four-power council, security during the transition after the war, European questions, and Far East machinery.

Pending a full Council of the United Nations, the four Moscow powers should form a Four-Power Council at once. It would have a standing committee in Washington. Its charge would be building the larger body, in which the Big Four would act as a presidium. An inter-Allied military commission would handle security, backed by international naval and air bases at agreed points. China also asks to be told of all European discussions, to share in decisions on Germany's surrender, and to build a Far Eastern Committee and a unified Far East command.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d399:
The Iranian Ministry of Foreign Affairs sent the American Legation in Iran an aide-mémoire at Tehran on 1 December 1943, while the three Allied leaders met in the capital. Written in formal, grateful language, it sets out what Iran hopes to gain from hosting the conference.

Iran, the note says, has cooperated fully under the Tripartite Pact, declared war on Germany, and borne economic hardship beyond her power in the Allied cause. In return she expects two things from the Allies. They should weigh the troubles and damage the war has inflicted on her. And they should make a special effort to hand back the vital threads of the country's affairs now in their hands, leaving security to Iran's own forces. The written promises of Iran's integrity and full independence, it urges, should be strengthened by moral and material help in every field.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d499:
The Combined Chiefs of Staff presented this formal report to President Roosevelt and Prime Minister Churchill on December 6, 1943, closing the military work of the Second Cairo Conference. It gathered the chiefs' joint conclusions for the two leaders' approval. The State Department printed it in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

A final report of this kind is the summit's military bottom line: the strategy both staffs could jointly recommend after weeks of argument at Tehran and Cairo. Roosevelt and Churchill governed the war through papers like this one. For readers, it is one of the key documents of the conference, stating where the alliance agreed to strike, and in what order, in the decisive year ahead.
