It is kept in the Foreign Relations series, in the thick of the pre-summit traffic.
frus-1944-quebec-d199: An editors' note records that no account survives of the discussion at this luncheon meeting either. The time of the lunch and the names of its participants come from the President's Log. The Log's evidence is confirmed by Sir Alexander Cadogan's diary, cited by page. Beyond attendance and timing, the conversation at this table left no trace in the records the editors could find.
frus-1944-quebec-d299: Roosevelt and Churchill both put their initials to this aide-mémoire, dated 19 September 1944, days after their Quebec meetings ended. An aide-mémoire is a short written summary left behind to fix what was agreed. Filed as document 299 in the Foreign Relations volume on the conference, it carries unusual weight because both leaders personally marked the text as accepted.
frus-1944-quebec-d99:
Ambassador Winant wrote to Secretary Hull on August 25, 1944. John Gilbert Winant served as America's ambassador in London. The State Department printed his message in the Quebec 1944 volume. Paris was liberated on the day he wrote.

An ambassador's reports gave Washington the view from the allied capital. Winant enjoyed unusual trust among British leaders. His letters carried both facts and a sense of British feeling. For readers, the message shows London speaking into summit preparation. The Quebec Conference opened less than three weeks later. Reports like Winant's helped shape the American brief.
frus-1945-50-intel-d199:
A memorandum from the Director of Central Intelligence (Vandenberg) reached the National Intelligence Authority on 30 July 1946. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 199 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. At the time, a new National Intelligence Authority oversaw central intelligence, and the Central Intelligence Group did its daily work.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d299:
On 19 August 1948, staff wrote up the discussion at the 18th Meeting of the National Security Council for the President. It is document 299 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. An outside survey team led by Allen Dulles was then reviewing the CIA, and its findings would drive a round of reform debate.

After key talks, an aide would write up what was said for the file. The result is close to the room itself. Later memos cite such notes the way lawyers cite a witness: as the best proof of words once spoken. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d399:
Willis Machle, the CIA's assistant director for scientific intelligence, wrote to Director Roscoe Hillenkoetter on 29 September 1949. The memo is document 399 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Scientific intelligence tracked foreign advances in weapons, above all the atomic bomb. The Soviet Union had tested its first bomb just weeks before, in late August 1949. Machle's office had to judge what the test meant and how fast the Soviets would move. His memo puts that tense moment in front of the agency's director. His memo came at a moment when each fresh fact about Soviet arms could shift budgets and plans.
frus-1945-50-intel-d99:
Magruder wrote to McCloy once more on 15 November 1945. Three Magruder letters to the same patron within seven weeks trace the SSU's autumn in miniature. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

November found the unit still alive, still funded, and still unsure of its place in the coming central system. Magruder's steady letters were part of why: no crisis found the War Department uninformed or the unit undefended. Readers closing the SSU thread for 1945 can see the method plainly. Survival, for a leftover agency, is a correspondence conducted on time, every time, with the right man reading it.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d199:
Leave some heavy weapons behind: that is Churchill's parting idea in this excerpt of 27 November 1944. His message number 834 to Roosevelt is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It closes, for the moment, the argument over arming France.

Churchill agrees the point has not yet come, and that the allies should gather a good many arms from the Germans. Still, he presses one practical thought. When the American divisions start for home, there would be a strong case for their leaving part of their heavy weapons and equipment behind. The French could then take over the job in western Germany with tools already on the ground.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d299:
A morning walk is all that survives of this Malta meeting, as the editorial note in the volume frankly states. No record of the substance of the talk has been found, the editors write. What follows is gathered from Stettinius's own account, at pages 60, 62, and 63 of his book.

Stettinius and Eden were both quartered aboard H. M. S. Sirius in Grand Harbor during the Malta days. In the early part of the morning they went ashore together and took a walk. In its course, it seems, they “discussed some of the problems to be raised at Yalta.” Nothing more is known. The note preserves the outline of a conversation between the two foreign ministers on the eve of the great conference, and no more than the outline.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d399:
America answered Molotov on Poland in a formal proposal of February 8, 1945. On frontiers, Washington raised no objection to the Soviet first point. Poland's eastern boundary would follow the Curzon line, with changes in Poland's favor of five to eight kilometers in some areas. On payment for that loss, the paper agrees in part.

Poland should gain at Germany's expense: East Prussia south of the Koenigsberg line, Upper Silesia, and land up to the Oder. But the paper sees little justification for pushing Poland's western boundary to the Western Neisse River. Here the Oder-Neisse dispute, which ran for decades, enters the record in careful language.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d499:
Stalin agreed at once, in this letter to Roosevelt of February 11, 1945, given here in translation. He had received the President's letter of February 10. Soviet votes would rise to three once Ukraine and White Russia joined the Assembly. Stalin entirely agreed: the number of votes for the United States should also be increased.

The American total might rise to three, he wrote, as in the Soviet case with its two basic republics. If necessary, he was prepared to support the proposal officially. With sincere respects, the letter closes. In the event, the United States never took the extra votes. The exchange survives as a measure of how far Stalin would go, that week, to keep Roosevelt content.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d99:
Three stopgap plans for the peace are summed up side by side in this paper from the Division of International Security and Organization. It is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Each plan tries to fill the gap before a world body can start work.

Senator Vandenberg proposed an allied treaty to keep Germany and Japan disarmed for good, with instant power for the President to act. Senator Connally proposed an interim United Nations council of eleven states, to advise on disputes until the Charter took force. The third plan, an Emergency High Commission for Liberated Europe, would seat the three allies and France. It would help freed and former satellite states build popular, stable rule and meet urgent needs.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d199:
Edwin Pauley pressed for reparations to rank high on the agenda in a telegram extract dated July 7, 1945. The extract is document 199 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Pauley, the American member of the reparations commission in Moscow, sent the message to Secretary Byrnes as he traveled to Berlin.

Pauley considers it most important, he writes, that the conference agenda provide for the reparations matters deadlocked in Moscow. He adds the question of including France in the reparations commission. These are questions of high policy that must be determined, he argues, and he asks Byrnes to see that they are given a high place on the agenda. The full text appears later in the volume, where Pauley's dispute with the Soviet negotiator Maisky over the size of Germany's bill is set out.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d299:
General Schuyler, the American military chief on Rumania's Allied Control Commission, warned the War Department on June 28, 1945, against an early peace with Rumania. His top secret message answered British proposals for a quick treaty. Schuyler had seen the Rumanian government up close from Bucharest.

Joining peace talks with the present government, he argued, would in effect recognize it. Yet that government spoke for only a small share of Rumanians. Schuyler's warning put the military view plainly before Washington: a fast treaty could lock in a regime the United States did not trust, weeks before Potsdam.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d399:
The Ruhr's disposition is argued in a briefing book paper dated June 27, 1945. Its recommendation is plain: the United States should oppose separating the Ruhr from Germany. That bar covers internationalization, a separate Ruhr state, and annexation by one or more neighboring states alike. No route to separation is acceptable.

Proposals for the Ruhr, the discussion says, should be judged by two tests. They must serve long-range security, and they must allow the full use of the region's resources to restore European production and living standards. Security measures in turn must be effective, cheap in effort, and durable. A Germany stripped of soldiers and arsenals, it notes, could not launch a new war.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d499:
Truman bends to Churchill's difficulty in an extract of his top secret reply of July 3, 1945. He has just received the Prime Minister's message, he writes, and in view of the reasons given, he concurs with the suggestion that recognition of the new Polish government be delayed temporarily. Churchill's proposed twenty-four hour delay, though, lands on an awkward date.

That delay would mean according recognition on Independence Day. Truman therefore suggests, and hopes Churchill will concur, that recognition be postponed for forty-eight hours instead. The new time would be 7 p.m., Eastern War Time, on July 5. The brief extract shows the President trading speed for allied unity.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d599:
The United States Chiefs of Staff laid out the Pacific campaign plan in a top secret memo of June 29, 1945. It is document 599 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Its stated aim was Japan's unconditional surrender at the earliest date.

The plan works in three steps. First, forces based on Okinawa, Iwo Jima, the Marianas, and the Philippines will tighten the blockade and step up bombing. Next comes an assault on Kyushu, to destroy major enemy forces there. Last comes the decisive invasion of Japan's industrial heart through the Tokyo Plain. The chiefs also cut side operations in the Ryukyus, dropping landings on two islands for good. The men and gear saved would speed the build-up on Okinawa instead.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d699:
Ambassador Kirk relayed a British report on Soviet military moves in Rumania from Caserta on July 5, 1945. His secret wire is document 699 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The source was Air Vice Marshal Stevenson, head of the British team on Rumania's control commission.

Stevenson put Rumania's planned peacetime army at fifteen or sixteen infantry divisions plus one armored division. Russia would supply its arms and gear under a treaty then being prepared. Four pontoon bridges now crossed the Danube, and night truck movements ran south toward Constanta. That port's center had been emptied to house Russian troops, and its hotels seized for staffs. Marshal Tolbukhin's headquarters, Stevenson judged, would almost surely sit at Constanta. With reports from Hungary, Bulgaria, and Allied headquarters, he read a broad Soviet build-up in the making.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d99:
Acting Secretary of State Joseph Grew recorded a complaint from the French ambassador in a memorandum dated June 25, 1945. The extracts form document 99 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam. Ambassador Henri Bonnet came, without instructions, to warn that relations between France and the United States were drifting the wrong way.

Among his points is France's exclusion from the coming Big Three meeting. Despite all France had suffered, and her stake in the occupation of Germany and Austria, reparations, and the Far East, she had not been invited, and the snub hurt deeply at home. Grew listened, gave no assurances, and promised to pass the points to the President. The memo shows the resentment the closed Big Three system stirred among shut-out allies.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1099:
On 24 July 1945, midway through the Potsdam Conference, the Soviet team put a formal proposal on the table. It appears as Document 1099 in the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States. The talks in Germany brought Truman, Stalin, and Churchill together to set the terms of the postwar order.

Written proposals were how each side stated its terms so the others could accept, reject, or trade against them. The Soviet Union had lost more of its people in the war than any other ally. Its team pressed its case hard at Potsdam, and a paper of this kind fixes the stand Moscow took at that stage of the bargaining.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1199:
Truman wrote to Churchill on 23 July 1945, two days before the British leader's last day at the summit. The president kept up his direct exchange with the prime minister through the final Churchill week. Neither man yet knew the count's result, though both could guess.

Their letters show the British-American partnership working at the top, in the men's own hands. A note between them could clear a point faster than a day of staff talks. This one belongs to the closing days of the Churchill era at Potsdam. It is part of the last set of letters the two wartime partners exchanged as leaders.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1299:
Baruch, the American ambassador in Portugal, wrote to the Acting Secretary of State on 21 July 1945. Portugal was neutral, but its capital was a crossroads of the war's quiet traffic: trade, spies, and the Atlantic air route through the Azores.

An envoy in Lisbon reported a scene unlike any other post's. Both sides courted Portugal, and both watched it. Baruch's dispatch fed that odd picture into Washington during the summit. It is the Lisbon end of the Potsdam web. The peace was shaped by neutral ground as well as by battlefields and tables.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1399:
Jefferson Caffery, the American ambassador in France, wrote to Georges Bidault, the French foreign minister, on 1 August 1945. The volume prints six Caffery letters to Bidault from the turn of August 1945. Three letters from Caffery to Bidault bear that single date in the volume.

A third letter in a day points to business that kept generating paper: drafts answered, points clarified, positions nudged. Caffery was an old hand in the foreign service, and Bidault a resistance leader turned minister; their styles met on paper with care. For readers, the cluster of August letters shows how much of the peace was made outside the famous rooms. The Potsdam three decided the frame; men like these two fitted France into it.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-99: Standing in the run of unnumbered items after document 710, this editorial note belongs to the apparatus of the Potsdam volume. Foreign Relations editors wrote notes like this to fill small holes in the story the papers tell. The note may cite a source file or a related text in another volume. It helps readers trust the order and completeness of what surrounds it.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d799:
Schoenfeld reported again from Hungary on July 17, 1945, in document 799. The representative in Budapest sent two letters as the conference opened. This one went to the Acting Secretary of State. It joined the second Potsdam volume beside his other reports.

Two letters on opening day suggest a post with much to say. Hungary's politics moved fast under the armistice. Readers can watch Schoenfeld sorting the urgent from the routine. The document extends the volume's Hungary file at its start. It shows a mission determined to be heard while the great decisions were still open.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d899:
Members of the American reparations delegation in Moscow answered Edwin Pauley's request in this secret telegram of July 18, 1945. Pauley had asked for figures on German capital assets and output. The reply gives estimates for the Soviet zone and for land east of the Oder-Neisse line.

About 40 percent of Germany's prewar movable and fixed capital assets lay in the Russian zone, Berlin included. Movable assets east of the Oder-Neisse were worth about 6 billion Reichsmarks in 1938. That area produced about 7 percent of German industrial and mining output. The senders warn that losing this land may cut Germany's power to pay by more than the raw shares suggest.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d999:
Secretary of State James Byrnes cabled George Kennan in Moscow on July 30, 1945. The message ties back to the American note just delivered to the Soviets on German assets in Spain. It passes on a report from the military attaché in Stockholm.

A Russian delegation there has surveyed interned German planes in Sweden. The planes are to be flown out as war booty, and newspapers have aired the plan. The papers also state that neither the United States nor Britain has asked about the remaining aircraft. The cable is short, and it asks Kennan for nothing beyond noting the report.
gao-gaoreports-b-296099: Gold Cross Safety took its June 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-296699: BAE Technical Services took its October 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Defense firms get the same full hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-297099: Europe Displays took its December 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-299599: Beck's Spray Service was back at GAO in June 2007 with another contract fight, and this ruling is the call. The firm challenged the award; the ruling tests the claims. Repeat players learn the protest ropes — and GAO keeps the bouts fair every round.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-199: Disaster insurance went head-to-head across the Atlantic in 2005, and GAO's report pits the U.S. style against Europe's. The review crosses the ocean for the compare. The uninsurable deserved the study. The uninsurable deserved the study. The compare was transatlantic.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-299: The gay-troops policy's cost defied counting in 2005, and GAO's report says the financial cost and lost skills could not be computed. The review admits the unmeasurable. The discharged deserved the honest attempt. The cost could not be computed. The discharged deserved the honest attempt.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-399: Nonoxynol-9 and HIV research got a GAO check in 2005, and the report covers HHS's efforts to study and inform the public. The review reads the science. The public deserved the honest facts. The efforts were examined. The public deserved the honest facts.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-399: Alaska Native contracting needed tailored oversight in 2006, and GAO's report says the increased use of special provisions called for custom supervision. The findings demand the fit. The report warns that the unique program deserved unique watching. The oversight had to be tailored.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-799: Donor-advised funds needed sunlight in 2006, and GAO's report says collecting more data could help address concerns. The findings demand the transparency. The report warns that the charity middlemen deserved scrutiny. The data had to be collected. The middlemen deserved a look.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-99: Mercury waste rules needed clarifying in 2006, and GAO's report says EPA had to clarify which wastes could be treated and disposed. The findings demand the definitions. The report warns that the toxic metal deserved clear rules. The types had to be clarified.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-299: The TSA's staffing math was useful but flawed in 2007, and GAO's report says the allocation model helped place screeners, though its assumptions needed work. The findings grade the formula. The report asks whether the right airports got the right crews.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-399: Wall Street's disaster drills were improving in 2007 — GAO's report says the financial markets had come far, though pandemic planning lagged behind. The findings credit the progress made. The report's foresight proved eerie: the next crash might wear a surgical mask.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-699: Blood money in the war zones got a review in 2007 — GAO's report examines the Pentagon's condolence payments to Iraqi and Afghan families. The findings weigh the solatia practice. The report treads the moral math: what a life is worth when America takes it by mistake.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-99: The Forest Service's logging shortcuts got a GAO review in 2007, and the report examines the use of categorical exclusions for vegetation projects. The findings probe the practice. The report warns that the fast-tracked cutting needed a closer look. The forests deserved the scrutiny.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-399: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on VA Health Care: Additional Efforts to Better Assess Joint Ventures Needed. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-599: GAO published its findings on US Postal Service: Mail-Related Recycling Initiatives and Possible Opportunities for Improvement in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-99: This 2007 GAO report takes a hard look at tax Compliance: Qualified Intermediary Program Provides Some Assurance That Taxes on Foreign Investors Are Withheld and Reported, but Can Be Improved. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
garland-prairie-folks-1899:
Prairie Folks bears rights dates of 1892 and a Chicago imprint of F. J. Schulte from 1893. Garland opens with the same pioneer verses used in his later farm book. Settlers, he writes, face a dazzling sky, blue and clear as steel in winter.

Farmers, schoolteachers, and small-town dreamers people these Middle West tales. The tone runs gentler than the angry realism of Main-Travelled Roads. Character studies warmed by fondness replace protest here. Readers still get the full range of prairie life, from comedy to pathos. No writer knew that world better, and the 1899 gathering shows his affection at its clearest.
geneva-bible-new-testament-1599:
English exiles at Geneva printed a Bible in 1560 that became the household Bible of Protestant England. The 1599 edition of its New Testament is the text here, with the famous Geneva study notes kept in place. William Whittingham led the team of translators.

The notes in the margins explain hard verses, name the lessons for church and state, and sometimes scold kings and bishops. Readers know it as the Bible of Shakespeare, Milton, and Bunyan, and the one the Pilgrims carried to America. Its plain, direct English shaped the language of faith for a century. The King James version later took its place but kept much of its wording.
harsnett-discovery-fraudulent-practises-:
Samuel Harsnett opened England's possession controversy with his Discovery of the Fraudulent Practises of John Darrell in 1599. Darrell, a Puritan minister, had made his name casting out devils. Harsnett denounces the famous dispossessions as outright counterfeit, staged by Darrell and coached into his patients.

He reconstructs how fits were rehearsed and symptoms suggested. The attack aims to disgrace Puritan exorcism and to defend the established church's ban on it. Darrell's party answered in print the next year. The pamphlet war that followed filled shelves. This Discovery is its opening shot, and it still reads like a prosecution speech.
hastings-dictionary-bible-vol2-1899:
Volume Two of Hastings's Dictionary of the Bible appeared in 1899, covering entries from Feign to Kinsman. James Hastings kept his team of scholars to a high, even standard. The dictionary was meant to serve study, preaching, and teaching alike.

Articles explain hard words, trace customs, and set out the theology of the Old and New Testaments. Archaeology, then a young science, adds fresh finds from Egypt and Palestine. The tone stays reverent but honest about hard questions. For a generation, this was the first place English readers turned when a Bible name or place puzzled them.
hertz-principles-of-mechanics-1899:
Heinrich Hertz's Principles of Mechanics Presented in a New Form appeared in English in 1899, translated by D E Jones and J T Walley. Hertz wrote the work in German near the end of his short life; it appeared after his death in 1894. It was his last book and his boldest.

Hertz tried to rebuild mechanics without the concept of force, which he found murky. In its place he put masses linked by rigid connections, some of them hidden, moving by the straightest paths. The scheme influenced Wittgenstein's picture theory of language and later philosophy of science. The book is hard, strange, and admired: a great experimenter's attempt to make physics rest on images the mind can fully grasp.
history-japanese-literature-aston-1899:
W. G. Aston wrote A History of Japanese Literature in 1899, the first such history in English. Aston, translator of the Nihongi chronicles, knew the sources at first hand from years in Japan. His survey runs from the oldest songs and chronicles through the great age of the novel and drama to his own century.

Poetry, prose, theater, and popular fiction each get their place in the long arc. Aston writes with a diplomat's clarity and a scholar's love for his subject. Later histories have added much, but his remains the foundation, the first map of a whole literature for Western readers.
holmes-auriferous-gravel-man-1899:
William Henry Holmes, a geologist with the United States survey, took up the California gold gravel claims in 1899. Men had claimed stone tools and a skull from deep gold beds as proof of old man in the west. Holmes had dug in those fields and knew the ground well.

He goes through the famed finds one by one, the Calaveras skull first of all. Each, he shows, is a hoax, a plant, or a late thing sunk in old beds by chance. His paper shut the case for deep age man in the gold state for good.
inge-christian-mysticism-1899:
William Ralph Inge, later famous as the gloomy Dean of Saint Paul's in London, gave the Bampton Lectures printed in 1899 as Christian Mysticism. The lectures survey the mystical tradition from the church fathers to the moderns. Inge writes as a scholar who also practiced the life he describes.

He traces Plotinus's influence on Christian prayer, the medieval mystics, and the quiet teachers of the inner way. Inge defends mysticism as the vital core of religion rather than a fringe oddity for specialists. The book made his name and remains a landmark history of Christian mysticism in English.
ireland-bewitching-relation-1699:
Ireland left few witchcraft prints, which makes Daniel Higgs's 1699 relation the more prized. The Wonderfull and True Relation tells of a young girl in Ireland said to be bewitched. It even prints a receipt, or cure, meant to free her from the spell.

Accusation and remedy sit side by side in the text, charge first and folk cure after. Readers see both the fear a strange illness raised and the means a household used against it. Irish cases rarely reached print at all in this period. The small pamphlet thus holds an outsized place in the record.
jackson-zoroaster-1899:
Abraham Valentine Williams Jackson, a Columbia professor, gave the lectures printed in 1899 as Zoroaster, the Prophet of Ancient Iran. Jackson had traveled in Persia and India to study the faith at its sources. The book helped found Iranian studies in America.

He rebuilds the prophet's life from the hymns of the Avesta, the scriptures that bear Zoroaster's name, and from Greek reports. The lectures weigh legend against history with a scholar's care and a traveler's eye. For English readers, Jackson's life of Zoroaster long stood as the classic account of the prophet. He writes for students, but his book reached travelers and teachers far beyond Columbia.
james-talks-to-teachers-1899:
Talks to Teachers, published in 1899, gathers James's lectures to teachers on psychology, joined with addresses to students on some of life's ideals. James had lectured to teachers for years and wrote down his counsel with a practitioner's warmth.

He warns teachers against turning psychology into rigid rules, and urges attention to habit, interest, and the child's own native impulses. The student addresses praise ideals like tolerance and the strenuous mood, life lived with effort and faith. The book shaped American teaching talk for a generation. Its humanity, more than its science, has kept it in print.
jenner-further-observations-variolae-179:
One year after his first Inquiry, Edward Jenner issued Further Observations on the Variolae Vaccinae in 1799. The London sequel adds fresh cases of cowpox vaccination to the record. Early critics had raised doubts and reported failures. Jenner answers them point by point with new evidence.

He sorts true cowpox from other sores that could mislead a doctor. Careful rules for taking and using the matter run through the pages. The aim was to make the new practice safe in other hands. Together with the Inquiry, the sequel built trust in vaccination. Readers see a claim being tested in public. The tone stays modest and exact.
jewett-queens-twin-1899:
Houghton Mifflin issued The Queen's Twin and Other Stories at Boston in 1899. Jewett dedicated the book to Susan Burley Cabot. Contents list A Dunnet Shepherdess, Martha's Lady, and The Night Before Thanksgiving beside the title tale.

The title story concerns a Maine woman sure she is Queen Victoria's twin, born in the same hour. Her whole village kindly humors the fond belief. Other tales treat aging, loneliness, and the odd dignity of country folk. The opening pages note how Maine's busy fleet once bound its coast to foreign shores. The book reads as a late, mellow harvest from a fond observer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-middleman-judah:
Judah Middleman was an English rabbi of the first half of the nineteenth century, remembered for one unfinished book. Joseph Jacobs and Israel Cohen give him a short entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He wrote in Hebrew, answering a Christian critic of the Talmud, and reached English readers the same year through a translator.

His Netibot Emet defended the traditions of the Talmud against Alexander McCaul's Old Paths, a well-known attack of the day. Only the first part ever appeared, published in 1847 as Paths of Truth in M. H. Breslau's English version. The bibliography points to Jacobs and Wolf's Bibliotheca Anglo-Judaica for what little more is recorded of him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moabite-stone-1:
The Moabite Stone is the only surviving inscribed monument of ancient Moab, and Joseph Jacobs and J. Frederic McCurdy tell its dramatic rescue in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Found at Dhiban in 1868 — a black basalt slab three and a half feet long — it was smashed by local Arabs who feared losing their talisman. A squeeze taken beforehand saved the text.

Clermont-Ganneau recovered most fragments and pieced the stone together; it stands in the Louvre beside the squeeze. The inscription runs thirty-four lines in old Hebrew characters, cut about 860 B.C. for Mesha, king of Moab, who boasts that Chemosh delivered him from all his attackers. The article prints a translation of its first two-thirds — a king's own voice from Israel's world.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mordecai-ben-ju:
Mordecai ben Judah Aryeh Löb Ashkenazi was a Dutch ritualist of Amsterdam in the early seventeenth century, noticed by Joseph Jacobs and S. J. Levinson in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was a disciple of the cabalist Abraham Rovigo, and his service to his master was editorial: he arranged and corrected Rovigo's commentary on the Zohar, the Eshel Abraham.

The commentary was printed with the text at Fürth in 1701, his preface to it a year earlier. His own book is humbler and more practical: Miḳweh Yisrael, a treatise on circumcision in Judæo-German, published in 1710 with David of Lida's Sod Adonai appended. Between the Zohar and a circumciser's handbook, his short bibliography maps the two poles of his world.

kropotkin-memoirs-revolutionist-1899:
Peter Kropotkin published Memoirs of a Revolutionist in 1899, first in English in a leading American magazine. The memoir tells how a Russian prince and army officer became the leading theorist of anarchism. Kropotkin wrote it in exile, looking back over a dramatic life.

He recalled boyhood at the Tsar's court, geographic work in Siberia, and the slow turn against the state he served. Prison in Russia, a daring escape, and years among European socialists followed. The book mixes adventure with the growth of an idea, anarchist communism, in one man's mind. It remains a classic of radical autobiography, valued for its candor and its picture of nineteenth-century Russia.
leadbeater-clairvoyance-1899:
C. W. Leadbeater taught fans how hid sight works in Clairvoyance, his hand book of 1899. Leadbeater claimed he could see the glow round folk, past lives, and far places at will. He sorts sight by kind: sight of the near glow, sight through space, and sight through time and past ages.

Drills and warns fill the last parts of the guide. He tells the pupil to test each sight with care and calm. Groups took the book as their chief text on the theme. Its scheme still shapes how the occult talks of sight.
leland-aradia-1899:
Charles Godfrey Leland put out Aradia in 1899. He said a Tuscan witch named Maddalena gave him the core of the text. The book claims to be the gospel of the witches of Italy. Diana, the moon queen, stands at its heart.

Spells, chants, and tales tell how Diana sent her child Aradia to Earth. Aradia was to teach witch craft to the poor and help them fight the rich. Some doubt how much of the text is old lore. The book still lit the spark of the new witch faith of our day.
leo-astrology-for-all-1899:
Alan Leo made star lore a trade and a craze in Britain. His Astrology for All came out in 1899. Leo wrote for the plain reader, not the math adept. He ran a press that sold charts and books by post to all.

The book teaches the signs, planets, and houses in short, clear steps. A reader can cast a rough chart and read its main traits at home. Leo drops much of the old doom talk for a bright, keen tone. The book marks the birth of the new, mass star lore of our age.
marx-value-price-profit-aveling-1899:
Marx addressed the General Council of the International in 1865, and the speech became Value, Price and Profit. His daughter Eleanor Marx Aveling edited the first English edition in 1899. Fellow council members had claimed that wage rises were useless. Marx answers them with his full theory of value in brief.

He explains surplus value, the source of profit in his system, with plain examples. Wages, prices, and profit fall into one connected account. He closes on the limits of trade union struggle under capitalism. Many readers find this his clearest short statement of his economics. It bridges his lectures and the vast Capital. The speech form keeps it lively.
memoirs-of-the-court-of-st-cloud-being-s: This final St. Cloud volume closes the long secret correspondence. The glittering imperial court fades as disaster looms near. The last letters carry a clear note of doom. The sad end of Napoleon's glittering world.
mungo-park-travels-interior-districts-af:

Park crossed from the Gambia toward Segu, was robbed and held prisoner by a Moorish chief, escaped, and at last saw the Niger flowing east. Fever and hardship cut the journey short before he could follow the river to its end. His plain, brave telling made the book a classic of exploration. Each chapter takes a leading remedy and gives its strongest signs in plain, lively words. Nash compares near neighbors side by side, so a reader can spot the small point that decides a case. The handbook was likely the most used of its kind in its era, carried in many a doctor's bag.

Edward William Nelson, a naturalist with the Signal Corps, spent years near Bering Strait in Alaska, and his great report came out in 1899. Frank Norris published McTeague in 1899, after years of study in Paris and at Harvard. Norris set the novel on Polk Street in San Francisco, where he watched the city's dentists, saloons, and rooming houses. He worked in the naturalist manner of Zola, treating character as a product of heredity and habit.

The story ends in Death Valley, with murder and handcuffs in the sand. Critics rank McTeague as the masterpiece of American naturalism, and its force has not faded.

The Malolos Congress adopted the first Philippine constitution in January 1899, founding the First Philippine Republic. Filipino revolutionaries had thrown off Spanish rule and proclaimed independence at Kawit the summer before. plos-pbio-0020199:
Edward J. Vowles and William Amos looked for a hidden pattern around human microsatellites in PLOS Biology in 2004. Microsatellites are short DNA stretches repeated many times, and they mutate fast. The authors found signs that distant species have independently evolved similar repeats in similar places, a pattern called convergent evolution.

If repeats arise again and again at the same spots, some force must favor them or favor the conditions that create them. That challenges the view of microsatellites as pure junk DNA. They are used widely as markers in genetics and forensics. Knowing they can converge keeps researchers from misreading shared repeats as proof of shared ancestry.
plos-pbio-0020399:
P. J. Hastings, Andrew Slack, Joseph F. Petrosino, and their team tested how bacteria adapt under stress in PLOS Biology in 2004. When starved, bacteria were said to boost helpful mutations. Two routes were proposed: copying a useful gene many times, called amplification, and raising the point mutation rate.

The authors found the two routes work apart from each other, not as one program. Stress can bring out both, but each has its own machinery. Sorting that out cooled a heated debate about whether mutations can be directed. The careful answer is no shortcut: bacteria gain variation by separate, blind means, and selection still does the choosing.
plos-pone-0000099:
Heather M. Scobie and John A. T. Young tested a detail of anthrax in PLOS ONE in 2006. Anthrax toxins enter cells through a docking protein on the cell surface, called anthrax toxin receptor 2. One spot on that receptor, residue T118, grips the metal ions that help the toxin's protective antigen bind.

The natural guess was that this grip is essential for toxin entry. The team found it is not: binding and entry still worked without it. Negative results of this precision save other labs from dead ends. They also refine the map of the toxin-receptor contact, the very surface that anthrax drug and vaccine design aims to block.
plos-pone-0000199:
Kundan Sengupta, Madhvi B. Upender, Linda Barenboim-Stapleton, and colleagues published this cancer cell study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Extra or missing chromosomes, aneuploidy, are a hallmark of carcinomas; in colon cancer, an extra copy of chromosome 7 appears early and persists. The authors introduced aneuploid chromosomes artificially into colon cancer cells.

The introduced chromosomes, they report, take up a conserved position inside the cell nucleus. Where a chromosome sits in the nucleus can affect which genes it can switch on. The result suggests the nucleus organizes even abnormal chromosome sets by rules, a clue to how cancer cells live with their scrambled genomes.
plos-pone-0000299:
Xue Han and Edward S. Boyden published this neuroscience methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It presents tools for optical control of neurons with multiple colors of light. Different wavelengths can activate, silence, or desynchronize neural activity, with timing precise to a single spike. Light-sensitive proteins inserted into neurons make that control possible.

Controlling neurons with light, the field of optogenetics, was just emerging. Adding colors lets researchers switch different cell groups independently in the same brain. This paper helped expand that toolkit, which went on to transform the study of brain circuits.
plos-pone-0000399:
Marcos R.H. Estécio and colleagues measured a chemical mark on DNA across cancers, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The mark is methylation, and in a repeated DNA element called LINE-1, cancer cells often carry too little of it, a state called hypomethylation. The team also measured microsatellite instability, a sign that a tumor's DNA repair is faulty.

The authors report that LINE-1 hypomethylation varies widely between cancers. It also runs opposite to microsatellite instability. Tumors high in one tend to be low in the other. That pattern suggests two distinct routes by which tumors scramble their genomes. Sorting cancers by route could help predict their behavior and response to treatment.
plos-pone-0000499:
Eva Vojtech, Lindsay A. Turnbull, and Andy Hector tested a simple predictor of plant competition outcomes, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. When grasses grow in monocultures, species differ in how much light their leaves intercept. The team asked whether those differences predict short-term competitive outcomes when species grow together under productive conditions.

If the winner can be predicted from a single plant's light capture, competition models get simpler and stronger. Light is the currency grasslands run on, so interception is a natural candidate predictor. Field tests like this discipline ecological theory, which often multiplies factors faster than experiments can check them.
plos-pone-0000599:
Michael Eddleston and colleagues compared two killers in rural Sri Lanka and found poisoning ahead, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The study assessed the importance of poisoning versus road traffic injuries as a cause of death in rural Sri Lanka. Pesticide self-poisoning is a leading cause of death in rural Asia.

Where poisoning outranks crashes, prevention priorities differ sharply from Western patterns: restricting access to the most toxic pesticides saves more lives than road campaigns. Eddleston's group built much of the evidence for pesticide regulation in Sri Lanka, where bans on the worst compounds later cut deaths dramatically. Local cause-of-death counts are what make such policy arguable.
plos-pone-0000699:
Dejan Vučinić and Terrence J. Sejnowski built a compact imaging system for watching fast brain activity in three dimensions. Their 2007 PLOS ONE article describes a multiphoton microscope designed for that job. At its heart sits a femtosecond laser made from Yb:KYW crystal, which they designed for use with acousto-optic deflection. Sound-driven deflectors steer the beam without moving mirrors.

Two-axis deflection lets the system scan a volume quickly, which fast neuronal events demand. Compact and simple were design goals, not afterthoughts. Neuroscientists often need custom rigs to record many cells at once in living tissue. A smaller, simpler system lowers the barrier for labs wanting 3D recordings of brain activity.
plos-pone-0000799:
André M. Comeau, Françoise Tétart, Sabrina N. Trojet and colleagues found that antibiotics can feed the viruses that kill bacteria, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Bacteriophages, viruses of bacteria, shape the biosphere hugely, yet comparatively little was known about how the external environment affects phage production. The team reports that sub-lethal concentrations of certain antibiotics can substantially stimulate phage growth.

Beta-lactam and quinolone antibiotics are named in the title, and the effect is called phage-antibiotic synergy. Stressed bacteria apparently become better phage factories. The synergy suggests pairing phages with antibiotics in therapy, where the drug boosts the phage precisely when bacteria are weakened. It also warns that antibiotic pollution may stir phage ecology.
plos-pone-0000899:
Laurent Gillet, Janet May and Philip Stevenson tested whether vaccinating virus carriers could sharpen their antibodies, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Herpesviruses stay in the body for life. Carriers still spread the virus even though they make antibodies against it, so those antibodies are clearly not the best they could be.

The team used a mouse gammaherpesvirus to ask whether a later vaccine dose improves neutralization, the ability of antibodies to block the virus. The question reaches beyond one virus. If carriers can be helped to neutralize better, infection control gains a new lever. The study frames that hope as a testable claim.
plos-pone-0000999:
Erik Postma questioned whether evolution papers earn inflated impact scores outside their own field, in a solo PLOS ONE article from 2007. Impact factors are used to judge journal quality, yet fields differ sharply in how much they cite. A paper's score may say more about its neighborhood than its worth.

Postma tests one specific suspicion: that evolutionary biology papers placed in general journals gain an extra lift. Fair comparisons should stay inside a field, in theory. His analysis checks whether even that fix holds. The paper is a measurement of measurement itself, aimed at how hiring and funding panels read scores.
plos-pone-0001099:
Kristin Scott, Caroline White and Huntington Willard studied a barrier that fences off silent DNA at a yeast centromere, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Heterochromatin is the packed, silent form of DNA. It forms by nucleation and spreading along the fiber, and barrier elements stop that spread so silencing stays in its place.

At fission yeast centromere one, the team examine a barrier that depends on RNA polymerase III, one of the cell's gene reading machines. A barrier made from active transcription machinery is an elegant fence: the reader itself blocks the silencer. Centromeres need their silent zones fenced precisely, or chromosome handling suffers.
plos-pone-0001199:
Genes are often switched on by several transcription factors acting together. Their cooperation is limited by physical constraints, such as how far apart their binding sites can be. Ryan Shultzaberger and colleagues used DNA sequence analysis to work out those constraints, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They studied transcriptional initiation complexes, the assemblies that start a gene being read.

By determining the structural rules, the authors aim to understand what defines functional cooperativity between factors. The logic runs both ways: known constraints also help predict which DNA sequences will work. The paper treats gene control as an engineering problem with measurable tolerances.
plos-pone-0001299:
Forests drop leaves and twigs constantly, and that litter feeds the soil's release of carbon dioxide. Emma Sayer, Jennifer Powers, and Edmund Tanner tested what happens when litter input rises. Such a rise is expected under higher atmospheric CO2 and shifting rainfall. Their report appeared in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Litterfall is a major flux of carbon from vegetation to soil.

The authors report that increased litterfall in tropical forests boosts the transfer of soil CO2 to the atmosphere. More litter does not simply lock carbon away; it speeds the soil's own breathing. That feedback matters for predicting how forests respond to climate change.
plos-pone-0001399:
Lin Yang and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on flu tracking in Hong Kong. Clinic rates for flu like illness are a common gauge of flu spread in a city. But many other germs cause like signs, so the gauge can mislead. Flu acts in unlike ways in the tropics too. The team checked how well clinic and lab data line up.

They compared the timing of clinic visits with lab proof of flu over the same span. Close sync would mean the cheap clinic gauge can be trusted. Gaps would mean lab checks must play a larger role. The results help health teams read flu seasons with more care.
plos-pone-0001499:
Xiao-Jian Sun and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study that maps a family of gene tag enzymes in zebrafish. These enzymes place most of the methyl tags on DNA wrapping proteins. Some are vital for embryo growth. The team set out to list the full family in fish and track when each member acts.

Their genome wide survey named the fish set and charted its use as embryos grow. Peaks at set stages hint at which members drive each growth step. A full roster is the base for knock out tests to come. It also lets labs compare fish and human tag systems side by side.
plos-pone-0001599:
Newton Opiyo and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on newborn resuscitation training in a Kenya hospital. Birth suffocation kills up to 1.6 million newborns a year, near all in poor lands. Sound revival at birth can cut that toll, but staff training in such lands is often stale. The team tested fresh training at Pumwani Hospital.

They weighed how staff acts changed after the training course. Gains in sound steps at birth would show the course works in real wards. Cheap training that sticks is one of the best buys in child health. The study gives managers proof for rolling it out more widely.
plos-pone-0001699:
Ilja G. Sligte, H. Steven Scholte, and Victor A. F. Lamme asked whether the mind keeps more than one visual memory store, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Visual short-term memory holds a few items for later report, and classic work says that store is small. Yet when people are cued during the delay to shift attention to one stored item, the store looks much larger.

That contrast hints at two stores: a small, sturdy one and a larger, fragile one. The full text gives the memory tasks, the cueing tests, and how performance split between the two patterns. The answer shapes how psychologists model attention and awareness, since a fragile store may hold sights we can use but cannot easily report.
plos-pone-0001799:
Jian-Ming Deng, Tao Li, Gen-Xuan Wang, and their co-authors examined scaling rules for plants in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The energetic equivalence rule, built from metabolic theory and the self-thinning rule, is treated as one of nature's fundamental laws. It predicts how metabolic rate scales with body mass and population density. Yet evidence was mounting that these scaling relationships break down in places.

The team studied trade-offs between metabolic rate and population density of plants. The full text gives the plant data and where the rule holds or fails. Scaling laws guide predictions of how forests store carbon and respond to crowding, so knowing their limits changes real forecasts.
plos-pone-0001899:
Birte Forstmann and colleagues scanned brains to see how free choice changes decisions, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Picking our own path feels like control, yet at times people would rather let others choose for them. The team wanted to see which brain areas switch on when a choice is truly ours, and which switch on when it is handed over.

Using brain scans, they compared trials where people chose for themselves with trials where the choice was made for them. The setting and the sense of agency, not just the act, shifted brain activity. The work helps explain why the same task can feel like a chance or a burden.
plos-pone-0001999:
Erika Schlaepfer and Roberto Speck studied how tripping a virus alarm turns immune cells against HIV, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The alarm, TLR7/8, senses single-stranded viral RNA. The pair had found that setting it off, by viral RNA or by lab-made drugs, changed lymph tissue in ways that hurt HIV.

They then used selective drugs to split the work of TLR7 from that of TLR8. As the title states, natural killer cells and CD8 cells mediated the anti-HIV activity after the trigger. Knowing which cells do the work helps aim drugs that wake them on purpose.
plos-pone-0002099:
Andrew Bassett and co-authors studied a chromatin factor in the fruit fly's silent genome zones, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Heterochromatin is the tightly packed, mostly silent form of DNA, yet little was known about how such a structure forms. The fly gene in view matches a human gene tied to alpha-thalassemia and mental retardation, a condition called ATRX.

The team show that the fly factor, dATRX, is important in the formation or maintenance of heterochromatin. A factor that builds silent zones helps explain how genomes keep restless DNA, such as jumping genes, under lock.
plos-pone-0002199:
Johanna Jakobsdottir, Yvette Conley, Daniel Weeks, and co-authors studied genes tied to age-related maculopathy, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The disease damages the center of the retina and is a common cause of vision loss in older people in rich countries. Variants in two genes, CFH and LOC387715, were already known to raise the risk.

The team examined two more genes, C2 and CFB, which sit in the same immune pathway as CFH. They asked how the four genes act together to shape a person's risk. Untangling joint effects like these is a step toward tests that can flag who should be watched most closely for vision loss.
plos-pone-0002299:
David Fouchet, John O'Brien, and Dominique Pontier asked whether visiting sick people is as risky as common sense says, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Keeping distance from infection seems the obvious way to avoid disease. But that view overlooks how repeated small exposures keep acquired immunity topped up and efficient.

When immunity has partly waned, a fresh low-level exposure can refresh it without causing illness. The authors model when contact with the sick could protect rather than harm. Their analysis gives a counterweight to blanket avoidance, suggesting health advice about visiting may deserve a second look in some cases, though not careless exposure.
plos-pone-0002399:
Shen and other authors present their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Named on the byline are Hongbin Shen, James J. Chou, among others. Its subject is memBrain: Improving the Accuracy of Predicting Transmembrane Helices. Predicting transmembrane helices in membrane proteins gives useful clues about protein shape when no full structure is known.

Many predictors have been built on amino acid hydrophobicity scales or on pure statistics. The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002499:
Janic joined co-authors to publish a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. Named on the byline are Branislava Janic, A. S. M. Iskander, Ali M. Rad, among others. Its subject is effects of Ferumoxides – Protamine Sulfate Labeling on Immunomodulatory Characteristics of Macrophage-like THP-1 Cells. Superparamagnetic Iron Oxide (SPIO) complexed with cationic transfection agent is used to label various mammalian cells.

Labeled cells can then be use as an in vivo magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) probes. The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002599:
Pellegatti led the team behind a 2008 research article in PLOS ONE. Named on the byline are Patrizia Pellegatti, Lizzia Raffaghello, Giovanna Bianchi, among others. Its subject is increased Level of Extracellular ATP at Tumor Sites: In Vivo Imaging with Plasma Membrane Luciferase. There is growing awareness that tumour cells build up a “self-advantageous” microenvironment that reduces effectiveness of anti-tumour immune response.

The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time.
plos-pone-0002699:
Thierry Genoud and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008 on the protein phosphatase 7 regulates phytochrome signaling in arabidopsis. Authorship is credited in the record to Thierry Genoud and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. The psi2 mutant of Arabidopsis displays amplification of the responses controlled by the red/far red light photoreceptors phytochrome A (phyA) and phytochrome B (phyB). The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002799:
Feng-Jie Sun and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was evolutionary patterns in the sequence and structure of transfer RNA: a window into early translation and the genetic code. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Feng-Jie Sun, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules play vital roles during protein synthesis. It goes on to note a further point. Their acceptor arms are aminoacylated with specific amino acid residues while their anticodons delimit codon specificity. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002899:
Rita Costa, Frederico Ferreira-da-Silva, Maria Saraiva and co-authors studied how the protein transthyretin guards against amyloid beta in 2008. In Alzheimer's disease, amyloid beta peptide builds up in the brain. Transthyretin is a four-part protein made mainly in the liver and in a fluid-making part of the brain.

Published in PLOS ONE, the work reports that transthyretin protects by cutting the peptide, and that a protease blocker called a Kunitz inhibitor can stop that cutting. That gives a concrete mechanism, not just a link. It also suggests a path that future Alzheimer's treatments might try to strengthen.
plos-pone-0002999:
Agustín Estrada-Peña, Pelayo Acevedo, Francisco Ruiz-Fons and co-authors studied habitat, wild boar, deer, and tick-borne Anaplasma in 2008. Foci of tick pathogens occur at fine spatial scales set by climate, host numbers, and landscape. Some hosts feed ticks but do not multiply a pathogen, which may dilute risk for other hosts.

The PLOS ONE paper gives evidence that host habitat use matters in predicting that dilution effect for deer exposure. Wild boar presence alone is not enough; where hosts actually spend time counts. Disease ecologists mapping tick risk need that habitat detail. Details of samples, measures, and analysis are set out in the full article text.
plos-pone-0003099:
Gisela Lundberg, Anders Rosengren, Ulf Håkanson and co-authors tracked MYCN gene copies in neuroblastoma in 2008. Amplification of the oncogene MYCN on double minutes, small extra DNA circles without centromeres, is common in this childhood cancer. How cells retain and amplify those circles without centromeres was unclear.

The team shows binomial mitotic segregation of the double minutes: copies split by chance at division. Randomness itself thus drives amplification, as the title says. Published in PLOS ONE, chance-based inheritance explains how tumors can quickly gain many copies of a growth gene. Details of samples, measures, and analysis are set out in the full article text.
plos-pone-0003199:
Connie J. Mulligan, Andrew Kitchen and Michael M. Miyamoto update a model of the peopling of the Americas in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The authors re-assess support for their three-stage model in light of a recent report that found nine non-Native American mitochondrial genome sequences that should not have been in their first analysis. Removing those sequences changes the data set.

They report what the removal does to the model's support, in an updated three-stage account. Readers see science correcting its own inputs in public. The paper is useful both for its migration model and as an example of transparent revision.
plos-pone-0003299:
Ji'An Pan, Xiaoxue Peng, Yajing Gao and colleagues map viral protein interactions in SARS coronavirus in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Analyses of viral protein-protein interactions are an important step to understand viral protein functions and their underlying molecular mechanisms. In this study, the team adopted a mammalian two-hybrid system to screen genome-wide intraviral protein-protein interactions of SARS-CoV.

Readers get a network map of which viral proteins bind each other during replication. Such maps reveal assemblies that single-protein studies miss. Interaction hubs can become drug targets, since breaking a central contact may disable several viral steps at once.
plos-pone-0003399:
Marianne David-Jürgens and co-authors mapped touch areas in aging rat brains for this 2008 paper. Growing old dulls touch and movement skills in rats and people. It is unclear if that loss comes from fixed damage or from flexible change. The team compared brain maps for the front paws and the hind paws.

The two maps did not age in the same way. One region changed more than the other as the rats grew old. That uneven pattern points to local change, not simple wear everywhere. The result helps separate true decline from change the brain can still adjust.
plos-pone-0003499:
Gaynor Dolman studied mate choice in Australian rainbow skinks for this 2008 paper. These lizards live in tropical rainforest patches cut off long ago. Such refugial isolation can split populations apart over time. Female preference can drive that split faster than genetic mismatch can.

Dolman found female preference differing between the isolated groups. Choosing local males builds pre-mating isolation between populations. That barrier can hold visible differences in place. The work shows taste itself can act as an engine of divergence. Mate choice is one of the strongest forces in all of evolution.
plos-pone-0003599:
Aleksey Y. Ogurtsov and co-authors linked gene form to expression in this 2008 paper. Protein kinases are enzymes that pass signals by tagging other proteins. Their expression patterns differ across tissues and conditions. Gene architecture means the layout of a gene's parts.

Expression patterns of kinases correlated with that architecture. They also correlated with how fast the genes evolve. How a kinase gene is built thus tracks when it is used. It also tracks the pace of its change over evolution. Kinases are top drug targets, so their patterns guide drug hunts as well.
plos-pone-0003699:
Yi Zhang and John G. Turner published this plant study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Plants that get hurt again and again grow stunted, with smaller leaves. The effect cuts crop yields after insect feeding, yet its basis was poorly understood. The team looked at jasmonates, the plant's own wound signals.

They found that wound-made jasmonates stunt growth by holding back mitosis, the division of cells. In effect, the alarm system doubles as a growth brake. The work shows how a plant trades size for defense when attack keeps coming, at a real cost in yield.
plos-pone-0003799:
Eric A. Moulton, Rami Burstein, Shannon Tully, and colleagues published this migraine study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Migraine is usually studied during attacks, when pain is present. The team instead looked between attacks, at a brainstem center that normally turns pain signals down on their way up.

They found this descending modulatory center works abnormally in migraine patients even when they are headache-free. The interictal dysfunction suggests migraine is a standing brain disorder, not just a series of painful episodes. A faulty pain brake between attacks may help set up the next one.
plos-pone-0003899:
Joseph M. Dybas, Carlos J. Madrid-Aliste, Fa-Yun Che, and co-authors checked gene predictions for a widespread parasite in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article concerns Toxoplasma gondii, a single-celled parasite. It infects a large share of people worldwide, often with no symptoms. In people with weak immune systems, it can return and prove fatal.

Computer programs predict the parasite's genes from its DNA sequence. The authors tested those predictions with lab data to see which hold up. Sound gene lists are the base for work on drugs and vaccines. The study helps clean up a genome that many labs rely on.
plos-pone-0003999:
Frederico Augusto Vieira Castro, Diana Mariani, Anita Dolly Panek, and co-authors studied two plant chemicals in yeast in 2008. Quinones help plants defend themselves and interest drug researchers. Several cancer drugs carry the quinone chemical core. The pair studied here was menadione and plumbagin.

Their PLOS ONE article traces how those compounds kill yeast cells. The yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae serves as a simple model for cell harm. Knowing the killing route helps judge both risks and drug promise. Quinones act through oxidative stress, and details of that path matter. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004099:
Thomas Rotolo, Philip M. Smallwood, John Williams, and co-authors presented a sparse neuron labeling method in 2008. Genetic labeling in mammals had not yet served very complex neurons well. Studying such cells needs only a few labeled at a time. Dense labeling tangles their branches beyond tracing.

Their PLOS ONE article directs labeling to specific cell types, sparsely. Genetic switches limit labeled cells to a chosen population. Individual neuron shapes can then be drawn in full. The method opens detailed anatomy of the most branched nerve cells. The study ran in PLOS ONE, an open journal read by labs around the world.
plos-pone-0004199:
Satoko Oyama and colleagues published this brain study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The gene DTNBP1 is a recognised susceptibility gene for schizophrenia, and its protein, dysbindin-1, is reduced in the brains of patients. What dysbindin-1 actually does in the central nervous system was little known.

The authors hypothesised a link to the DNA-dependent protein kinase complex, a machine best known for repairing broken DNA. They report that dysbindin-1 interacts with this complex, and that the interaction depends on which isoform, or version, of dysbindin-1 is present. The link gives the schizophrenia gene an unexpected second life in DNA repair.
plos-pone-0004299:
Riccardo Storchi and colleagues published this neuroscience methods study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Neural activity often proceeds by motifs, patterns spread across the cortical networks involved. Neurons are correlated with each other, so estimating all possible dependencies quickly grows out of control. The nesting of oscillation frequencies adds to the tangle.

The authors present a way to extract essential discharge patterns from multisite recordings of ongoing spiking activity. Characterising the real patterns, rather than every theoretical one, is a step toward reading what a resting brain is doing. The recordings came from many sites at once.
plos-pone-0004399:
During reproduction, DNA strands swap pieces in a process called recombination. The swaps cluster in short hotspots, with long quiet stretches between. Prithvi Mani, Vinod Kumar Yadav, Swapan Kumar Das, and co-authors searched the genome for what marks those zones. Their 2009 PLOS ONE paper uses data from the HapMap project. That project mapped common DNA variation across people.

The uneven spread of hotspots hints that DNA itself carries clues. The authors tested whether structural motifs, shapes the DNA sequence can form, predict recombination. Their genome-wide analysis backs a role for such motifs. If sequence shape steers swapping, heredity maps can be read more finely. The work links DNA form to one of genetics' basic engines.
plos-pone-0004599:
A blood test combining several markers may sort ovarian cancer from harmless conditions, report Suraj Amonkar, Greg Bertenshaw, Tzong-Hao Chen, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Most women whose symptoms suggest ovarian cancer turn out to have benign conditions. Methods to distinguish the two groups would spare many women needless surgery and fear, while speeding real cases to treatment.

The team describes the development and preliminary evaluation of a multivariate index assay. Instead of one marker, the assay combines several serum measurements into a single index. Early evaluation shows how well that index separates cancer from benign disease. Ovarian cancer is often caught late, so any test that sorts patients better at first presentation is valuable.
plos-pone-0004699:
Nora Klöting and colleagues compared tiny RNA levels in two kinds of human belly fat, for PLOS ONE in 2009. MicroRNAs are small RNAs that tune gene use in growth, cell change, and energy balance. In mammals they have been shown to shape how fat cells form and mature.

Fat deep in the belly and fat under the skin act in unlike ways. The team asked if their microRNA sets differ too. A split could help explain why deep belly fat links more to diabetes and heart risk. It could also point to new ways to shift fat behavior.
plos-pone-0004799:
Abdallah Sayyed-Ahmad and Yiannis Kaznessis determined the orientation of protegrin-1 in model bilayers using an implicit solvent membrane model, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Continuum models that describe solvent and membrane effects promise better understanding of antimicrobial peptide action. In such methods, a lipid bilayer is represented without tracking every single molecule, which speeds calculation while keeping key physics of the membrane environment.

Protegrin-1 is a potent antimicrobial peptide that kills by disrupting membranes. Its angle and depth in the bilayer shape how it acts. Model results can guide design of new antibiotics. They also save costly experiments.
plos-pone-0004899:
Ying Wang, Gro Amdam, and Olav Rueppell linked PDK1, and HR46 homologs tying social behavior to ovary signals in honey bees, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Genetic basis of division of labor in social insects is a central question in evolutionary biology. Honey bees are models because of well characterized age correlated division of labor. Transitioning from nursing to foraging while ovaries regress and hormone profiles shift dramatically.

Two genes connect ovary state to behavior timing. Reproductive ground plan hypothesis gains support. Social evolution reuses reproductive physiology. Bee declines make behavioral genetics relevant. Follow up work can check whether the same pattern appears in other settings.
plos-pone-0004999:
Gibbons carry wildly rearranged chromosomes. The family includes fifteen species in four genera. Chromosome numbers range from 38 to 52. Lucia Carbone and colleagues mapped one rearrangement in PLOS ONE in 2009. It is an inversion, a flipped chromosome segment. This one is unique to the northern white-cheeked gibbon.

The inversion marks that species' separate evolutionary path. Gibbon chromosomes changed rapidly as the genera split. Mapping single events helps reconstruct that history. The finding aids the tangled family tree of these small apes. It also gives conservation geneticists a marker for this endangered species. Distinct lineages need distinct protection plans.
plos-pone-0005099:
Growing nerve branches need guidance to reach their targets. Proteases help clear their path. Bertrand Gonthier and colleagues studied one such partnership in PLOS ONE in 2009. They focused on cortical dendrites, the receiving branches of brain cells. A guidance signal called semaphorin-3A can promote their growth. The effect needed an enzyme, MMP-2.

A signal called PKC controls MMP-2's recruitment. With PKC active, MMP-2 arrives and the growth effect proceeds. Without it, the promotion fails. The finding links three players in brain wiring. Guidance cues, signals and enzymes must cooperate. Brain wiring errors underlie many disorders. Mapping these hand-offs shows where wiring can go wrong.
plos-pone-0005199:
Melanoma, the deadliest skin cancer, provokes a strong response from the patient's own immune system. That response leaves antibodies in the blood that flag tumor proteins. Forgber and colleagues used proteome serology in PLOS ONE in 2009 to find those flagged proteins.

The method screens tumor proteins against patient serum to find antigens tied to the cancer. Such antigens can become markers for diagnosis or targets for therapy. Mining the patient's own immune response is a smart shortcut, since the body has already picked out which tumor proteins stand out. For people with this skin cancer, a blood test of that kind could mean fewer scans and less time spent in doubt.
plos-pone-0005299:
Most ocean microbes will not grow in a lab, so their genomes stay out of reach. Standard DNA surveys of seawater mix thousands of species into one blur. Woyke and colleagues took a one-cell-at-a-time approach in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Single-cell methods let the team reconstruct genomes from individual marine microbes. Assembling the marine metagenome cell by cell reveals who is actually there and what they can do. That detail matters for understanding ocean chemistry, since microbes drive much of it. Most sea germs have never been seen under a lens, let alone grown. So a one-cell road to their genes opens a world that was closed to science for a long time.
plos-pone-0005399:
Gene regulatory networks contain toggle switches that hold cells in one of two stable states, a form of memory. Widder and colleagues explored how bistability can arise in PLOS ONE in 2009, including in switches built from a single component.

Monomeric bistability means one molecule type can sustain two stable states alone. Autoloops, where a gene regulates itself, shape that behavior in their analysis. A minimal memory device built from one part is a useful blueprint for synthetic biology. Small parts with memory are the bricks of smart gene circuits, and a brick made of one part is cheaper to build. Less prone to fail than one that needs two or three to hold state.
plos-pone-0005499:
Daniela Brunert and colleagues studied the sense of smell in mammals for a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Nitric oxide is a gas that cells use as a signal for blood flow, defence, and nerve messages. In the smell centre of the brain it helps form memories of odours.

The team showed that odours themselves trigger the making of nitric oxide in smell-sensing nerve cells. That ties the signal directly to the act of smelling, not just to later steps in the brain. It helps explain how the nose and brain turn a scent into a lasting memory.
plos-pone-0005599:
Roland Friedrich and Angela Friederici studied logic and language in the brain in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Formal logic and natural language share a deep feature: both build meaning from rules of structure. A sentence can be checked for whether its structure is valid.

The team asked which brain areas handle the syntax of logical statements, as opposed to ordinary sentences. Finding the areas shows how much machinery logic and language share. That bears on how reasoning is taught and how the brain handles symbols in general. Logic may be the cleaner test case, since its rules are fixed in advance and free of word meaning disputes.
plos-pone-0005699:
Barbara Mintzes, Steve Morgan, and James Wright reviewed twelve years of drug ads aimed at the public in Canada in 2009. Canada bans full ads for prescription drugs as a health safeguard, while the United States allows them. In 2000, Canada loosened the rules to permit simple reminder ads.

The authors call the outcome a cautionary tale. Reminder ads name a drug but say little about what it does or its risks. That gap can push demand without giving patients balanced facts. Their review feeds the debate on whether drug ads serve patients or mainly sales.
plos-pone-0005799:
Rebecca Cotterman and Paul Knoepfler reported in 2009 that N-Myc, a gene known for driving tumors, also switches on stem-cell genes in neuroblastoma. Myc genes cause cancer when overactive, but normal Myc helps stem cells renew themselves. Neuroblastoma, a childhood nerve tumor, often rides on extra N-Myc.

The team found N-Myc controls genes tied to pluripotency, the ability to become many cell types, including lif, klf2, klf4, and lin28b. That link may explain the tumor's stubborn, stem-like core. It also ties cancer biology to the normal stem cell program in one set of experiments.
plos-pone-0005899:
Arach Goldar, Marie-Claude Marsolier-Kergoat, and Olivier Hyrien looked in 2009 for a universal pattern in when DNA copying starts. Origins of replication fire at scattered times through S-phase in all eukaryotes studied. The schedule is reproducible, yet the sequence rules for origins differ by species.

The team found a shared temporal profile of origin activation across eukaryotes. A common shape under varied rules suggests a deeper organizing principle. That principle could unify how cells schedule genome duplication. Keeping that schedule is vital; its breakdown invites the DNA damage seen in cancer.
plos-pone-0005999:
Tuberculosis kills a great many people who also live with HIV. Neeraj Raizada, Lakbir Singh Chauhan, Sai Babu and colleagues studied how to connect such patients to lifesaving care in India in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper follows a program effort to link HIV-infected TB patients to two things: cotrimoxazole, a drug that prevents other infections, and antiretroviral treatment for HIV itself.

No program study from India had yet recorded how well that delivery works. A workable link between TB clinics and HIV care can cut deaths that both diseases cause together. The paper gives health planners in similar settings a grounded model for joining two services that too often run apart.
plos-pone-0006099:
A brain recording is blind to which kind of neuron is firing. Susana Lima, Tomáš Hromádka, Petr Znamenskiy and colleagues gave recordings a name tag in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper presents PINP, a method for tagging chosen neuronal populations so they can be identified during in vivo electrophysiological recording in a living animal.
