Circuits mix many neuron types in tight quarters, and their roles cannot be sorted by signal alone. A tag that marks a population while it works lets scientists tie a cell type to its true job. The method serves the wider project of reading brain circuits part by part instead of as one blur.
plos-pone-0006199:
Species brought in for farming or trade can escape, go wild, and harm local nature. Xuan Liu and Yiming Li ran a 2009 PLOS ONE study on farmed animals in enclosures. They asked how those farms relate to wild populations of introduced species. Escapees can damage wildlife and cause heavy economic losses once they settle.

The study links the presence of aquaculture enclosures to where introduced species have set up wild populations. That link helps managers judge which escapes pose the greatest risk. Better siting and stronger containment can then prevent new invasions. The work turns past escapes into a guide for safer farming practice.
plos-pone-0006299:
Polycystic kidney disease is a common inherited condition in which cysts crowd out working kidney tissue. Hisashi Hashimoto and colleagues traced the fish version in medaka, a small Japanese fish, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. A growing list of cilia-related genes has been tied to the disease in recent studies.

The medaka pc mutant's disease is caused by a mutation in the glis3 gene, the team reports. A fish model lets researchers watch the disease unfold and test ideas cheaply. Each added causal gene clarifies the family of disorders. The work links fish genetics to a human health problem.
plos-pone-0006399:
Working memory keeps information alive for seconds after it vanishes, and cortical neurons fire in telling patterns during that delay. Sergio Verduzco-Flores and colleagues modelled those patterns in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Observed patterns include steady firing, ramping activity, and shifting sequences across trials.

Cross-regional networks with synaptic facilitation explain the cells' behaviour in their model. Short-term strengthening of synapses can hold a memory without constant input. The model unifies several firing patterns under one mechanism. It guides experiments on how brains hold thoughts. Tests of the model may show how the brain keeps a thought in mind.
plos-pone-0006499:
Illya Tietzel, Christelle El-Haibi, and Rey Carabeo studied human defense proteins against Chlamydia in PLOS ONE in 2009. Chlamydiae are bacteria that live inside cells and are sensitive to interferon gamma, an immune signal. In mice, a family of interferon-induced GTPases helps fight them. The human counterparts are the guanylate binding proteins.

The team tested whether human guanylate binding proteins strengthen the anti-Chlamydia effects of interferon gamma. Their title says they do potentiate those effects. Knowing which human proteins matter helps translate mouse findings to people. It may also suggest ways to support the body's own defense against a very common infection.
plos-pone-0006599:
Ana Miletic and co-authors studied a linker protein in T cell activation in PLOS ONE in 2009. When a T cell meets its target, signal clusters form and the cell's actin skeleton shifts fast. Actin is a core building protein of cells. The protein Vav links the T cell receptor to that skeleton. The team asked which of Vav's jobs drives this link.

Their title says Vav makes the link on its own, apart from its known enzyme role as a GEF. That means Vav also works as a scaffold, a frame that holds protein groups in place. Scaffold jobs like this are now seen as key in immune signals. The work redraws what this one protein does.
plos-pone-0006699:
Fiery Cushman and colleagues ran a behavioral game about blame and accidents in PLOS ONE in 2009. People often must judge harm that nobody intended. Punishment might follow the actor's intentions. Or it might follow the bad outcome that happened by chance. Standard economics games rarely allowed accidents at all. The authors built a game where a trembling hand could change the result.

Players decided rewards and punishments after moves went wrong by accident. The outcomes, not just intentions, guided how players responded. That bias matters for law, management, and everyday fairness judgments. The study shows how hard it is to judge intent alone. It gives moral psychology a cleaner way to study accidental harm.
plos-pone-0006799:
Scott Christley, Qing Nie, and Xiaohui Xie improved methods for inferring gene networks in PLOS ONE in 2009. One successful approach models networks with ordinary differential equations. Such models work backward from gene expression data. New data types keep appearing, though. The authors asked how existing network knowledge could join the inference.

Their method incorporates known network information into the modeling. Prior knowledge can steady estimates where data are thin. It can also speed the search for plausible networks. Gene networks guide research on development and disease. Better inference means experiments start from sharper maps of gene control.
plos-pone-0006999:
David Lewis, Zhiming Huo, Susan Barnett, and colleagues reported a vaccine safety finding in PLOS ONE in 2009. An earlier nasal flu vaccine had been linked to Bell's palsy, a temporary facial nerve paralysis. That vaccine carried an active bacterial toxin as an adjuvant. Which component caused the problem was unresolved.

The team gave a genetically detoxified mutant of the E. coli heat labile toxin through the nose. Facial nerve paralysis still followed in their tests. The result points at the toxin component itself, even in weakened form. It is a caution for any vaccine delivered through the nasal route.
plos-pone-0007099:
Jun Inoue, Akiko Misawa, Yukichi Tanaka, and colleagues studied tumors that vanish on their own in PLOS ONE in 2009. Neuroblastoma is the most common solid tumor in children. Its behavior varies widely. Favorable tumors, often found by urine screening, can regress spontaneously through programmed cell death.

The team linked that regression to a gene called LAPTM5. The gene sits in lysosomes, the cell's recycling compartments. A gene tied to tumors disappearing is a valuable lead. It might show how to push dangerous neuroblastomas down the same path, without harsh treatment.
plos-pone-0007199:
Thomas W. Plummer, Peter W. Ditchfield, Laura C. Bishop, and colleagues presented early human evidence in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their paper reports the oldest evidence of toolmaking hominins in a grassland-dominated ecosystem. Hominins are the group that includes humans and their close extinct relatives.

Major changes in late Pliocene hominin evolution are often linked to spreading grasslands in Africa. Deep sea records give indirect evidence for more grass over time. The authors bring direct site evidence into that debate. Anthropologists can use their findings to test how grassland life shaped early tool use.
plos-pone-0007299:
Victor Hugo Aquino, Alberto Anastacio Amarilla, Helda Liz Alfonso, and colleagues described a new dengue virus genotype in 2009. Dengue type 3 genotype V viruses had recently been detected in Brazil and Colombia. Dengue causes major epidemics of fever across tropical regions, and tracking genotypes helps officials follow its spread.

The authors describe another Brazilian isolate belonging to this genotype. Their family tree analysis includes dengue type 3 viruses from around the world. They find the South American viruses closely related to old Asian viruses. That link suggests a long-distance introduction into the Americas.
plos-pone-0007399:
Jolena N. Fleming-Waddell, Gayla R. Olbricht, Tasia M. Taxis, and colleagues studied a muscle mutation in sheep in 2009. Callipyge sheep develop extreme postnatal muscle growth in the loin and hindquarters. A single nucleotide change in an imprinted gene domain on sheep chromosome 18 causes the trait, which interests meat producers greatly.

That change raises expression of surrounding transcripts when inherited from the father. The authors test effects of genes DLK1 and RTL1, but not MEG3 or MEG8, on muscle gene expression. Their results narrow which genes in the domain actually drive callipyge muscle growth.
plos-pone-0007499:
Ying-Chi Lin and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on two fatty compounds that fight Staphylococcus aureus. One, glycerol monolaurate, slows the bacterium's growth and shuts down its toxin output. The toxin in question causes toxic shock syndrome. A flaw limits the first compound: a bacterial enzyme breaks it down. The team compared it with a tougher relative, dodecylglycerol.

They tested both compounds in lab cultures and in living animals. The comparison covered killing power and control of toxic shock toxin-1. A more durable compound would keep working where the first one degrades. That durability matters for uses like skin treatments or protective products. The study weighs whether the sturdier molecule can replace its fragile cousin. It is a practical step toward better anti-staph defenses.
plos-pone-0007599:
Lora Shahine and colleagues published a clinical study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on differences in fertility treatment outcomes. Disease rates and treatment responses can differ among patients of diverse ethnic backgrounds. Earlier reports showed Indian women fare worse with in vitro fertilization than Caucasian women. Poor embryo quality was one proposed explanation. The team compared outcomes while accounting for how good the embryos actually looked.

The gap in success persisted despite similar embryo quality. That rules out the simplest explanation and redirects attention. The difference likely lies in the womb environment or in how implantation proceeds. Knowing where a gap sits is the first step to closing it. Fertility medicine aims to treat individuals, and group-level data like this sharpen that aim. The study flags a disparity that clinics should not ignore.
plos-pone-0007699:
Angelo Quaranta and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It asks why amphibians react more strongly than mammals to foreign chemicals, called xenobiotics. Amphibian numbers have fallen sharply around the world since the 1980s.

The authors weigh the common claim that amphibians are simply more sensitive to threats. They look for traits that set amphibians apart from mammals. Thin skin, a life split between water and land, and slow chemical defenses all play a part. The answer matters for conservation, since frogs often serve as an early warning of pollution.
plos-pone-0007799:
Nagafumi Doi and co-authors published a discussion paper in PLOS ONE in 2009. It tackles a puzzle in schizophrenia genetics. Genes that raise the risk of schizophrenia persist in the human gene pool. They survive despite strong natural selection against them.

Why would harmful variants not be weeded out? The authors review the evidence from evolution and population studies. New mutations may keep replacing the variants that selection removes. Other balances may also help the genes persist. The paper weighs which explanations fit the facts best. The paradox guides how geneticists hunt for schizophrenia genes.
plos-pone-0007899:
Sophia Vijay and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It tests whether TB clinics in India can offer HIV testing to every TB patient. Provider-initiated testing and counselling is recommended worldwide for TB patients. TB and HIV fuel each other, so finding HIV early matters.

Whether the policy would work under India's TB control programme was unknown. The team evaluated it across two districts of South India. They weighed feasibility, effectiveness and the impact on the TB programme itself. Their findings can help health officials roll out joint testing without breaking TB services.
plos-pone-0007999:
Denver Fowler and colleagues measured the talons of birds of prey for PLOS ONE in 2009. Raptors kill with their feet, yet how claw size varies from toe to toe had drawn little study. The team compared talon size across species with unlike hunting styles.

Claw patterns matched how each bird holds and stills its prey. Species that squeeze and pin prey with force carry a different claw layout from those that strike and release. Talons thus read as tools shaped by technique, a link that helps decode the hunting lives of living and fossil raptors alike.
plos-pone-0008099:
Jai Kaushik and colleagues put a local probiotic candidate through its paces in PLOS ONE in 2009. The candidate is a strain of Lactobacillus plantarum, a friendly germ, found in India. To earn the probiotic label, a strain must survive the gut, do some good, and do no harm.

The strain endured acid and bile, clung to gut lining, held harmful germs back, and passed safety checks. Each passed test adds a line to its case for use in foods and supplements. A well-tested local strain may suit local diets and makers better than imports.
plos-pone-0008199:
Paloma Cejas and co-authors studied KRAS mutations in colorectal cancer in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. KRAS faults in primary tumors predict resistance to certain antibody therapies. That makes KRAS a true marker of whether a key growth pathway is active. The team compared primary tumors with their related metastases, the secondary tumors that spread elsewhere.

They asked whether KRAS status could help predict spread to the lung. Matching primary and metastatic samples show how stable the marker stays. If the pattern holds, a simple gene test might flag patients at risk of lung spread. That would help doctors plan follow-up care.
plos-pone-0008299:
Matthew A. Pettengill, Verissa W. Lam, and David M. Ojcius studied a persistent bacterial infection in PLOS ONE in 2009. Chlamydiae infect most of the world population as intracellular bacteria. Inflammation helps contain their early spread but also damages tissue. Low oxygen in infected tissue is part of that picture. Most infections clear, yet some persist quietly.

The authors found the danger signal adenosine induces chlamydial persistence. It acts by stimulating A2b receptors on cells. Persistence helps the bacteria survive treatment and immunity. Understanding that switch could lead to ways of waking and clearing hidden infections.
plos-pone-0008399:
Smadar Peleg-Grossman and colleagues studied a plant protein's two faces in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Legumes form symbiotic partnerships with Rhizobium bacteria. The bacteria provide nitrogen the plant can use. Nodulation factors from the bacteria start the root changes that trap them. The NPR1 protein was the focus of the study.

NPR1 regulates both pathogenic and symbiotic interactions between Rhizobium and plants. It acts in legumes and non-legumes alike. One protein balancing defense and friendship is a notable finding. It may help extend nitrogen-fixing partnerships to more crops.
plos-pone-0008499:
Agata Leszczynska and co-authors use yeast to study statin drugs in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Statins lower cholesterol in humans. Faults in lipid metabolism underlie diseases such as atherosclerosis and type II diabetes. High cholesterol is a primary risk factor for coronary artery disease. That disease is a major cause of early death in developed countries. Yeast offer a simple system to probe lipid effects.

The team express human-related genes in yeast and add statins. They watch how cellular lipid metabolism changes. Yeast screens can reveal statin effects that cell studies in humans miss. The system may also help find new lipid drug targets.
plos-pone-0008599:
Carey Lambert, Chien-Yi Chang, Michael J. Capeness, and colleagues reported a microbiology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their subject was Bdellovibrio bacteriovorus, a small bacterium that hunts and kills other bacteria. Its prey are Gram-negative kinds, a broad group that includes many germs harming people, farm animals, and crops.

Rather than study the whole life cycle, the team profiled the opening attack. They catalogued the genes switched on as the predator makes its first bite, a working set they name the predatosome. That profile shows which tools the hunter deploys first when it invades prey. It also helps judge whether such predators could one day serve as living germ control.
plos-pone-0008699:
Hortensia Sanchez-Calderon, Lourdes Rodriguez-de la Rosa, Marta Milo, and colleagues searched for genes guided by a growth signal. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study centers on the inner ear of unborn mice. The signal, IGF-I, helps ear cells survive and mature. In humans, broken IGF-I causes deafness along with poor growth. Which ear genes answer to it was only partly known.

Using a gene chip on the prenatal cochlea, the team found fresh target genes. Two control proteins, MEF2 and FOXM1, stood out as likely helpers. The list gives hearing researchers new leads on how the ear is built.
plos-pone-0008799:
Beau Fenner, Michael Scannell, and Jochen Prehn expanded the partner list of a key immune switchboard. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The NF-kappaB pathway steers responses to infection and stress. NEMO sits near its top, passing signals onward. A fuller map of NEMO's partners would reveal new control points. Protein microarrays can test thousands of possible partners at once.

Scanning arrays with NEMO surfaced many new candidate interactions. The enlarged network, called an interactome, suggests fresh signaling branches. Each new partner is a lead for follow-up experiments. The map helps explain how one switchboard serves so many cell messages.
plos-pone-0008899:
Renee Laird and Sandra Hayes mapped how two kinases set the volume of an unusual T cell's signals. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Lck and Fyn belong to the Src kinase family. Both help relay signals from the common alpha-beta T cell receptor. Gamma-delta T cells use a different receptor with murkier rules. Whether the same kinases help, hinder, or split duties there was open.

Experiments separated the roles of Lck and Fyn in gamma-delta signaling. The pair did not simply duplicate their alpha-beta jobs. Signal strength in these cells follows its own tuning. Gamma-delta cells matter for early defense and cancer watching, so their rules count.
plos-pone-0008999:
Dragana Antic and co-authors explained how an embryo decides its left from its right, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Early embryos carry a small pit where each cell bears one tiny beating hair, a cilium. The hairs beat together and sweep fluid across the pit. That flow tells the embryo which side is which, before organs form.

The team studied this in mouse and in the frog Xenopus. They found planar cell polarity, a tissue-level compass, positions the cilia at the cell's rear. Tilted to the back, the hairs can push fluid in one useful direction. Without that tilt, the left-right axis would be set wrongly.
plos-pone-0009099:
Jean-Marc Collombet and co-authors settled whether a puzzling protein family truly belongs to animals, in PLOS ONE in 2010. DING proteins are named for their distinctive starting sequence of amino acids. Some members have been linked to arthritis, atherosclerosis, and blocking HIV. Sceptics doubted eukaryotes make them at all, suspecting bacterial contamination instead.

The team stained mouse tissues to hunt for the proteins in place. Clear signals inside the mouse tissue showed the proteins are endogenous. Animals genuinely produce their own DING proteins, the images proved. That verdict lets disease researchers take the family seriously as native players.
plos-pone-0009199:
Hiyaa Singhee Ghosh, Michael McBurney, and Paul Robbins published this aging study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Two control systems meet in it. One is mTOR, a pathway that senses food, energy, and stress and steers growth and aging. The other is SIRT1, an enzyme linked to the longer life seen when animals eat less.

Their central finding is that SIRT1 holds mTOR back, acting as a brake on it. That brake connects two famous aging pathways that were often studied apart. It suggests the benefits of eating less may run partly through quieting mTOR. The result gives aging researchers a clearer map of how these controls interact.
plos-pone-0009299:
Ara Parlakian and co-authors published this cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cancers spread to many organs, but almost never to skeletal muscle. Why muscle resists being a home for metastasis was not understood. The authors grew muscle-forming cells together with metastatic cancer cells to find out.

In mice and in culture, the muscle cells exerted strong effects on the cancer cells. Melanoma and carcinoma cells changed character under that influence. The muscle cells also selectively blocked the cancer cells' growth. The work hints that muscle tissue carries an active defense, one that might be borrowed for therapy.
plos-pone-0009399:
Naoki Saijo and Hiroaki Gomi published this motor learning study in PLOS ONE in 2010. When a screen cursor is rotated away from the hand's true motion, people adapt. Their reaches soon bring the cursor back to the target. Remove the rotation suddenly, and errors swing the other way.

The authors examined how people learn this visuomotor rotation. They found that learners use multiple strategies at once, not a single mechanism. Some adjust by feel, others by aiming off on purpose. Knowing the mix explains why adaptation speeds differ between people and why skills persist or fade.
plos-pone-0009499:
Mireia Margeli and co-authors studied breast cancer samples in Spain for PLOS ONE in 2010. Some breast tumors make little of the protein BRCA1. That protein helps repair DNA damage. Tumors with low BRCA1 may answer in a distinct way to drugs that damage DNA. The team measured BRCA1 message levels in tumors after chemotherapy given before surgery.

They then compared those levels with how patients fared over time. BRCA1 levels carried information about prognosis after that treatment. Reading them could help doctors sort patients by likely outcome. It is a step toward matching breast cancer care to the biology of each tumor.
plos-pone-0009599:
Latisha Heinlen and co-authors read old blood samples for the first signs of lupus in PLOS ONE in 2010. Lupus is an autoimmune disease with many faces. Its mark is a flood of antibodies against the body's own parts. The team had serum from 129 people taken before they fell ill, while they served in the United States military. They tested which autoantibodies appeared first.

Antibodies against two targets, 60 kD Ro and nRNP A, most often came first. They showed up years before symptoms. Knowing the opening shots of lupus may help doctors spot the disease earlier. It also tells researchers where the loss of self tolerance begins.
plos-pone-0009699:
A mother's immune experience during pregnancy may shape her baby's defenses after birth. Muhammad Jubayer Rahman and colleagues tested that idea in mice for a 2010 PLOS ONE report. Pregnant mice received mycobacterial antigens, pieces of the germ family that includes tuberculosis bacteria.

The researchers then checked how the pups' immune systems responded after birth. Comparing treated and untreated mothers showed whether exposure before birth carried lasting effects. Work like this informs debates about vaccination and infection during pregnancy. It may also help explain why newborns differ in how strongly they respond to vaccines.
plos-pone-0009899:
Names in genome databases can be wrong, and one wrong name can mislead years of work. Katherine Evans-Roberts and colleagues checked a suspicious gene name in the plant Arabidopsis thaliana. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Arabidopsis is the most studied plant in genetics.

The gene, GYRB3, was thought to encode a DNA gyrase subunit. Gyrase is an enzyme that twists and untwists DNA so it fits in the cell. The team showed GYRB3 does not encode that subunit after all. Correcting the record keeps plant genetics honest.
plos-pone-0009999:
The authors were Qingyu Qin, Guanghong Liao, Michel Baudry, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE mouse work asked what disturbed cholesterol balance does to the brain. The brain holds more cholesterol than any other part of the body, so faults in handling it can do deep harm. A severe case is Niemann-Pick Type C disease, which steadily destroys nerve tissue.

The team linked disturbed cholesterol to loss of the guard protein p53. They also linked it to damage in axons. Axons are the long fibers that carry nerve signals. Two other proteins, p38 MAPK and Mdm2, sat in the chain they traced. The findings help explain how a lipid fault can turn into nerve damage.
plos-pone-0010199:
The authors were Michaël Schwarzinger, Rémi Flicoteaux, Sébastien Cortarenoda, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study surveyed French adults about pandemic flu vaccination. In July 2009, French authorities launched a mass campaign against the A/H1N1 pandemic strain. The team ran an online survey of 2,253 adults on attitudes and behavior toward that campaign.

They found low acceptability of vaccination in the general population. Their question was whether public health policy itself fueled public dissonance, or distrust. The episode offers lessons for any future mass vaccination drive facing a doubtful public.
plos-pone-0010299:
The authors were Sante Roperto, Roberta De Tullio, Cinzia Raso, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study examined bladder tumors in cattle linked to papillomavirus. The protein calpain 3 is normally specific to skeletal muscle. Its absence causes a form of limb-girdle muscular dystrophy in people. Recent work also suggested it can promote cell death in some melanoma cells.

The team found calpain 3 in these cattle urothelial tumors in an active form. The enzyme was proteolytically active, meaning it could cut other proteins there. Its presence opens a new line on how virus-linked tumors grow in farm animals.
plos-pone-0010399:
Gerd Birkenmeier and colleagues described a chemical change that may control a detox enzyme in PLOS ONE in 2010. The enzyme, glyoxalase 1, helps clear toxic by-products inside cells. It works with a partner enzyme and uses glutathione, a common cell protector. Human glyoxalase 1 comes in several forms, but why was unclear. The team examined changes added to the enzyme after it is built.

They found a modification tied to the cell's oxidation state. When oxidation rises, the enzyme's form shifts; its activity may shift too. Such redox control lets cells tune detox work to current stress. The finding connects a housekeeping enzyme to the cell's wider alarm system. It may matter in diseases where oxidation runs high, such as diabetes.
plos-pone-0010499:
Wei Tian and co-workers described a new lab-made compound that freezes cell division and kills tumor cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. Many strong cancer drugs work by stopping mitosis, the splitting of a cell into two. The search continues for such drugs with fewer side effects. The team found a compound, LJK-11, from a family called quinazolines. It blocked a key step: the assembly of microtubules, the cell's division machinery.

Without working microtubules, tumor cells stalled in division and then died by apoptosis. A new chemical scaffold gives medicinal chemists fresh material to refine. Potency in dishes must still survive animal and safety testing. The study adds one more candidate to a proven drug strategy. It also details the mechanism clearly for followers.
plos-pone-0010599:
Branka Bogunovic and colleagues studied how the immune system shows protein pieces to T cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A cell enzyme called GILT cuts certain chemical bonds in swallowed proteins. That cutting helps prepare the pieces displayed on the cell surface.

Using mass spectrometry, the team compared displayed pieces with and without working GILT. The menu of self pieces changed clearly when GILT was missing. Some pieces appeared only when the enzyme was present. The work shows GILT shapes what T cells learn to treat as self, which matters for both infection defense and autoimmunity.
plos-pone-0010699:
Jun Li, Jose Ribeiro, and Guiyun Yan catalogued gene structure variants in the malaria mosquito, in PLOS ONE in 2010. One gene can make several proteins when its message is cut and rejoined in different ways. In humans most genes do this. In Anopheles gambiae the scale of such variation was unmapped.

Comparing gene copies across mosquitoes, the team found wide variation in gene structure. Many genes produced alternate forms that could change what the protein does. The mosquito's protein toolkit is thus larger than its gene count suggests. Control programs that target a single gene product may need to reckon with all of its forms.
plos-pone-0010799:
Guang Xue He and colleagues followed drug-resistant TB patients in Heilongjiang, China, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A 2004 survey there found multidrug-resistant TB in a small share of new patients and a large share of those treated before. All patients then received the standard first-line drug course, and the team returned four years later.

Follow-up showed how many stayed cured and how many fell ill again. Outcomes for resistant cases on standard drugs were poor beside those of drug-sensitive cases. Standard treatment is a weak answer to resistant TB. Long follow-up data like these push programs to test for resistance first and fund the costlier regimens that resistant cases need.
plos-pone-0010899:
John Weete, Maritza Abril and Meredith Blackwell published this fungal evolution study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Ergosterol, a fat-like molecule in cell membranes, has been called the fungal sterol for more than a century, since most fungi seem to use it. The authors tested that label by laying sterol data across a modern family tree of the fungi.

The pattern proved messier and more ordered at once. The earliest-branching fungi lean on cholesterol and similar sterols, while ergosterol dominates only in later branches. Some lineages break the trend with their own signatures; one fungal order favors a near relative of ergosterol, another a different methyl sterol entirely. Weete and colleagues turn a textbook simplification into an evolutionary story, useful for targeting fungi, since many antifungal drugs attack ergosterol.
plos-pone-0010999:
Pierre Perrot, Julie Rousseau, Anne-Laure Bouffaut and co-authors published this case report in PLOS ONE in 2010. Osteosarcoma is the commonest bone cancer of young adults, treated with chemotherapy and surgery that can leave soft tissue defects. Surgeons sometimes fill those defects with the patient's own fat, a technique called lipofilling, which the authors now question.

They report a patient whose osteosarcoma returned at the original site thirteen years after the first illness, and only eighteen months after a fat grafting procedure. Because such late recurrence is highly unexpected, they tested fat grafts and the progenitor cells abundant in fat in preclinical models, and found both promoted tumor growth. Perrot and colleagues raise an uncomfortable safety question for reconstructive surgery after bone cancer, urging caution until the risk is measured.
plos-pone-0011099:
Greenstein, Su and Brown reported a drug test in PLOS ONE in 2010. They worked with the germ that causes a wasting gut disease in cattle, related to the germ behind a similar human illness. Two thyroid drugs, both from a class called thioamides, were tested in culture dishes.

Both drugs stopped the germ from growing in culture. That result suggests old drugs for another illness might be reused against this hard to treat infection. Farm losses from the cattle disease are large, so even a lead matters. The finding now needs tests in living animals to see if the effect holds.
plos-pone-0011199:
Del Rio, Seegers and Gomes-Solecki tested a Lyme vaccine idea in PLOS ONE in 2010. They used a friendly gut bacterium as a carrier, engineered to make a surface protein of the Lyme disease germ. The team measured the immune response to this oral style vaccine in animals.

The response was shaped by a fat tag attached to the vaccine protein. That detail matters, since the tag can raise or lower immune strength. A needle free vaccine carried by a safe gut germ would suit wide campaigns. The study tunes that approach for a disease spread by ticks across many regions.
plos-pone-0011299:
Xu, Deng, Peng and colleagues studied a rice gene in PLOS ONE in 2010. The rice version of a chromatin remodeling gene known from a model weed proved to be the focus. Mutants let the team test whether rice embryos can develop normally without this gene's action.

Embryo development failed without it, showing the gene is essential in rice. A gene that reshapes how DNA is packed can control whole developmental programs. That knowledge informs crop science, since seed formation sets yield. It also shows deep conservation: the same gene family guides embryos in very different plants.
plos-pone-0011399:
Frédéric Gambino and colleagues tracked brain connection growth in 2010 in a mouse model of Rett syndrome. Rett syndrome is a severe developmental disorder, mostly in girls, that disrupts movement, speech, and learning. The team focused on connections running from the cortex into the lateral amygdala, a hub for fear and emotion.

They charted how those connections mature over time and where growth in the Rett model departs from normal. Specific junctions matured on an altered schedule, pointing to a defined circuit where the disorder distorts emotional wiring. Narrowing the fault to one pathway helps focus the search for treatments. It also suggests that therapies may need to arrive while that circuit is still maturing, before its altered pattern sets.
plos-pone-0011499:
Lorella Marselli and co-authors read gene activity in 2010 in the very cells that fail in type 2 diabetes. Insulin-making beta cells sit in small clusters inside the pancreas, mixed with other cells, so studying them requires plucking out just those clusters. The team used laser capture microdissection, a microscope-guided method that cuts out chosen tissue under direct view, on pancreas samples from diabetic donors.

The resulting profiles show how the inner programs of beta-cell tissue differ in people with the disease. Those differences are candidate causes of failure, not just consequences, and each one is a defined lead for follow-up. Getting the tissue pure enough to trust was half the achievement. The study gives diabetes research a cleaner window on the failing cell itself, rather than on the whole mixed organ.
plos-pone-0011599:
Xiaoli Pang and colleagues tracked stomach flu outbreaks in Alberta and Canada's north from 2000 to 2008, in PLOS ONE in 2010. One virus type, called GII.4, causes most norovirus outbreaks around the world. Fresh forms of this type show up every few years, and each one tends to arrive with a new wave of illness.

The authors matched outbreak records with the virus forms found each season. They show how the arrival of a new form changed when and where outbreaks struck. Health teams can use that past pattern as a warning: spot a new form early, and the next wave is easier to predict.
plos-pone-0011699:
Shannon O'Grady and co-authors used isotope analysis to detect disturbed water balance in the body, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Isotopes are commonly used as tracers in disease research, in labelled form. Far fewer studies had asked whether disease itself shifts the natural isotope ratios found in body water, and what such shifts might reveal.

The team showed that abnormal water handling leaves a detectable signature in stable isotope ratios. Reading that signature could flag hidden fluid problems before symptoms appear. An early-warning measure of this kind may prove useful wherever water balance quietly goes wrong.
plos-pone-0011799:
Refugio Robles-Sikisaka and co-authors read the gene traces of a shrimp virus outbreak, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The virus IHHNV is a small DNA virus found across the world. It has caused heavy losses in wild and farmed shrimp on Mexico's north Pacific coast since the early nineteen nineties.

By comparing virus genes in wild Penaeus shrimp, the team found the marks of fast growth in the virus's numbers. Those marks trace how the outbreak raced through wild stocks. Knowing that growth pattern helps fish farms plan against fresh outbreaks of the same kind.
plos-pone-0011899:
Simon Thrush and a large team surveyed in 2010 the animals living on Antarctica's coastal seafloor. These benthic communities sit in near-pristine water crossed by sharp gradients of ice, light, and food supply. The team asked how habitat type, distance between sites, and local productivity each shape how species composition changes from place to place.

That change, called beta diversity, shows how connected the seafloor communities are. Where composition shifts mainly with distance, populations are isolated; where it follows habitat, local conditions rule. Knowing which force dominates helps predict what warming and ice loss will do to Antarctic seafloor life, and which areas most need protection.
plos-pone-0011999:
Joshua Cinner and Örjan Bodin mapped in 2010 how tropical coastal households spread their work across many activities. Diverse livelihoods are a survival staple in developing countries, especially where families depend on natural resources such as fisheries. A household fishing, farming, and trading is insured against any one source failing.

The team used network analysis to picture these livelihood landscapes: the web of activities and how households connect through them. A network view shows which activities cluster together and which households hold the web together. For resource managers, that map matters because rules aimed at one activity, such as fishing, land on households whose real economy is the whole web.
plos-pone-0012099:
Xue Wang, Jiangqin Zhao, Shixing Tang, and co-authors studied bird flu infection in ferrets for PLOS ONE in 2010. The H5N1 bird flu virus kills many of the people it infects, yet doctors still know too little about how it moves through the body. Ferrets catch flu in ways much like humans, so the team used them to track the virus during severe illness.

They paid close attention to virus in the blood, which is rare in normal flu. Cases where the virus reached the blood lined up with the worst outcomes in the animals. That link suggests blood-borne virus is a warning sign of fatal disease, and it helps explain why this strain can be so deadly.
plos-pone-0012199:
Roger Bate and Kimberly Hess tested the quality of drugs bought from internet pharmacies for PLOS ONE in 2010. Medicines ordered online are widely suspected of being fake or weak, and regulators report that sites hiding their address sell counterfeits more than half the time. The authors set out to measure what buyers actually receive from website pharmacies.

Their checks found the picture less grim than the warnings suggest for the sites they sampled. That does not make every web pharmacy safe, but it argues for judging by testing rather than by fear alone. Evidence of this kind helps regulators target truly dangerous sellers instead of treating the whole online trade as one risk.
plos-pone-0012299:
Céline Frère, Ewa Krzyszczyk, Eric Patterson, and co-authors collected whale DNA from breath instead of flesh, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Genetic data answer key questions for whale and dolphin conservation, from family ties to population size. The standard method fires a dart that takes a small skin sample, an approach many consider too invasive for repeated use on wild animals.

The blow a whale exhales at the surface carries cells, and the team shows it carries usable DNA too. A breath sample can be gathered from a boat without touching the animal at all. Gentler sampling means more animals can be studied more often, improving the science while lowering the cost to the animals themselves.
plos-pone-0012399:
Jonathan Goldwasser, Pazit Cohen, Eric Yang and colleagues fed a grapefruit compound to study liver fat control, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Naringenin gives grapefruit its bitter bite, and the team asked how it changes the genes that run fat and sugar handling in the liver. Faulty handling drives diabetes, obesity, and clogged arteries, so food compounds that tune it draw interest.

The compound switched on some control proteins, including PPAR alpha and PPAR gamma, and eased others, reshaping fat burning and storage programs. The gene pattern hints at why grapefruit diets show metabolic benefits in some studies. It also warns that strong food compounds can act like drugs, with real effects on the liver.
plos-pone-0012499:
Rui Gu, Anae Shampang, Toufic Nashar and colleagues built an oral HIV vaccine from a common cold-like virus, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. A vaccine against HIV has eluded decades of work, so fresh delivery routes are welcome. Their carrier is a live coxsackievirus, taken by mouth, engineered to display an HIV protein called Gag p24.

After oral dosing, animals mounted T cell responses specific to the HIV protein. A mouth-delivered vaccine would be cheap, needle-free, and easy to ship, all prized for global campaigns. Early animal responses do not guarantee protection, but they earn the approach a place among strategies worth refining.
plos-pone-0012599:
Bulgarelli and co-authors studied leaf stripe, a fungal disease that travels in barley seed. The fungus harms barley crops, and some barley lines resist it through genes called Rdg genes. Their 2010 paper focuses on one of them, Rdg2a, which follows the CC-NB-LRR pattern common in plant defence genes.

They report that Rdg2a gives the plant full protection without the usual burst of cell death at the infection site. Most plant resistance relies on those dying cells to trap the fungus, so a quieter route is notable. Seed breeders may use Rdg2a to build tougher barley with less tissue damage.
plos-pone-0012699:
Gustavsson, Agardh, Zetterqvist and co-authors measured a sticky molecule on mouse eye vessels in diabetes. The molecule, VCAM-1, helps white blood cells cling to vessel walls, an early step in inflammation. Diabetic retinopathy, a leading cause of blindness, is thought to involve just such inflammation in the retina.

Their 2010 study raised blood sugar and blood fats, separately and together, to see which drives VCAM-1 up. Both mattered, which fits the mixed metabolic picture of real diabetes. Pinning down these drivers helps target the earliest, most treatable stage of eye damage.
plos-pone-0012799:
Johnson, Kazgan, Bretz and co-authors starved fruit flies of their main energy sensor and watched metabolism go wrong. Animals must balance energy use when food runs short. A protein complex called AMPK is a central part of that balancing act, sensing low fuel and switching the body to saving mode.

Their 2010 study cut AMPK function in flies and saw altered metabolism plus food-seeking behaviour that persisted as if the flies were still starving. The pairing of body and behaviour effects shows how deeply one sensor shapes survival. Fly work often maps onto human metabolism.
plos-pone-0330399:
Elliot Sloyan and co-authors reviewed antenatal classes about labour and post birth pain in 2026. Classes aim to prepare parents, but how much they actually teach about pain, and how women feel about that teaching, had not been mapped.

Following standard review methods, the team searched twelve databases and found seventeen studies that fit. They charted what classes covered, how they were delivered, and what outcomes and experiences were reported. Coverage of pain after birth looked especially patchy. The map gives course designers a clear view of missing topics, such as recovery pain, that parents meet unprepared.
plos-pone-0331699:
Zhenhua Liu and three colleagues turn kelp waste into a useful industrial material in this 2026 study. Kelp farming in East Asia leaves mountains of residue after alginate extraction. That residue is rich in cellulose. The team first extracted kelp cellulose. Dilute acid then broke it down into microcrystalline cellulose, a powder used in food, drugs, and cosmetics.

Careful testing showed the process preserved the cellulose's basic chemistry. Its natural crystal form survived the acid bath. Crystallinity rose slightly, and heat resistance improved. The particles came out as small flakes rather than the rods seen in commercial products. Chain length and yield, about eighty-five percent, closely matched the commercial standard. Seaweed waste, normally a disposal problem, could thus become a saleable ingredient with the right processing.
plos-pone-0335299:
Nanvuma and colleagues, in a 2026 study, evaluate a program in Uganda that trains young health researchers to lead their own clinical studies. Building research skill in lower-income countries is a stated global health goal, and the Infectious Diseases Institute in Kampala runs a structured model to do it. The team checked whether the model works, is practical, and is welcomed.

Eighty trainees answered a survey, and twenty took deeper interviews. Nine in ten would recommend the program. Most said it helped them reach career goals and widened job options. Current trainees reported more scientific benefit than alumni did, a gap the authors flag. Interviewees praised close mentorship, both technical and personal, along with training in softer skills, chances to present work, and networking. The authors conclude the model works, while noting room to raise scientific gains for graduates.
plos-pone-0336199:
Akshay Singh and Stuart J. Hesketh test whether morning caffeine can erase the daily dip in women's muscle performance. Strength and endurance naturally peak later in the day. Their 2026 study brings thirteen healthy women through three sessions. One session runs in the evening with a dummy pill. A second runs in the morning with the dummy. A third runs in the morning with caffeine. Each session tests leg strength and endurance to failure.

Morning placebo performance lagged the evening clearly. Morning caffeine not only closed the gap but pushed peak force above evening levels, and endurance jumped by more than two-fifths over morning placebo. Effort also felt easier. Muscle signals suggested caffeine worked through the brain's drive rather than the muscle itself. Early training need not mean weaker training.
plos-pone-0341299:
Kate Bergh and colleagues explored how drinking and HIV risk intertwine. Their focus was adolescent girls and young women in South African communities with heavy HIV burdens. The data come from a large review of a joint prevention program across eight provinces. It paired a household survey of fifteen-to-twenty-four-year-olds, in program and comparison districts, with blood spot tests for HIV.

Questionnaires captured drinking and sexual behavior. Interviews added lived texture, showing how drinking can become an urgent, consuming pursuit. Viewed through syndemic theory, alcohol, violence, and HIV reinforce each other rather than acting alone. Programs that treat drinking as a side issue miss one of the gears driving infection in exactly the group carrying the heaviest burden.
plos-pone-0343199:
Bill Jonathan Serrano Orellana maps how work-related well-being differs across Ecuador's twenty-four provinces in the years after the pandemic. National averages hide deep local gaps in job quality, pay, and poverty. Using official survey data, the study combines eleven indicators, from youth joblessness to underemployment, into yearly maps that show provinces and indicators together, then checks whether the yearly pictures agree.

One stable gradient dominated, driven by job quality and income rather than headline unemployment. Three groups persisted: an Amazonian core stacking poverty and weak jobs, a stronger Andean-coastal group, and a fragile middle. No province group caught up with another across the period. Serrano Orellana argues labor policy must be territorial, since the gaps barely move year to year.
plos-pone-0343399:
Diabetic foot ulcers can end in amputation, and Lianawati and colleagues followed patients at a hospital in Central Java, Indonesia, to time that path. Their 2026 PLOS One study tracked about eight hundred eighty patients with type 2 diabetes across five years.

Amputations occurred at a rate of roughly fourteen per hundred patient-years. The rate soared in patients whose ulcers had turned gangrenous, reaching many times the average. Statistical models weighed which traits hastened amputation, using adjusted risk ratios. Data on timing like this are scarce for Indonesia, and the authors offer them to guide earlier wound care that might save limbs.
plos-pone-0345899:
Habtamu Guaguahu Feleke and three co-authors map vaccine gaps in Ethiopia. They study the country's two newer childhood vaccines. One fights pneumococcus, and one fights rotavirus. They used a 2019 national survey of more than two thousand children aged one to just under three. They charted where missed doses cluster. They also charted which local factors track with the gaps, using spatial tools that let effects vary by place.

Nearly half the children had not finished the newer vaccines. The gaps clustered in the south and east, including the Somali region. Missing vaccine cards were tied to the gaps. Home delivery, no postnatal care, and large households were tied too. Very young first-time mothers were another factor. The authors urge targeted catch-up work in those clusters. They also urge stronger card and tracking systems across the country.
plos-pone-0347499:
Xie Xiaoting and colleagues randomised one hundred forty orthodontic patients, aged twelve to thirty-five, between an artificial-intelligence-assisted digital workflow and conventional fixed braces. Both groups treated the same class of bite problem, and trained examiners, kept blind to group, scored tooth alignment with a standard rating index before, during, and after treatment.

The digital group's final scores were clearly better, and more than eight in ten achieved at least a seventy percent improvement, against half of the conventional group. Younger patients and those starting with worse scores improved most. No serious harms occurred. The authors caution that results cover short-term tooth position only, and longer, wider trials are needed.
plos-pone-0347599:
Xiaowei Zha and Shen Cao searched spinal cord injury data for genes that steer macrophages, immune cells whose behaviour shapes whether the injured cord heals or deteriorates. Comparing gene activity in injured and healthy samples and filtering with three machine learning methods, the 2026 study settled on three hub genes, all more active after injury.

The genes tied into immune pathways and were far more active in the repair-oriented type of macrophage than in the inflammatory type. A drug database search flagged thirty-seven existing compounds, including familiar medicines, that might nudge these genes. Lab checks in injury models confirmed the genes switch on. The authors offer them as targets for future therapies.
plos-pone-0347699:
Yaping Chen, Lu Zhang, and Akot Deng mined Chinese social media, restaurant reviews, and location check-ins to ask what kinds of leisure spaces make city residents satisfied with life. Deep learning models scored service quality across catering, entertainment, personal care, retail, and sports venues, then weighed each type's influence on reported life satisfaction.

Quality beat quantity decisively: excellent service lifted satisfaction, while simply having more venues did almost nothing. Restaurants and other food spaces mattered most, then entertainment, with sports trailing. Effects varied by district and function. The authors advise city planners to invest in the quality of everyday leisure spaces rather than their raw number.
plos-pone-0347799:
Abdirahman Ibrahim Said and colleagues measure low blood calcium among diabetic patients at a regional hospital in Jinja, Uganda, and hunt for what predicts it. Calcium problems are an overlooked companion of diabetes and can worsen outcomes, especially where testing is scarce. Several hundred adult outpatients were enrolled in order, answered structured questions, and gave blood, with low calcium set at a standard cutoff.

Nearly three in ten patients fell below the cutoff, a high share. Many traits looked linked one by one, from body size to glucose control and medication habits, but in the full model only occupation survived: civil servants showed markedly higher prevalence than farmers. Said and colleagues say the surprising job link deserves study of diet, sunlight, and work patterns in this population.
plos-pone-0347999:
Li Quan and co-workers measure how much sky a driver can see and test whether that simple number predicts driving strain. Busy streets flood drivers with information, but complexity has been hard to score. Their 2026 study builds three-dimensional street models, computes a sky view index for each scene, and puts twenty-four drivers through virtual roads while tracking eyes and steering.

The index lined up strongly with measured driving load. In a middle band of the index, safety scores improved markedly, suggesting neither a sealed tunnel of buildings nor a bare open road is ideal. City designers could use the measure to shape streets that keep drivers alert without overwhelming them, and car makers could use it in training simulators.
plos-pone-0348199:
Md Fantacher Islam, Jarrod Mosier, and Vignesh Subbian built a formal computer ontology, a structured map of concepts, for non-invasive breathing support in acute care. Masks and high-flow nasal oxygen are used ever more widely to keep patients off ventilators, but terminology varies and guidance is scattered. Their 2026 proof of concept organises machines, settings, patient traits, and outcomes into one queryable framework with built-in rules.

The map holds one hundred forty-five classes and nearly a thousand logical statements, enriched with standard definitions. Test queries on six sample patients returned the expected treatment inferences, including cases where early support avoided a breathing tube. The authors offer it as groundwork for consistent records and future decision support.
plos-pone-0348599:
Xin Han and seven colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One earthquake engineering study on the design response spectra that building codes use to set how strongly structures must resist shaking. These standardized curves differ between countries and, the authors show, deviate appreciably from spectra computed from real earthquake recordings. The team assembled more than twelve hundred strong-motion records and grouped them by earthquake size, distance, and ground type.

From the averaged recorded spectra they derived an improved mathematical shape for the design curve, then built a genetic-algorithm procedure to fit its parameters to any dataset. Tests on four independent earthquake records showed the refined curve tracking the frequency-by-frequency character of real shaking better than the conventional code shape. The authors offer the framework as a reference for future code updates.
plos-pone-0348699:
Yanfei Zhu and colleagues built a blood-test model for catching pancreatic cancer earlier, when treatment still has a chance. The disease is usually found late and kills quickly. Tiny RNA molecules circulating in blood carry early signals, but earlier models were rarely checked on independent data. The 2026 team trained a random forest on twenty such markers from public datasets totalling about eight hundred samples.

The model separated cancer from non-cancer with good accuracy in training and held up respectably in outside datasets using different technologies. An explanation method named the markers driving each decision, keeping the system transparent. The authors call it a foundation for prospective testing, not a clinic-ready test.
plos-pone-0348799:
Ahmed Alneami and a large team combined satellite images with soil chemistry to map salty, degrading land in a Saudi Arabian salt flat. One hundred and eighteen soil samples from a grid across the flat were tested for saltiness and related properties. The samples were then matched against what the Sentinel-2 satellite sees from orbit. That built a prediction model that can draw the whole map from imagery alone.

The model held up respectably in validation, explaining about two thirds of the variation in soil salt. Samples confirmed fierce salinity in places, with some readings deep into ranges that kill vegetation. The authors offer satellite mapping as a cheap, repeatable watch over land degradation in dry regions, in line with United Nations goals for protecting farmland from salt and desert spread.
plos-pone-0348899:
Quan He and co-workers search for tiny RNA signals that explain why hepatitis B sometimes passes from mother to baby despite vaccines and antibody shots. Their 2026 study compares blood RNA from babies born to infected mothers in a Guangxi registry, contrasting the few who were infected with those who stayed clear after full preventive care.

Sixty-two small RNAs differed between the groups. Following their predicted target genes led to three genes already tied to the virus, governed by four of the altered RNAs. The groups were very small, so the signals are early clues, not proven markers. Still, they point to molecular levers that better prevention might one day pull.
plos-pone-0349099:
Zhonghua Lv and colleagues tested a probiotic bacterium as a weapon against Helicobacter pylori, the stomach germ behind ulcers and much stomach cancer. In dishes, their strain of Lactobacillus casei slowed the germ's growth, dulled its key enzyme, clumped together with it, and blocked it from sticking to stomach cells. The team then gave the probiotic to infected mice.

Treated mice showed calmer stomach linings, with lower levels of several inflammatory signals and a quieter master inflammation switch. Their stomach microbe communities also shifted toward a healthier balance, with the Helicobacter share shrinking. The authors describe a multi-pronged effect: direct attack, blocked attachment, calmer immunity, and a rebalanced gut community, together making the probiotic a candidate companion to antibiotic therapy.
plos-pone-0349199:
Luqi Gao, Qihao Wang, and Chao Zhu built the first combined genetic map of age-related eye disease, treating several ageing eye conditions as one shared trait rather than separate problems. Using genome-wide data and a modelling method that can invent a combined trait from its parts. They searched for DNA variants that raise risk across the group. Then they asked which tissues and eye layers those variants act through.

Eleven locations in the genome passed the significance bar. Follow-up analyses tied the signals to particular genes and to the retinal and ocular tissues where ageing does its damage. Because eye diseases of ageing share patients and possibly roots, the authors argue a joint genetic landscape can reveal causes that single-disease studies miss. They present their catalogue as a starting point for that research.
plos-pone-0349299:
Taylor Mullin and colleagues tracked teen HPV shots in the United States. Data came from a national vaccine survey. Years ran from 2021 to 2023. Over one hundred and twenty six thousand teens took part. Ages ran from thirteen to seventeen. Provider records set each teen shot status. The vaccine can prevent several cancers.

Completion held steady each year. Rates sat near sixty two to sixty four percent. About fifteen percent started but never finished. About twenty two percent never started. Older teens finished more than younger teens. Girls finished more than boys. Steady rates during pandemic recovery show resilience. Early starts still need a strong push.
plos-pone-0349399:
Jinhua Zhang measured how the writing of sixty-six students at a Chinese application-oriented university grows more complex as their English improves. Compositions were analyzed at three levels: word choice, sentence structure, and whole-text coherence. Writing complexity is a window into second-language development, yet students at practically focused universities are rarely studied this way.

Different complexity measures responded to proficiency at different rates, and both vocabulary and sentence skills developed in a nonlinear pattern, with spurts and plateaus rather than steady lines. Coherence, by contrast, tracked writing quality consistently at every level. The practical advice follows directly: teaching should target the dimension that is actually moving at each stage instead of treating writing skill as a single ladder.
plos-pone-0349499:
David Warne and colleagues developed a statistical method for spotting vaccine hesitancy while a vaccination campaign is still running. Their approach uses the counts health officials already collect: reported cases, deaths, and doses given. It applies Bayesian methods, which state openly how uncertain each estimate is.

By fitting epidemic models to those counts, the method can flag when uptake is being held back by hesitancy rather than by supply or access problems. It also points to which behaviors drive the slowdown. That gives public health teams a chance to adjust messaging or outreach during an outbreak instead of after it.
plos-pone-0349599:
Zahra Dianat Maharlouei, Davood Azadi, and Majid Fekri worked on cleaning farm soil poisoned by both heavy metals and oil-related chemicals near Kerman, Iran. Such soil cuts crop yields and lets toxins into food. The team collected native bacteria from polluted sites, paired them with biochar made from rice husks, and tested the mix on maize in a greenhouse.

The bacteria-loaded biochar cut the share of metals plants could take up by roughly half and removed about seventy percent of the hydrocarbons. Less metal reached the maize shoots, soil carbon rose, and the plants grew about twice as heavy as untreated ones. Because the bacteria came from the same soils, the approach suits dry regions like Kerman and avoids imported fixes.
plos-pone-0349999: Sarhan and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a well-known child behavior survey in a hard setting. The Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire asks about a child's emotional state and conduct. The team tested how well it works among teen girls from Palestinian refugee families living in Jordan and in Palestine itself. A survey is only fair if it means the same thing in the group being asked.
plos-pone-0350099:
Katya A Nogales Crespo and colleagues mapped HIV related policies across fifteen European countries to see which rules help or hinder prevention, testing, treatment, and care for key groups. Hundreds of policies and dozens of studies were screened against fifty seven policy areas drawn from world frameworks. Most countries covered forty or more areas, yet scope varied widely.

Across twenty seven core areas, two hundred and forty eight policies were judged relevant. Coverage was uneven by population: not every key group was named or served in every country. Laws on paper also faced rollout barriers found in the literature. Europe cannot meet its AIDS ending goals, the authors warn, while policy patchwork leaves key groups behind.
plos-pone-0350199:
Jaewon Seol and co-authors modelled the future Korean range of Lindera, a group of relict trees from an ancient warm era, in 2026 work. Such leftovers of past climates are sensitive sentinels for what warming will do to East Asian forests.

Six modelling methods were blended for four species under three climate futures. Temperature swings across seasons and growing season rain mattered most. As warming deepened, good habitat shifted north and uphill, and southern and central Korean habitat shrank badly. Even the widest ranging species lost most of its ground in the harshest future. The maps give conservationists time to plan refuges.
plos-pone-0350299:
Eyerusalem Asfaw and co-authors measured digital health literacy among health workers in eastern Ethiopia in 2026. Clinics are digitising fast, and staff who cannot use the tools well become the bottleneck, a gap little measured in the region.

Four hundred one workers at three public and private hospitals answered a structured questionnaire in mid 2025. About half reached an adequate level. Internet access and digital training and confidence stood among the factors linked with adequacy. The near even split frames a clear workforce task: access and skills, not willingness, are what hospitals must supply.
plos-pone-0350399:
Benjamin Kingsley Harley and co-authors tested a compound from the leaves of Paullinia pinnata against Candida fungi in 2026. These yeasts cause common infections, including in pregnancy, and drug resistant strains narrow treatment choices.

Leaf extract killed or slowed several Candida species, including resistant strains and patient isolates, across a range of doses. A purified triterpenoid compound carried much of the activity. Mixes with standard antifungal drugs and tests against biofilms, the yeasts' protective layers, were also run. Plant compounds that still work on resistant yeasts are valuable leads, though safety in people is a separate, untested question.
plos-pone-0350499:
Xiaohui Liu, Miki Shimohigashi, and Yasuyuki Shimohigashi studied how industrial chemicals related to plastic hardeners act on the estrogen receptor, a protein that switches genes on in response to hormones. Some of these chemicals mimic estrogen, raising health concerns. Their 2026 lab study used human cells carrying either the full receptor or a shortened version missing its front section.

Natural estrogen switched on both receptor forms, and standard blocking drugs shut both down. Two halogen-bearing chemicals, though, behaved oddly: they activated the full receptor yet blocked the shortened one. A third related chemical activated both forms. The results show the receptor's front section decides whether these chemicals act as mimics or blockers, a detail that matters for judging their safety.
plos-pone-0351299:
Takuya Nishino and colleagues studied sleep drug use and falls among older hospital patients in Japan. Records from two hospitals from 2018 to 2024 covered more than sixty thousand patients aged sixty five and older who stayed fall free for the first week. Sustained sleep drug use in days four to seven was classed as none, older sedatives, newer sleep drugs, or both.

About six percent fell in the next month. Every drug class raised fall hazard by roughly forty percent versus no sustained use. Head to head matching found no clear safety gap between older and newer drug classes. Newer marketing does not equal safer walking, the authors warn; all sleep drugs in hospital deserve fall precautions.
plos-pone-0351399:
Cancer and metabolic syndrome, the cluster of belly fat, blood sugar, and blood fat problems, often arrive together. Minsoo Yeo, Mi-Jeong Lee, and Wanhyung Lee asked how the pair relates to depression, using a Korean national health survey of more than fifty-seven thousand adults, in this 2026 PLOS One paper.

People with cancer reported depression more often than others. Metabolic syndrome alone showed no clear link. But cancer patients whose blood fat readings were poor faced notably higher depression odds, suggesting the combination deserves attention. The authors urge clinics treating cancer to watch mood and metabolic health together rather than in separate visits.
plos-pone-0351499:
Quick treatment decides how well stroke patients recover, yet in poorer rural counties the first clinicians on hand are rarely brain specialists. Xia Huang and colleagues surveyed such workers in a county in southwestern China for this 2026 PLOS One study.

First the team adapted a standard stroke knowledge questionnaire into Chinese and checked that it measured steadily. Then about two hundred fifty staff answered it. Roughly seven in ten scored well overall, with the weakest marks on fast, early treatment steps. Nurses scored below doctors, and staff at smaller facilities scored below hospital staff. Working alongside a neurologist seemed to help.
plos-pone-0351699:
Yunkyeong Hwang and colleagues tested a cheap blood score as a forecast of death in kidney disease. The score is the ratio of two white cell types in a routine count. Their patients had chronic kidney disease but were not yet on dialysis. Over twenty-six hundred patients at one Korean center were followed for years. A second measure mattered too: how uneven the red blood cells are.

Across all patients, the ratio forecast nothing once other factors were counted. Split by red cell spread, the picture changed. In patients with even red cells, a high ratio more than doubled the risk of death. In patients with uneven red cells, it said nothing at all. A free number from a standard blood test can carry real signal, but only when read beside its partner measure.
plos-pone-0352099:
Abel Sefasi and co-authors optimized a low-cost way for Malawian farmers to multiply banana planting material, since a shortage of clean suckers caps the country's banana yields. The method grows suckers from cut stems inside simple structures. Trials crossed three structures, from a standard chamber to a mulched open bed, with three bedding materials, measuring growth and the number of suckers harvested from the Williams variety.

The standard chamber grew the tallest plants and by far the most suckers. Sawdust and loam soil were the best bedding for sucker counts, while rice husks grew the longest roots, and chamber plus sawdust topped plant height. No single recipe wins every trait, so growers can tune the mix: chambers and sawdust for numbers, husks when root quality matters for transplant survival.
plos-pone-0352199:
Ji Su Lee and five colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One study using machine learning to separate the weather patterns behind two common itchy skin diseases in South Korea. One is atopic dermatitis, the other allergic contact dermatitis. Both flare with the environment, but possibly in different ways. The team modeled monthly case counts from national insurance claims in six cities over six years against temperature, humidity, rainfall, and air pollution.

The models predicted both diseases accurately, and average temperature was the leading factor for each, but at different thresholds. Above its threshold, atopic dermatitis tracked with fine particle pollution, while contact dermatitis below its threshold was tied to low humidity. The authors say the split pathways can help time public health advice and clinic staffing to the conditions that drive each disease.
plos-pone-0352399:
Maria Jimenez-Serrania and three colleagues go hunting for drug side effects in pharmacy records before official systems notice them. Their 2026 pharmacovigilance study covers two modern diabetes drug families, the gliptins and the gliflozins. Community pharmacists surveyed treated patients with six months of recall. Metformin users served as the control group. Candidate drug-event pairs from the 2021 pharmacy data were then compared with Spain's spontaneous reporting database for later years.

Several early signals surfaced. One gliptin was linked with dry mouth. Another paired with bone fracture and with renal impairment. A gliflozin was tied to unusual fatigue. The statistical method, adapted from a validated Bayesian network, screened each pair for disproportion. Spontaneous reporting is slow and patchy by design. Pharmacists, who hear complaints first, could give regulators a head start. The authors frame these as candidate signals for confirmation, not established harms.
plos-pone-0352499:
Bartlomiej Arendarczyk and six colleagues measure the hidden land cost of Britain's food imports. Their 2026 study tracks farmland used abroad to feed the United Kingdom. Imports supply nearly half of what the country eats. The team reconstructed the import footprint from 2010 to 2020. A food system model then projected it forward under four future scenarios.

About eleven million hectares of farmland worldwide currently serve British food and feed imports. That rivals two-thirds of all farmland inside the United Kingdom itself. By mid-century the footprint stays near ten to twelve million hectares in every scenario. By 2100 it could reach sixteen million under the highest path. Diets, yields, and trade patterns all shift the number. The study reframes British food security as a land question spread across other continents.
plos-pone-0352999:
Lei Miao, Fengwei Hou, and Guanghong Li present this 2026 PLOS One computational study on how chemicals produced by gut bacteria might influence Alzheimer's disease through inflammation. Starting from a library of gut-derived compounds, the team predicted their protein targets, overlapped them with Alzheimer's-related targets, and used network analysis and virtual docking to rank the most plausible connections.

A small set of inflammation genes, several of them classic immune messengers, sat at the network's center, and a few gut compounds fit neatly into those proteins in simulation. The authors are careful to call this hypothesis generation rather than proof: docking scores show shape compatibility, not real biological effect. The value is a prioritized map for laboratory studies of the gut-brain connection in Alzheimer's.
