Amirhossein Jafarian and Rob Wykes build a mathematical model that reads hidden brain chemistry from electrical recordings, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. Their data come from rats bred to have absence seizures, in which slow brain waves build before each burst of seizure activity. The leading theory blames drifting potassium levels around brain cells, which cannot be measured continuously in a living brain.

Their slow-fast model treats the slow waves as a filtered echo of those potassium shifts, and statistical machinery fits the model to recordings and infers the hidden chemical trace. The inferred states stayed consistent across long recordings with seizures the model had never seen. A window into seizure build-up could one day feed warning systems.
plos-pone-0353699:
Hala Mohamed Said, Islam Al Sawi, and Heba Alaa-Eldeen Said evaluate a flipped classroom for adult English learners in Egypt, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. In a flipped model, students meet the material before class and spend class time practising. Nearly three hundred learners in a continuing education programme rated the approach across five dimensions of good teaching, and wrote open comments that were also run through sentiment analysis.

Ratings were strongly positive, with building knowledge scoring highest. Confidence, motivation, engagement, and digital skill predicted how much learners felt they gained, while earlier flipped experience made no difference. The written comments matched the scores: more participation, more confidence, more collaboration. Adult language programmes, the authors suggest, should not fear the flip.
plos-pone-0353799:
Bhat and colleagues compared two drug plans for a hard-to-treat blood infection in a 2026 study. The germ, a pneumonia-causing bacterium, no longer responds to a key family of strong antibiotics, leaving few choices. Records from several hospitals covered adults treated from 2019 through 2023 with either an older drug family or newer alternatives.

Patients on newer alternatives cleared fever more often and left hospital alive more often than those on the older drugs. Kidney harm was also less common in that group, while germ clearing from blood was similar. The older drug family itself predicted higher risk of death. The results favor moving away from the older drugs when a newer option is available.
plos-pone-0354699:
Maike Wang, Gang Zhang, and Duansong Wang published this 2026 robotics control paper for wheeled robots that follow a planned path. Recalculating the ideal path at every instant wastes computing power when the robot is cruising steadily. Their layered design reruns the smart planner only when a trigger condition fires, while a simple fast controller handles the motors continuously.

In simulated lane changes and figure-eight runs, planner calls fell to a small fraction of the always-on version while tracking stayed strong. Repeated randomized trials supported the design's steadiness under messy conditions.
plos-pone-0354799:
Chizu Nishi led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study of Group B Streptococcus carried by pregnant women in Japan. The germ is a leading danger to newborns. From screening swabs at an Osaka hospital between 2021 and 2023, they sequenced just over two hundred isolates to learn their types, danger genes, and drug resistance.

Three family lines made up most isolates, while a famously aggressive line stayed rare. All isolates still responded to penicillin-type drugs and vancomycin, though resistance to other antibiotics varied. Nishi frames the survey as a baseline before any future vaccine arrives.
plos-pone-0354899:
Carlos Rivero-López and colleagues lay out in 2026 a plan to build the first formal reporting guide for medical theses. Thesis work is produced worldwide, yet its shape varies widely by school and country, with no shared reporting standard. The project is based at a major university in Mexico and follows established steps for building such guides.

Work will start with a review of thesis parts, then move through expert voting rounds and a face to face meeting. Students will test a draft checklist for clarity and ease of use. The final guide and a companion explanation will be shared openly once complete.
plos-pone-0354999:
Xiaoqing Li and Xiaoling Ji measure how efficiently China's universities, research institutes, and companies innovate together, in this 2026 study. Collaboration is usually judged as one block. The authors instead split it into two stages, research and development, then transferring results into use. They applied a game-based efficiency model that also credits each input's contribution fairly. That design fixes known weaknesses of simpler efficiency scores.

A clear pattern appeared: the system is strong at research but weak at transfer. The central region performed best overall with balanced stages, while the east led in research yet lagged in transfer, and western and northeastern regions were badly imbalanced. Resources, the authors find, tilt toward transfer while companies' leading role stays underused. They recommend stronger technology markets and region-specific policies to close the transfer gap.
plos-pone-0355199:
Jac Neirin Airdrie and colleagues ran a virtual reality pilot. It asked whether a mother's attachment style shapes how she responds to stepping into a child's shoes. Their 2026 study placed nineteen British mothers inside a child avatar. The avatar faced a virtual mother who was either harsh and critical or warm and supportive. Empathy, parenting attitudes, and mind-reading were measured before and after.

Empathy scores did not budge, contrary to earlier studies. Attachment style did not explain the flat result. Yet attitudes toward effective parenting genuinely improved. Attachment possibly moderated the gain. Mothers' own accounts described real perspective-taking and changed behavior intentions. The authors conclude the simulation has promise. It needs stronger empathy measures and better immersion before bigger trials.
plos-pone-0355399:
Le Chi Kien and coauthors published a 2026 engineering study in PLOS ONE on placing wind turbines and solar units inside local power distribution grids at the lowest total cost. Renewable output swings with the weather, and poorly placed units can worsen power quality through harmonic distortion. The team used a tweaked nature-inspired search method, a modified coyote optimization algorithm, and tested it on two standard model grids of different sizes, modeling wind and sunshine with probability curves.

Against five rival methods, their approach found cheaper twenty-year plans, saving roughly a quarter of total cost in both test grids. Energy losses fell by about two-thirds, voltages moved into the best operating range, and harmonic distortion stayed within the international standard. The authors present the method as a practical planning tool for utilities adding renewables without sacrificing power quality, and the savings held at both grid sizes.
plos-pone-0355499:
Muhammad Suleman led a team of eight authors screening natural compounds against herpes simplex virus, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. The virus hides from the immune system with help from a protein called UL21. Blocking that protein's evasion trick could let immunity clear the virus more effectively.

Suleman's team used computer docking, molecular dynamics, and energy calculations in stages to test natural-product scaffolds against UL21. Their pipeline names compounds worth taking into lab tests. Computer screening cannot prove a drug works, but it narrows a huge field to a short list cheaply. For a virus carried by much of the world's population, even early leads toward new antivirals are worth pursuing.
plos-pone-0355599:
Sasmita Kumari Pradhan and Suryakanth V Gangashetty describe a smart home system that reads daily activities from household sensors, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Homes fitted with connected sensors could support safety checks, health monitoring, and energy savings, but only if software can tell cooking from falling, or rest from wandering. Their framework feeds cleaned sensor readings into a bidirectional memory network that reads sequences forward and backward.

An attention layer then highlights which moments in the stream matter most for each decision. On a standard smart home activity dataset the system classified activities with accuracy near ninety-seven percent, alongside strong scores for spotting the exact span of each activity. The authors still flag noise, privacy, and the jump to new homes as open challenges. Even so, the design suits continuous, quiet monitoring of people living alone.
plos-pone-0356199:
Massinissa Benyahia and coauthors published a 2026 evaluation in PLOS ONE of two rapid tests for bloodstream infections in intensive care patients at a French university hospital. In sepsis, every hour of delay in matching antibiotic to germ costs lives, yet standard identification and sensitivity testing take days. The team compared a molecular panel that names bacteria from positive blood cultures, and a new instrument that sniffs the gases bacteria release to test drug sensitivity, against standard laboratory methods.

The panel identified every isolate correctly, and together the tools cut identification time by most of a day and sensitivity results by over half a day. The rapid instrument averaged under six hours and agreed with standard testing in nearly all drug-bug combinations, though a few serious errors occurred. Both tools, they conclude, belong in routine workflows to speed sepsis care, with standard methods guarding against the rare big mistake.
plos-pone-0356299:
Raisha Binte Islam and Syed Toukir Ahmed Noor study risky patterns of childbearing among married women in Bangladesh using national survey data. Risk here means giving birth very young or after the mid thirties, spacing births too closely, or having many children. The authors examine nearly twenty thousand women and track how these patterns changed across survey rounds and which traits raise or lower the odds.

Well over half of the women showed at least one risky pattern, and a quarter showed several at once. Later marriage, more schooling, media access, and an educated husband all linked to lower risk, while rural homes and lower wealth linked to higher risk. Risk also clustered among poorer women. Islam and Noor say family planning efforts should focus where wealth and schooling are lowest.
plos-pone-0356599:
Edward Ken Essuman and colleagues survey women who cook for households in Ho Municipality, Ghana, about food safety at home. Home kitchens cause much foodborne illness in poorer countries, yet training rarely reaches them. Several hundred women answered interview questions on hygiene knowledge and daily habits, scored against a short knowledge checklist.

Awareness looked strong: most women reported good personal hygiene while cooking and knew that poor hygiene spreads germs. Practice lagged badly behind. Fewer than half washed hands before cooking, only about a fifth regularly washed food items, and many tasted food with bare hands or reused one spoon across pots. Essuman and colleagues argue that campaigns must target habits and kitchen conditions, not just knowledge.
plos-pone-0356799:

The study tested whether a language's prestige shapes how much a translation borrows features from its source text, comparing translations in both directions. Among the corrections, the notice restates how earlier scholars defined translation universals and the laws of interference and growing standardization, and clarifies the wording of the prestige hypothesis itself. Anyone reusing the study's data or quoting its framing should follow this corrected version, which points to the proper open-data record for the underlying corpus.
plos-pone-0356999:

Their 2026 paper describes the electronics, validates them on the bench, and proves the system in living rats, healthy and with chemically irritated, overactive bladders.

Bench tests showed clean, faithful signals, and the live recordings captured eighteen standard bladder measures matching published values. The device sharply registered the disease model's signature changes, including much shorter gaps between contractions. Commercial rigs for this work are pricey and bulky; a validated, affordable alternative could widen who can run careful bladder studies and how easily results get reproduced.
plos-pone-0357099:

Viruses infect everything there, but their ecological role was nearly unmapped. The team sequenced viral communities from several mats and linked viruses to hosts.

Each site held a distinctive viral community, although about two fifths of viral types appeared everywhere, in shifting abundances. Different viruses preyed on different mat members. Viruses, they argue, shape these communities by killing hosts and reprogramming survivors' metabolism, a real force in deep-ocean food webs.
plos-pone-0357499:

Fourteen patients and survivors at a Korean hospital sat for hour-long interviews with an art therapist, talking about their usual colors, attached memories, and whether diagnosis changed their choices.

Every woman had meaningful color memories. Four themes organized their reasons. Color served social life first: managing how others see them and easing interaction. Next came self-image, including colors and shapes that conceal a changed body. Colors also summoned positive feelings directly. And a smaller theme recorded real shifts in preference after diagnosis, toward or away from certain shades as identity shifted. Clothing color, they suggest, is a small but genuine recovery resource, and color-based interventions deserve testing for mood and social confidence in oncology care.

Patrick's study gave English readers a full door into ancient scepticism. That philosophy later shaped Hume and modern thought on the limits of knowledge.
sibylline-oracles-terry-1899:
Milton Spenser Terry translated the complete Sibylline Oracles into English in 1899. The Oracles are prophetic poems composed by Jewish and Christian writers over centuries. Their authors spoke in the voice of pagan prophetesses, the Sibyls.

Doom, moral warning, and messianic hope mix across the collection's books. The poems foretell the rise and fall of kingdoms in hexameter verse. Church Fathers quoted the Oracles as proof of Christian claims. That ancient endorsement kept the texts copied and read for centuries. Terry's translation gave English readers the whole strange collection at once. Prophecy with many authors speaks here in one urgent tone throughout.
spencer-gillen-the-native-tribes-of-cent:
Baldwin Spencer and Francis James Gillen wrote the founding classic of Australian anthropology in The Native Tribes of Central Australia, published in 1899. Spencer, a biologist, and Gillen, a telegraph officer at Alice Springs, worked from the Horn expedition and years of residence. Arunta totemism, the Alcheringa dream times, initiation, and magic fill their record.

Their account shaped how the whole world thought about early religion for a generation. Durkheim and Freud both built on its pages, whatever later fieldwork revised. The book remains the great early source on Arrernte life, written close to the people it describes.
spr-proceedings-vol14-1898-1899:
Parts thirty four and thirty five make volume fourteen, dated 1898 and 1899. As the century ends, the SPR Proceedings keep their mix of trial, case, and dispute. Thought transference work takes new statistical forms under careful hands. The census of hallucinations still frames how apparition cases get weighed.

Trance sittings, including the long Piper record, fill many pages with transcripts. Thompson and other mediums of the period appear in the case files. Skeptical members publish their counter readings in the same binding. Volume fourteen closes the society's Victorian era in fitting style. Its evidence fed the next century's arguments. The record stays open for readers to judge.
still-philosophy-of-osteopathy-1899:
Andrew Taylor Still, a Kansas doctor, set out the ideas behind osteopathy in his Philosophy of Osteopathy in 1899. Still had lost faith in the drugs of his day and built a new way of healing with his hands. He saw the body as a machine whose parts must sit and move rightly.

When structure goes wrong, Still taught, function suffers, and a lesion, a spot of strain or blockage, lies behind much disease. Free the body's own flows, he held, and nature does the healing. As the founding text of osteopathy, the book still anchors how the field tells its own story.
tob-0099:
George Lincoln Burr, a historian of Cornell, surveyed the literature of witchcraft itself: the books through which Europe learned to hunt witches and, eventually, to stop. Demon-hunters' handbooks, skeptics' rebuttals, and trial narratives pass in review. Burr writes for readers who want the whole craze mapped through its printed remains.

From the Malleus Maleficarum's authority to the doubts of Scot and others, the walk covers roughly three hundred years of fear and law. Burr's scholarship helped found the modern academic study of witch trials. For anyone entering the subject, his guide remains a key orientation to Europe's witch craze and its paperwork.
tob-10099:
Thomas Commerford Martin, an electrical engineer, edited a volume gathering Nikola Tesla's talks and articles. Tesla was then explaining the alternating-current system that would come to power the modern world. Martin's collection let readers hear the inventor in his own vivid words rather than through newspaper summaries.

Inside are Tesla's induction motor, his work on high-frequency currents, and early tests with wireless transmission. Lectures and papers show both finished inventions and research still in progress. For anyone curious how a new electrical age argued for itself, Martin's volume preserves Tesla presenting his ideas, experiments, and hopes at the moment they were new.
tob-10499:
Flavius Josephus lived through the Jewish revolt against Rome and then wrote its definitive history, The Wars of the Jews. He had served as a commander in Galilee before being captured and later attached to the Roman side. His account runs through the siege of Jerusalem and the Temple's burning in 70 AD.

The narrative ends with episodes like the last stand at Masada, where defenders chose death over surrender. Josephus writes eyewitness narrative with a general's eye for siege warfare, logistics, and morale. Flawed and self-interested as he may be, his history is the essential source for one of antiquity's great catastrophes, read ever since.
tob-10799:
The second volume of H. P. Blavatsky's Isis Unveiled came out in 1877 and takes up the faiths of the world. She argues that all faiths spring from one old stock of secret wisdom. The churches, she charges, have buried that stock under dogma and priestcraft. The book is huge in scope, fierce in tone, and stuffed with odd lore.

She ranges over the early church, the Gnostics, and the faiths of the East, with quotes piled high. Set beside the first volume, on science, it launched the movement known as Theosophy. Read it as a gauntlet thrown down, not as calm scholarship, and note how much later occult thought starts here.
tob-10899:
Edward J. Ruppelt headed the United States Air Force's Project Blue Book investigation, and his 1956 Report on Unidentified Flying Objects gives an insider's account. Ruppelt coined the term UFO itself, preferring it to flying saucer. His book reviews the best cases, the investigations, and what the files actually showed.

Radar sightings, pilot reports, and famous incidents are weighed without hysteria for hoaxes, balloons, or honest mistakes. Ruppelt stays balanced and unsensational, while admitting some cases resisted explanation on the evidence then available. The result is often called the soberest book on the subject, written by the officer who had run the official inquiry.
tob-4099:
G. R. S. Mead's 1906 English Corpus Hermeticum presents the Greek dialogues of Hermes Trismegistus to modern readers. Mead, a theosophist and careful scholar, translated works like the Poimandres, where Mind reveals God and man to Hermes. His English is lucid where the Greek is dense and strange.

Renaissance magi had treated these dialogues as their bible, older than Moses and full of secret power. Mead brought that whole inheritance into the occult revival of his own day. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry. Mead's version nonetheless fixed the Hermetica in the modern imagination.
tob-4199:
Ignatius of Loyola, founder of the Jesuits, built the Spiritual Exercises out of his own conversion and years of guiding others in prayer. Elder Mullan's translation follows the saint's text closely. The Exercises form a four-week retreat, led by a director, with each week shaped around a stage of the soul's turning.

Retreatants picture Gospel scenes, examine conscience, and learn the discernment of spirits: how to tell consolations and desolations apart and choose well between them. Jesuits and lay seekers have made the retreat for nearly five hundred years. Few manuals of prayer have formed so many lives, or lasted with so little change.
tob-4299:
Mead's Pistis Sophia appears again in this further record of his 1896 translation. The Coptic Gnostic gospel stages the risen Savior teaching his disciples the mysteries of the soul's ascent. Pistis Sophia, a fallen wisdom-power, repents through the rulers' realms in psalms of grief and hope.

Jesus expounds her songs as maps of the spirit's fall and return. The cosmology is elaborate: treasuries of light, archons, and aeons in ranked array. Verified from the 1919 edition, the entry keeps Mead's famous version in circulation. For many modern readers, this strange gospel was Gnosticism's first open door.
tractatus-septem-de-lapide-philosophico-: Tractatus septem de lapide philosophico, 1599. The seven treatises on the philosophers' stone. This book preserves that alchemy. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
tristan-iseult-gottfried-weston-vol1-189:
Gottfried von Strassburg wrote the deepest medieval version of Tristan and Iseult in German verse around 1210. Jessie Weston translated it into English, and this first volume came out in 1899. Gottfried never finished his poem, but what he left stands near the top of medieval literature.

The tale opens with Rivalin, Tristan's father, and his courtship in Cornwall. Then comes the voyage to Ireland and the fateful drink the lovers share by mistake. Gottfried looks inward, studying love as both joy and wound. Weston's first volume carries the story from its roots toward the potion that changes everything.
tristan-iseult-gottfried-weston-vol2-189:
Jessie Weston's second volume of Gottfried von Strassburg's Tristan and Iseult appeared in 1899. It continues the German master's unfinished poem from the point where suspicion closes around the lovers. The translation lets English readers follow the tale to the place where Gottfried's own life cut it short.

Tristan and Iseult pass through tests, exile, and uneasy returns to court. Gottfried probes their hearts with a care few medieval poets match. Then the poem stops, mid-story, and no ending from his hand exists. Later writers finished it in their own ways, but readers still prize Gottfried's part above theirs. The great love story was never completed.
un-ga-res-54-99:
Three years into Guatemala's peace, the General Assembly passed Resolution 54/99 in December 1999 to keep the UN watch in place. The Verification Mission in Guatemala had its term stretched through 1999 by a vote of 1998. The Assembly had the mission's ninth report on human rights before it. It also had the report of the Commission for Historical Clarification, the truth body that had named the crimes of the civil war.

The mission's role in the peace is stressed, and the need for all sides to back it is pressed. Both sides had voiced their wish for the mission to stay in the land. The Secretary-General's counsel on its work is weighed: how to shape it to meet the needs of the peace through the end of the year 2000.
un-ga-res-999:
Two days after its first Suez cease-fire call went unheeded, the UN General Assembly returned to the crisis with Resolution 999, adopted on 4 November 1956. The text notes with regret that not all sides had agreed to obey Resolution 997. That call had put an instant cease-fire first, with a halt to all movement of troops and arms into the area, and a pull-back behind the truce lines.

The Assembly states the 2 November call again, in full force. The Secretary-General is given power to arrange the cease-fire with the sides at once. He must report back on how the call is being kept, within twelve hours of the vote if he can.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
In resolution 54/99, adopted on 8 December 1999, the General Assembly again renews the United Nations Verification Mission in Guatemala, the ceasefire-to-peace operation known as MINUGUA. The text works from the mission's latest verification reports and from the findings of the country's Commission for Historical Clarification on the civil war.

The mandate runs through 2000. Guatemala's government and former insurgents are urged to finish carrying out the peace accords and the truth commission's recommendations. The Assembly frames full implementation as a condition for lasting peace and democracy. The resolution also asks for better international help in investigating the killing of a bishop. The case had tested public faith in the settlement. Each yearly renewal kept the peace process under sustained international scrutiny.

Resolution 999 (ES-I) of 4 November 1956 records the Assembly's frustration that its Suez cease-fire demand had not been obeyed. It reaffirms that demand and again calls on the parties to comply at once. The Secretary-General is authorized to arrange implementation of the cease-fire and the halt to force and arms movements. He must report within twelve hours. With the Truce Supervision Organization's help, he is to obtain the withdrawal of all forces behind the armistice lines. The Assembly decided to meet again as soon as his report arrived.
un-sc-res-1199:
When the Council met on 23 September 1998, it adopted Resolution 1199 on Kosovo. Serb security forces and the Yugoslav army had used heavy force against Kosovo Albanians. More than 230,000 people had fled their homes. Tens of thousands lacked shelter as winter neared.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council demands an instant halt to the fighting. Belgrade must pull back the units used against civilians and let foreign monitors move freely. Refugees must be able to return home with aid groups at their side. Kosovo Albanian leaders are told to reject violence and seek their goals by peaceful means alone.
un-sc-res-1299: The record catalogued as Resolution 1299, dated 2000, preserves one formal decision of the United Nations Security Council. The Charter gives the Council power to bind member states, which is why its resolutions are kept with such care. Here the primary source stands on its own, with the formal phrasing that lawyers and historians rely on. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-1399:
Fighting flared in the Congo's Moliro pocket in March 2002. Rebel troops of RCD-Goma seized the town on Lake Tanganyika. On 19 March 2002 the Security Council condemned the attack. It called the capture a major breach of the Lusaka ceasefire. That ceasefire had held since January 2001. Peace talks between Congolese parties were under way. No side, the Council stressed, could grab land while a peace process ran.

RCD-Goma had to pull out of Moliro at once and without conditions. All parties had to return to the defensive lines set by the Harare plans. RCD-Goma also had to leave Pweto, which it held against the same plans. The demands defended the ceasefire's basic bargain.
un-sc-res-1499:
The plunder of the Congo's natural resources kept a panel of experts at work under a Security Council decision of 13 August 2003. A transitional government had just been formed in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The panel's chairman had briefed the Council on 24 July that the looting continued, above all in the east. The panel had also opened dialogue with the people, firms, and states named in its reports.

The Council asked the Secretary-General to extend the Expert Panel's mandate. It repeated its demand that all states concerned act at once to end the illegal exploitation of Congo's wealth. The panel would pass governments the information required under resolution 1457 and keep updating its findings. It could remove from its lists the names of parties that settled their cases. The text ties the resource trade to the illicit flow of small arms that fed the war.
un-sc-res-1599:
Timor-Leste's support mission gave way to a smaller office on 28 April 2005. The Council praised the peace and stability the Timorese had built and UNMISET's work in its consolidation phase. The prime minister had written in January about the road ahead. The Secretary-General judged that a United Nations presence should stay past 20 May 2005, at a reduced level. Justice, policing, and public administration still needed help.

The Council established the United Nations Office in Timor-Leste, UNOTIL, as a one-year follow-on political mission. It would stay until 20 May 2006. Its mandate centered on building state institutions, training the national police, and backing democratic governance and human rights. Advisers would pass on skills and knowledge to Timorese staff as they worked. A special representative would lead the office. Donors and agencies were urged to keep their support flowing as the country took over its own affairs.
un-sc-res-1699:
Police work meets diplomacy in Resolution 1699, adopted in September 2006. It strengthened cooperation between the United Nations and Interpol, the global police network. The Council wanted Interpol's tools, including its databases on stolen documents, used more fully against listed terrorists.

Inside, sanctions committees are urged to share information with Interpol and to make use of its special notices for listed people. The text is short and practical rather than dramatic. It matters because modern sanctions only work when border officers can identify a name, and this resolution wired the UN's lists into police channels.
un-sc-res-1799:
Congo sanctions were given a short renewal by the Security Council on 15 February 2008. Illegal weapons kept flowing within and into the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Armed groups and militias still held ground in North and South Kivu and in Ituri. The Council said it would review the measures of resolution 1771 (2007) and adjust them as security, army integration, police reform, and disarmament allowed.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extended the arms measures of resolution 1493 (2003), as widened by resolution 1596 (2005), to 31 March 2008. The transport controls of resolution 1596 ran for the same six weeks. So did the money and travel measures aimed at embargo breakers and armed group backers. The Group of Experts' mandate was extended over the same period. The brief rollover kept every tool in place while the Council prepared a fuller reset of the regime.
un-sc-res-1899:
UNDOF's renewal in December 2009 carried a new standard clause. On 16 December 2009 the Security Council extended the Golan force until 30 June 2010. The Secretary-General had reported on the mission in November. Alongside the usual terms, the Council welcomed the force's work on conduct. UNDOF was applying the zero-tolerance policy on sexual exploitation and abuse. Its personnel had to meet the United Nations code of conduct in full.

The parties again had to carry out resolution 338 at once. The Secretary-General owed a report at the term's end. The conduct clause now appeared in most mission renewals. It marked a shift in how the Council wrote mandates after abuse scandals elsewhere.
un-sc-res-199:
Congo's crisis was handed to African diplomacy on 30 December 1964. The Council deplored the recent events in the country and noted the worsening state of affairs. It held that the answer lay in national reconciliation and restored public order. The Organization of African Unity had passed its own Congo resolution on 10 September 1964.

The Council asked all states to keep out of the Congo's domestic affairs. It appealed for a cease-fire on the terms of the African body's September resolution. Mercenaries were to be withdrawn from the Congo as a matter of urgency. The Organization of African Unity was encouraged to press its efforts to bring the government and the factions to reconciliation. All states were asked to help it reach that goal. The African body had to keep the Council fully informed, and the Secretary-General would follow the Congo and report when the time was right.
un-sc-res-399: Western Samoa asked to join the United Nations in 1976. On 1 December 1976 the Security Council examined its application. It recommended to the General Assembly that Western Samoa be admitted to membership. The vote was unanimous, and the text is one sentence. The Pacific island state had been independent since 1962. It took its seat as the world body kept growing.
un-sc-res-799:
Israel sent hundreds of Palestinians to Lebanon in December 1992. The move came on 17 December, from land held since 1967, including Jerusalem. On 18 December 1992 the Council condemned the act in strong terms. It said the act broke the Fourth Geneva Convention. That treaty guards people under foreign rule in war. The Council said it covers all the land Israel held.

Israel had to bring all those sent away back home at once, and keep them safe. The Council voiced firm protest against any such act. It also backed Lebanon's freedom and its borders. Those expelled spent months in a camp in south Lebanon. Their case drew world focus to the rules on forced removal.
un-sc-res-99:
Judge Sergei Alexandrovich Golunsky resigned from the International Court of Justice in 1953 because of ill health, and Resolution 99 deals with the empty seat he left behind. The Security Council adopted the text on 12 August 1953, with no member objecting.

The resolution notes that the vacancy must be filled under the terms of the Court's Statute. Under Article 14 of that Statute, the Council fixes the date of the election. It decided the vote would take place during the eighth session of the General Assembly. The record is brief, but it shows how the Council handles one of its steady duties: keeping the world court at full strength.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Fighting in Kosovo brings a Chapter VII response in Resolution 1199, adopted on 23 September 1998. Serbian security forces and the Yugoslav Army had used excessive, indiscriminate force, killing civilians and driving over 230,000 people from their homes. Refugees were flowing into Albania and elsewhere, and tens of thousands inside Kosovo lacked shelter. A humanitarian catastrophe loomed.

The Council demands an immediate ceasefire and an end to hostilities by all parties. It orders the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to halt security-force action against civilians, pull out units used for repression, and allow continuous international monitoring. It also orders that refugees return safely with aid access. It calls for urgent talks with the Kosovo Albanian leadership on a political settlement with greater autonomy. It backs the new Kosovo Diplomatic Observer Mission and demands full cooperation with the Yugoslavia tribunal's prosecutor. If the measures are not taken, further action will be considered.

Security Council resolution 1299, adopted on 19 May 2000, rapidly reinforces UNAMSIL in Sierra Leone as security on the ground deteriorates. The Council expands the mission's military component to a maximum of 13,000 personnel. That includes the 260 military observers already deployed. It thanks states that sped up troop deployments or offered support. Acting under Chapter VII, it exempts arms supplied for the sole use of states cooperating with UNAMSIL and the Sierra Leone government from the restrictions of resolution 1171 (1998).

A lakeside town's fall broke Congo's truce in March 2002. Rebel troops of RCD-Goma seized Moliro by force. The Lusaka truce had held since January 2001. Peace talks among Congolese were in full flow. Resolution 1399 passed with no dissent on 19 March 2002.

The grab was damned as a grave breach. RCD-Goma had to quit Moliro at once, with no terms set. It had to quit Pweto too. All sides had to fall back to the lines the Harare plan set. Kisangani had to be cleared of arms. Rwanda was told to use its clout on the rebels. No side could grab land while talks ran. UN troops in both towns won the Council's thanks and a plea for safe work.

Resolution 1499, adopted unanimously on 13 August 2003, extends an investigation into the looting of Congo's wealth. An expert panel had documented how natural resources, especially in the east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, were being plundered during the conflict, feeding the trade in small arms. A transitional government had just been installed in Kinshasa.

The Council asked the Secretary-General to extend the panel's mandate until 31 October 2003 so it could finish its remaining work. The panel was also updating its findings and resolving cases with named individuals, companies, and states through dialogue. The resolution kept international attention on the link between resource theft and Congo's war.

Resolution 1599, adopted unanimously on 28 April 2005, creates a small political office to succeed Timor-Leste's big peacekeeping mission. UNMISET was ending on 20 May, but the Secretary-General judged that a reduced UN presence was still needed; Timor-Leste's prime minister had asked for continued support back in January. Young state institutions remained fragile, above all in justice and administration.

The Council created a small UN office for Timor-Leste, known as UNOTIL, for one year. Instead of troops, it would field civilian advisers to help build state institutions, train police, and support democratic governance and human rights. The mission shrank from thousands of peacekeepers to a few dozen specialists, marking Timor-Leste's graduation from UN administration.

Cooperation between the United Nations and Interpol on sanctions is deepened on 8 August 2006. Interpol already helped the Al-Qaida and Taliban sanctions committee, notably through special notices that alert police worldwide to listed people. Scope for the same help across the other sanctions committees was now seen.

The Secretary-General is asked to take the steps needed to increase that cooperation. All sanctions committees are invited to consider closer work with Interpol, each drawing its own conclusions. Sanctions, the Council stresses, are applied through national law, often criminal law, so stronger police cooperation would help states enforce asset freezes, travel bans, and arms embargoes against listed people and groups.

Resolution 1799, adopted on 15 February 2008, is a short bridge for the sanctions regime on the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The Council condemned the continuing illicit flow of weapons into and within Congo. Armed groups and militias in North and South Kivu and in Ituri kept the east insecure, and the Council said it would keep watching how the embargo and related measures worked.

Acting under Chapter VII, it extended the arms measures first imposed in 2003, as amended since, until 31 March 2008. The six-week span was deliberate: members intended to review the whole regime and adjust it to progress in army integration, police reform, and disarming Congolese and foreign armed groups.

The last Golan renewal of the 2000s came in the year's final days. The chief's report of 18 November 2009 had found the zone calm. UNDOF's term was close to its end. Resolution 1899 passed on 16 December 2009.

The force won six months more, to 30 June 2010. The Council rang its old bell once more: act on the 1973 text at once. A long clause on staff conduct stands out in this text. The force must hold the UN's zero-tolerance line on sexual abuse. Troop states must probe and punish such acts by their own men. A report was due at the term's end. Few files show peace work's twin face so plainly: a still line abroad, and strict rules for the watchers.

Congo's chaos at the end of 1964 is addressed in Resolution 199, adopted unanimously on 30 December. The Council noted with concern that Congo's crisis was deepening and deplored the recent violence there. It backed an African-led path out: the Organization of African Unity had resolved in September to pursue reconciliation, including removing the mercenaries fighting in the country.

All states were asked to keep out of Congo's domestic affairs. The Council appealed for a ceasefire on the African organization's terms and said the mercenaries should be withdrawn as a matter of urgency. The OAU was encouraged to keep working for a peaceful settlement and to inform the Council.

Resolution 299, adopted unanimously on 30 September 1971, concerns the application of Oman for United Nations membership. The Security Council reviewed the Gulf sultanate's request and found it ready to forward. Oman, at the southeastern corner of the Arabian Peninsula, had stayed outside the UN long after many neighbors joined.

The Council recommends that the General Assembly admit Oman, and that one sentence is the entire decision. Under the Charter, no state joins without this recommendation first. The resolution is a small formal step, yet it marks the point where Oman moved from the margins of the organization into full membership, with a vote in the General Assembly.

The first trust land to win freedom waited fourteen years for its UN seat. On 1 December 1976, the Council adopted Resolution 399 without dissent. Western Samoa had reached self-rule in 1962. The Polynesian state chose to firm up its house first. Close ties with New Zealand marked those years. A seat in New York was not its first concern.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit Western Samoa. The Assembly acted two weeks later. The country later shortened its name to Samoa, in 1997. It grew into an early Pacific voice in the Assembly. Seas, islands, and climate topped its list of causes from the start.

On 18 December 1992 the UN Security Council voted unanimously to condemn Israel for deporting hundreds of Palestinian civilians across the border into Lebanon one day earlier. The Council said the expulsions broke the Fourth Geneva Convention, the wartime treaty that protects civilians living under occupation.

Beyond condemning the move, the members demanded that Israel bring every deported person back to the occupied territories safely and at once. They also reaffirmed Lebanon's independence and asked the Secretary-General to consider sending an envoy to press the Israeli government and report back. The vote kept the expulsions at the top of the Council's agenda.

A judge of the International Court of Justice resigned because of ill health in 1953. Judge Sergei Alexandrovich Golunsky, named in the text, had submitted his resignation. His seat stood vacant for the rest of his term. Resolution 99 was adopted on 12 August 1953.

Under Article 14 of the Court's Statute, the Security Council fixes the date of the election for such a vacancy. The Council decided that the election would take place during the eighth session of the General Assembly. No single date was set in the text. The decision is a short, routine step in the Court's life. It kept the bench of the World Court on the way back to full strength.
un-un-res-special-report-of-the-secretar:
Crisis forced this special report of the Secretary-General on the United Nations Observer Mission in Sierra Leone, document S/1999/20, at the turn of 1999. Rebel forces were closing on Freetown, the capital, in a drive that would soon flood the city with violence. The small observer mission had to pull back for its own safety.

The report explains the emergency, the evacuation of observers, and what the attack meant for the peace effort. It asks the Council to weigh the mission's future in harsh new conditions. The document is the record of a mission overtaken by the war it watched.
un-un-res-united-nations-emergency-force:
The third report of the Secretary-General on the United Nations Emergency Force, document A/3899, reviews the force through 1957 and 1958. UNEF had cleared its first hurdles and now held set positions between Egypt and Israel. The report comes from the force's second year, when its methods were still being tested.

It describes observation posts, patrol habits, and the handling of minor border incidents. It also addresses supply lines and the force's money troubles. For readers tracing how peacekeeping grew up, this early report shows the experiment in its raw, formative stage.
veblen-theory-leisure-class-1899:
Thorstein Veblen published The Theory of the Leisure Class in 1899. Veblen, a Norwegian-American economist at the University of Chicago, studied the rich as an anthropologist studies a tribe. His dry, ironic book founded institutional economics and gave the language a lasting phrase.

That phrase is conspicuous consumption: spending not for need but to display rank. Veblen traced the leisure class from barbarian chiefs to modern wealth, arguing that honor, not usefulness, drives much spending. Dress, sports, manners, and even learning served as proof of standing in his account. Later scholars disputed his history, but his lens on status spending remains one of the sharpest tools in social thought.
waddell-among-the-himalayas-1899:
Laurence Waddell marched the Himalayas as a soldier and scholar in the 1890s and heard strange tales at altitude. Among the Himalayas, printed in 1899, is his travel book of the high ranges. Waddell served with the British Indian Army and dug in Tibet's lore as he went.

In its pages he sets down legends of hairy wild men who haunt the snows. His notice is among the first in the West to print yeti folk tales. The book mixes march, map, and myth in a soldier's clear prose. It planted the seed of the yeti in Western minds.
ward-naturalism-agnosticism-vol1-1899:
James Ward delivered the Gifford Lectures that became Naturalism and Agnosticism in 1899. Ward taught at Cambridge and held a pluralist view of the world. Volume one opens his case against naturalism, the view that nature alone explains all things. The lectures address scholars and general readers alike.

Ward tests the claims of science when science steps beyond its own field. He asks whether mind, will, and value can shrink to matter in motion. His answer defends a world of many real agents, not one blind machine. The volume sets up the argument volume two completes. It shows British idealism in debate form.
ward-naturalism-agnosticism-vol2-1899:
Volume two of James Ward's Naturalism and Agnosticism completes the Gifford Lectures published in 1899. Ward, the Cambridge pluralist, spends the first volume testing naturalism's claims. Here he carries the same argument to its second half. Agnosticism, the claim that deep truths lie beyond knowledge, also faces his questions.

Ward presses on the limits that both views set for mind and faith. He defends room for spirit, purpose, and a theistic reading of the world. The lectures keep a measured tone even when the stakes run high. Read after volume one, the book gives his full case. It captures a key British debate of the 1890s.
wells-tales-of-space-and-time-1899:
H. G. Wells set his short tales in a book in 1899. Tales of Space and Time holds five of his best short works. The tales range from the end of the world to a shop in London. Wells was then at the height of his first fame.

The Star tells of a rogue world that near hits Earth and remakes its skies. The Crystal Egg gives a shy shop man a live view of Mars. The Man Who Could Work Miracles closes the set with a clerk whose wishes all come true. The tales show Wells's range in brief, bright form.
white-yajurveda-griffith-1899:
Ralph T. H. Griffith translated the texts of the White Yajurveda into English in 1899. The White Yajurveda, or Vajasaneyi Samhita, is one of Hinduism's four Vedas. Its forty chapters hold the sacrificial formulas of Vedic ritual.

Priests chanted these verses while offering at fire altars in ancient India. Mantras accompany the building of altars, royal rites, and daily sacrifices. The collection also preserves hymns and prayers of great antiquity. Priests composed parts of the text more than three thousand years ago. Griffith's translation made the full Samhita readable in English. Austere and rhythmic, the formulas remain foundational to Hindu tradition today.
wilde-importance-of-being-earnest-1899:
Oscar Wilde's The Importance of Being Earnest first saw print in 1899, four years after its triumph. The subtitle calls it a trivial comedy for serious people, and many agree it is perfect. Its first run in London made Wilde the toast of the town in 1895.

Jack Worthing invents a wicked brother, Ernest, to escape to town and woo Gwendolen. His friend Algernon invents an invalid, Bunbury, for the same sport in the country air. False names, a handbag at Victoria Station, and Lady Bracknell's cross-examining tangle the lovers' plans. A lost manuscript and a christening plot sort the pairs out in the end. Wilde's lines sparkle so brightly that the play feels brand new each staging.
yeats-wind-among-reeds-1899:
W. B. Yeats published The Wind Among the Reeds in 1899, a book of poems rooted in Irish myth and legend. Yeats was an Irish poet helping to lead a revival of Irish culture. Lovers, heroes, and fairies from old tales move through these lyrics. Names like Aengus and the Sidhe recur in dreamlike settings.

The poems are musical, wistful, and full of longing for a lost beloved. Yeats wrote notes explaining the legends behind many pieces. The book marks the height of his early Celtic Twilight style. Later his verse grew harder and more public. These poems still charm readers with their mist and music. They show a young poet finding his voice.
